#6232. Ryanair Weighs Fare Hikes, Pay Freeze As Fuel Prices Soar

Irish discount carrier Ryanair is bracing for a difficult 2027 as jet fuel prices rise and European oil hedges expire.

In its most recent earnings report, the airline said it is considering temporarily freezing pay for workers, lowering crew ratios, and ramping up use of artificial intelligence. The company did not specify how long it would look to freeze wages, or how it would adjust staffing.

Ryanair has over 27,000 employees across its group.

Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said ticket prices will rise across Europe as lower-price oil hedges run out.

“The market customers have been insulated for the last 12 months,” O’Leary said. “But those hedges are rolling off. There’s still no resolution in the Middle East. Jet oil today is $170 a barrel. I mean, this is a very significant cost cliff we’re all facing next year. I believe you’re going to see air fares rise next year across Europe by 10 percent, maybe even 20 percent.”

In its earnings report, Ryanair said that while short-haul air fares will increase “materially,” it will not be enough to offset the expected €2 billion increase in fuel costs, necessitating the additional cost-saving measures.

Fuel prices have prompted several major European airlines and airline groups to cut capacity this fall and winter, and to retire some older, less efficient aircraft. Price volatility also pushed Lufthansa to accelerate the shutdown of Lufthansa CityLine, and made the U.K.’s EasyJet amenable to a roughly $7.7 billion takeover by Apollo Global Management.

The price shock has generally been worse in Europe and Asia than in North America, as those regions are more dependent on Gulf oil and lack domestic refining capacity.

#6231. Battleground Dem touts bipartisan record, but can’t name single issue she’d work with Trump on

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan told Fox News’ Bill Melugin she is more concerned about the Trump administration’s "continued grift" than finding common ground with the president.

A Democratic Senate candidate in Minnesota touted her bipartisan record Sunday but could not name a single issue she would work with President Donald Trump on, instead accusing his administration of "continued grift."

The exchange came as Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s Democratic Senate nominee, campaigns against Republican Michele Tafoya in a race Republicans see as a rare opportunity to flip a traditionally blue state. Flanagan’s answer underscored the sharply partisan nature of the Minnesota race, where she has cast Tafoya as a rubber stamp for Trump and pledged to oppose the administration at nearly every turn.

"I just want to be really clear that I’ve got a long track record of working with folks on the other side of the aisle," Flanagan told Fox News' Bill Melugin when asked if there were any policies she could see herself working with Trump on. Flanagan pointed to her work at the Children’s Defense Fund–Minnesota and her time in the Minnesota Legislature, where she served alongside a Republican majority and helped pass bipartisan legislation, as evidence of her ability to work across the aisle.

"I think that, you know, that proves that I have the ability to work with folks," she continued.

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, speaks during a primary election night party on Aug. 11, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minn. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)

"Right now, I’m deeply concerned about the Trump administration, the continued grift, making money hand over fist directly from the Oval Office," she continued in her response to Melugin on whether she would work with Trump on anything.

The Democratic Senate candidate went on to tell Melugin that what she has been "hearing" on the campaign trail is that voters want someone who will be a "check" on Trump, not his ally.

President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at Rock Hill Sports and Event Center on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, in Rock Hill, S.C. (Scott Kinser/AP)

"They’re interested in whether people are going to be a check on this guy, and roll back some of the devastating cuts and impacts on Minnesota," Flanagan concluded in her answer about working with Trump. "That’s the place I’m going to start."

Flanagan is facing Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter who has turned the race into a referendum on the massive fraud scandal that unfolded under the Walz administration. Tafoya has argued that Flanagan, who served as Walz’s No. 2 as lieutenant governor, should share responsibility for the scandal, while also tying her opponent to progressive positions, including Medicare for All and dismantling ICE.

MN SENATE CANDIDATE RIPPED FOR BLAMING WALZ FOR FRAUD DESPITE BEING HIS #2: 'KNOWS SHE'S COOKED'

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, joined by Gov. Tim Walz, speaks during a press conference, June 25, 2022, in St. Paul, Minn. (Aaron Lavinsky/Star Tribune via Getty Images)

Flanagan has repeatedly tied Tafoya to Trump, whose approval ratings are well underwater in Minnesota.

"Michele Tafoya is all in for Donald Trump — and he's all in for her," Flanagan said last month in a social media post.

But Tafoya appears to be putting some daylight between herself and Trump, as she highlights her support for abortion rights.

"I’m a pro-choice Republican not afraid to stand up to my party," Tafoya says in a new campaign commercial. "When Trump is right, I will work with him. When he is wrong, I will stand up for Minnesota."

Michele Tafoya before an NFL football game, when she worked as an NBC Sports reporter, on Nov. 25, 2021, in New Orleans. (AP Photo/Tyler Kaufman, File)

While the ad drew opposition from some Republicans, including Mercedes Schlapp, a senior fellow at the Conservative Political Action Conference, Trump subsequently signaled support for Tafoya at an Ohio rally he headlined.

"You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who’s a very respected person," the president said.

Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

#6229. Delta CEO Calls Heathrow Move ‘Short-Sighted’

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is pushing back against a planned terminal move at London Heathrow, calling the airport’s decision “short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers.”

In comments posted Monday on LinkedIn and published by Delta, Bastian objected to Heathrow’s decision to relocate the airline from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4. The move, planned for 2028, would separate Delta from joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic, which would remain in Terminal 3.

Bastian said the airlines’ shared operation has served millions of passengers for more than a decade, providing connections, premium amenities and access to their combined networks. He argued that splitting the carriers would undermine years of investment and the benefits of operating from the same terminal.

Delta will “pursue all available remedies to correct this decision,” he said, urging Heathrow to reconsider. Bastian did not outline specific legal or regulatory steps.

Virgin Atlantic has also challenged the plan. CEO Corneel Koster said separating the two airlines would complicate journeys, weaken competition and reduce passenger choice. The carrier is considering its options to contest the relocation, Sky News reported.

Heathrow says the changes will help ease congestion and make better use of its terminals. The airport began notifying airlines of the outcome of its terminal occupancy review on Oct. 27.

A Heathrow spokesperson told Sky News that the plan followed consultation with airline customers and would improve the passenger experience, strengthen operational resilience and provide room for growth.

Delta is one of five airlines slated to change terminals. Finnair and Japan Airlines would also move from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4, while LATAM would relocate from Terminal 3 to Terminal 2. China Southern would move from Terminal 4 to Terminal 5.

Delta consolidated its Heathrow operation in Terminal 3 in September 2016 to operate alongside Virgin Atlantic. In announcing that move, Delta cited easier connections and last-minute flight changes, along with access to Virgin Atlantic’s premium facilities for eligible passengers.

#6228. Ouch: Flying Blue Makes Earning XPs Through SAF 50% More Expensive

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has just rolled out a quiet devaluation, and it’s one that many savvy Flying Blue members won’t be happy about. The airline group has increased the cost to contribute toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and in turn, has reduced the ability to earn elite status through this method. And we’re not talking about a minor price increase either…

Personally I consider Air France-KLM Flying Blue elite status to be valuable, not just for the SkyTeam Elite Plus perks, but also for the more Air France- KLM specific benefits, like access to more award availability.

Earning Flying Blue elite status is based on the concept of XPs (“experience points”), and how many of those you rack up. One really innovative thing that Flying Blue has done is that it has been possible to earn XPs through environmental contributions:

As I see it, this is a win-win — this program can genuinely help you earn status, while doing something that’s good for the environment, and also contributing to Air France-KLM’s long term environmental goals.

Well, seemingly overnight, Flying Blue has increased the cost to purchase SAF, and in turn, earn XPs. With these changes, you earn one XP for every €15 contributed toward SAF, compared to the previous amount of €10.

A 50% overnight increase is rough. It gets even worse than that, though. There’s no longer any “rounding” with this, so for short haul economy flights you might find that you’re not offered any XPs if the contribution amount is €14, and you’re offered one XP if the amount is €28.

The past year or so has definitely been rough for the overall value of the Flying Blue program, including for elite members:

This is of course all frustrating, though I guess the other side of the equation is that Flying Blue Platinum status has become more valuable over time, but primarily through punitive measures:

How do we make sense of increasing the cost to contribute to SAF, and in turn, earn XPs? I wonder if Flying Blue management thinks that people will still buy SAF at the same rate as before? I know I certainly won’t, though maybe I’m in the minority (I’ll instead increasingly earn XPs through Flying Blue’s co-branded credit card in the US, since that opportunity was recently improved).

For that matter, I’m curious to what extent the number of people buying SAF matters to Air France-KLM? Does this materially contribute to any environmental initiatives, or is it not a priority?

I still get value from my Flying Blue Platinum status, and don’t have plans to change my strategy. Honestly, that partly comes down to how hard it has become to find award availability in business class on long haul flights through other programs.

But I’m definitely slowly becoming less enthused by the program. Then again, I guess that sums up the reality of miles & points more broadly — this isn’t what it once was, and it’s getting harder and harder to make the case for being loyal. It’s no different than World of Hyatt, where they’re clearly trying to cash in. I guess that is the goal of any for-profit business, eh?

Flying Blue has just devalued the rate at which you earn XPs for SAF contributions. You used to earn one XP for every €10 contributed, while you now earn one XP for every €15 contributed. A 50% increase in cost overnight is huge.

I always thought this was a unique aspect of the Flying Blue program, since it’s a win-win for consumers, the airline group, and the environment. Obviously they’ve decided on a different equation now, and for us members, this isn’t good news.

What do you make of this change to Flying Blue when it comes to earning XPs for SAF?

#6227. 1 Dead, 2 Injured After 2 Helicopters Collide On Mount Everest

Two helicopters have collided while attempting to land in Nepal's Mount Everest region, killing an Indian tourist and injuring two other people, according to initial reports. The accident happened on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, near Pheriche village, below Mount Everest's South Base Camp, during one of Nepal's busiest trekking periods. Two private helicopter companies, Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, operated the aircraft, which reportedly approached the same landing area when the collision occurred.

The incident has raised fresh concerns about helicopter operations in the Himalayas, where aviation plays an important role in transporting tourists, rescuing stranded trekkers, and supporting mountaineering expeditions. Although helicopters provide an essential transportation link in this remote region, operating at extreme altitudes presents considerable challenges for pilots and aircraft. Authorities are investigating the circumstances surrounding the collision.

According to ABC News, the collision occurred at Pheriche village, approximately 13,780 feet (4,200 meters) above sea level. Both helicopters were attempting to land in the area when they collided midair and crashed to the ground. A 47-year-old Indian tourist died, while a passenger from New Zealand and a Nepali pilot sustained injuries. All injured were later airlifted to Kathmandu for medical treatment.

The helicopters involved belonged to Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two private operators serving Nepal's mountainous regions. Fishtail Air confirmed its aircraft was transporting passengers, while an Air Dynasty representative said its helicopter was carrying cargo. The incident occurred during a particularly busy period for trekking tourism, with thousands of visitors traveling through the region after improved weather conditions.

Further details published by The Kathmandu Post identified both aircraft as Airbus AS350 helicopters. The Air Dynasty aircraft, registered as 9N-AOD, departed Lukla Airport on a cargo flight, while Fishtail Air's 9N-AJR took off from Gorakshep carrying two foreign nationals. The collision reportedly happened at approximately 08:12 AM local time, as the helicopters approached the helipad from opposite directions.

Footage verified by the BBC showed the helicopters' rotor blades clipping each other shortly before both aircraft came down. According to The Kathmandu Post, the collision occurred when the helicopters were still approximately 2–3 meters above the ground. The circumstances surrounding the accident remain under investigation, although preliminary reports point to a possible communication failure between the pilots.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal (CAAN) is investigating the collision. Its director general, Mukesh Dangol, suggested that communication difficulties could have contributed to the incident because the location is outside the coverage of Lukla Airport's air traffic control tower. He explained that pilots operating in the area must communicate directly with one another.

“Preliminary reports suggest miscommunication between the pilots, as the area is outside the coverage of Lukla Airport's air traffic control tower and pilots have to communicate with each other”.

The latest accident adds to a history of serious helicopter incidents in the Everest region. In July 2023, a Manang Air Airbus AS350 B3e crashed in the Lamajura area of Solukhumbu district while returning to Kathmandu following a sightseeing flight. All six people aboard the helicopter died, including five Mexican tourists from the same family and the Nepali pilot, according to The Kathmandu Post.

Helicopter operations in the Everest region have also faced growing criticism from local communities concerned about noise pollution, environmental damage, and the rising number of sightseeing flights. In December 2025, local authorities and Sagarmatha National Park issued directives restricting sightseeing helicopter flights over the park, except for rescue operations. The restrictions were scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2026.

Nevertheless, helicopters remain essential to Nepal's mountain tourism industry. With no road access to many settlements and trekking locations, aircraft provide a vital means of transporting supplies, supporting climbers, and evacuating people with altitude sickness or injuries. The latest collision will likely renew discussions about air traffic coordination, landing procedures, and operational safety in one of the world's most challenging environments.

Well, if Belarusian media is to be believed, these sanctions are now being lifted, so the country’s airline can once again buy planes from Boeing…

This was announced by Valentin Rybakov, the Belarusian representative to the United Nations. If true, this means that Belavia can once again purchase planes and parts directly from Boeing.

This all seems to be related to a visit to Belarus by an American delegation in September, where the country’s president, Alexander Lukashenko, met with US Special Envoy John Cole. This meeting included a larger lifting of sanctions. It also comes at a time when we’re seeing the Trump administration increasingly lifting sanctions on Russia in relation to the invasion of Ukraine.

In 2021, the United States imposed sanctions on Belarus, after the country engaged in what was referred to as a state sponsored hijacking. A Ryanair Boeing 737 was flying between Greece and Lithuania, and as the plane approached Belarusian airspace, an air traffic controller claimed there was a bomb onboard, and that the plane needed to divert to Belarus.

As it turned out, an opponent of the Belarusian government was onboard, so the real motive with this was to have him arrested. Obviously this violates all sorts of international laws and aviation treaties, which is why action was taken against the country. Then in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, additional sanctions were imposed against Belarus, given its support for Russia.

Obviously having sanctions imposed on you by both the United States and European Union makes it challenging to buy new aircraft, given the aircraft manufacturing duopoly we have (unless you consider the aircraft manufacturers in China and Russia to be competitors).

So most of Belavia’s aircraft acquisitions in recent times have been smuggled into the country using shady middlemen. For example, in 2025, Belavia acquired Airbus A330s through an imaginary Gambian airline, as one does.

Belavia can reportedly once again buy aircraft and parts from Boeing, after the United States lifted sanctions that were imposed around five years ago, when the country hijacked a Ryanair plane. This easing of sanctions comes as part of a larger reversal by the Trump administration, as it takes less of a stance against Russia and Belarus.

It’ll be interesting to see what comes of this, and if Belarus places some big Boeing aircraft order in the near future…

What do you make of the US lifting sanctions on Belarus on the airline front?

#6223. How a midterm tie gets settled in the case of the Senate

'Fox & Friends Weekend' co-host Griff Jenkins analyzes new Fox News Power Rankings and discusses pathways to Senate control ahead of the midterm elections.

In the World Cup, they play overtime, then rely on penalty kicks to settle ties.

The National Hockey League plays a short overtime, followed by a shootout. NHL games used to end in ties. In the playoffs, the teams keep going – until there’s a winner. In the 2020 playoffs, the Tampa Bay Lightning finally topped the Columbus Blue Jackets 3-2 after a staggering five overtimes. In other words. They played nearly THREE total games. That’s the equivalent of 26 innings in baseball.

Speaking of Major League Baseball, teams play extra innings. And keep playing until one team is ahead and the home team has completed an at-bat in the bottom of the inning. MLB modified its rules a few years ago, introducing a "ghost runner" on second base to start the 10th inning. That’s an effort to end the tie and finish the game sooner.

If only there were a method to settle a tie in the U.S. Senate.

THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND

Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Yes. In the case of a tie roll call vote, the vice president — who doubles as president of the Senate – can vote to break a tie vote. In fact, the VP doesn’t even have to cast a ballot if it’s a tie and the roll call vote is going the way he or she wants. By rule, tie votes go down to defeat in the Senate.

But what if we wake up Wednesday morning (if not Friday or Saturday morning or sometime in early December, depending on how hotly contested things are) to discover that the Senate is tied at 50-50?

There is nothing in the Senate’s 44 standing rules which serves as a tiebreaker. The Founders didn’t provide a system to bust up a tie and determine which side is in the majority or minority. And no, it’s not written down anywhere that the party of the President is automatically thrust into the majority.

Maybe soccer is on to something with penalty kicks. At least there’s a system. There’s nothing concrete to sort out which party controls the Senate if things are deadlocked at 50-50.

There was a tie was a Senate tie in 1881 after resignations and political maneuvering. The Senate was also tied for a period in 1954. Nearly ten percent of all senators died during the two-year Congress which stretched from early 1953 to early 1955.

However, the Senate featured two ties in recent Senate history. Both instances reflect what the Senate did to sort out which party captured the majority. One tie came after the 2000 election. The other in 2020. Both elections took a while to sort things out.

Democratic Senate candidate, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during a campaign event at the Georgia Theater on Sept. 13, 2026 in Athens, Ga. (Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images)

It took until early December, 2000 to determine that Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., defeated then-Sen. Slade Gorton, R-Wash., establishing a 50-50 Senate.

In fact, the tie for the Senate from the 2020 election wasn’t even established until two days into the new Congress on January 6, 2021. Yes. That was the day of the Capitol riot. Sens. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., both won runoffs to set the 50-50 split.

In early December, 2000, the Supreme Court finally settled the Florida election dispute between President George W. Bush and Vice President Al Gore. Republicans had held the Senate. But then Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, R-Miss., and Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, D-S.D., engineered a power-sharing agreement between the parties. This aligned with the election of Vice President Dick Cheney.

Lott would serve as the Majority Leader and the GOP technically had the "majority." But the bipartisan pact granted Daschle some special floor powers. Republicans chaired each committee. However, there was equal representation by both parties on each panel.

The full Senate had to ratify this agreement. And it did just that.

Such a process is subject to two filibusters requiring 60 yeas. One to bring up the proposal for debate. Another to terminate the debate. Then a simple majority to pass it. But none of that was a problem. The Senate greenlighted it with all 100 senators signing on.

Republicans feared Democrats would stall the agenda of President George W. Bush. So they got on board. Democrats agreed because they knew they were kinda, sorta in the majority. Otherwise, they were relegated to an outright minority.

Former Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., was well aware of those same dynamics in 2001. He insisted that Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., propound – word-for-word – the same accord in 2021 which Lott and Daschle hammered out.

Which brings us to a potential tie in 2027. Is there the political will in the Senate – let alone the votes – to agree to such a compact? President Trump is still president. And Vice President JD Vance is still President of the Senate. What would they say about that? Unclear.

Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump and Republican vice presidential nominee Sen. JD Vance joined family members and others at Ground Zero on Sept. 11, 2024, in New York City, to honor those killed in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks at the World Trade Center. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

The Senate isn’t compelled to present a dedicated "majority" or "minority." The concept of a "Majority Leader" is relatively new – only dating back to the early 20th Century. The Senate is a body of "equals." Thus, the Founders didn’t expect one senator to wield operational control of the Senate. You won’t find the words "Majority Leader" anywhere in the Constitution. Just Speaker of the House and President of the Senate.

If there’s a 50-50 Senate and an impasse, could Vance suddenly have more power? Maybe. As President of the Senate, he can’t debate. He can only preside over the body and break ties. Moreover, would Vance even want to assert more authority? It’s unclear what that could be. And what would all of this do to his plans to run for president in 2028?

EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING

In fact, a deadlocked Senate with no power sharing agreement could potentially hamstring Vance. It wasn’t that long ago that the Vice President spent much of his time presiding over daily Senate debates. But not anymore. If there’s no set majority, those responsibilities either fall to Vance, current Senate President Pro Tempore Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, or the possible Democratic Senate President Pro Tempore Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash. The latter two are the most senior senators from their respective parties. The President Pro Tempore is third in line to the presidency, following the Vice President and House Speaker. A power sharing agreement is what helps determine who presides over the Senate. Otherwise, Vance may be moored in the Senate.

So there is precedent for settling a "tie" in the Senate. But it hinges on the political will of senators. And if there are disputes about seating Members – say the Alaska Senate race or another contest becomes a conflagration – one can anticipate a toxic climate on Capitol Hill. Few may be willing to sign on to anything.

The Senate relies a lot on history and precedent to do things. But absent political will, senators may just resort to rock, paper, scissors.

Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

#6222. Frontier Shakes Up Leadership Team

Frontier is reshuffling its leadership team, hiring a new chief operating officer, and announcing the departures of two senior executives.

Michael Delehant will join the carrier as executive vice president and chief operating officer on Nov. 30. He will oversee all airline operations and report to CEO Jimmy Dempsey, Frontier said Monday.

Delehant most recently served as group managing director at Wizz Air, overseeing operational and commercial activities. He previously held senior positions at Vueling, including chief strategy and network officer, and worked in several leadership roles at Southwest.

Dempsey said Delehant’s experience would be “instrumental as we continue growing our airline and executing against our strategic priorities.”

The appointment comes as Trevor Stedke, senior vice president of operations, and Alex Clerc, senior vice president of customers, prepare to leave Frontier on Nov. 13. The airline did not give a reason for their departures in its announcement.

“I want to express my sincere gratitude to Trevor and Alex for their dedication and contributions to Frontier,” Dempsey said.

Frontier also promoted James Fenner to senior vice president and chief revenue officer. His responsibilities include pricing and revenue management, loyalty, and network planning.

Fenner has spent more than a decade at the airline, most recently serving as vice president of revenue and loyalty.

Bobby Schroeter will move into the role of senior vice president and chief marketing officer, overseeing the airline’s brand and customer experience. Both Fenner and Schroeter will report directly to Dempsey.

The changes follow Frontier’s third-quarter results, which showed a $104 million net loss, compared with a $77 million loss a year earlier. Excluding special items, the carrier reported a $40 million profit on record revenue of $1.36 billion.

#6220. Transfer Amex Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 30% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just launched a new 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While Flying Club is in some ways a niche program, this is a deal that has the potential to offer outsized value, and I’m sure it will interest many people. I’d probably speculatively take advantage of this, except for the fact that I moved a bunch of points last year when there was a 40% transfer bonus.

Between November 2 and November 30, 2026, the American Express Membership Rewards program in the United States is offering a 30% bonus on points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,300 Flying Club points for every 1,000 Membership Rewards points transferred. Transfers are generally instant.

For context, Amex seems to offer a transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club once or twice per year. The last promotion we saw was over the summer, and this is the second offer so far in 2026. When we do see these offers, they’re typically in the range of 30-40%, so this is on the low side of that range, but could still represent a great deal.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

In late 2024 we saw Flying Club introduce dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. While the changes are a mixed bag, what’s exciting is that on the low end, redemptions are cheaper than ever before. It’s now possible to fly one-way Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and the UK for under 30,000 points, and that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 30% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Amex points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through November 30, 2026, Amex is offering a 30% bonus when you transfer points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is definitely more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 30% bonus, award travel on Virgin Atlantic will be an even better value. There’s also lots of value to booking on partners, ranging from SkyTeam airlines, to Air New Zealand, to All Nippon Airways.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Amex transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club?

#6218. The Re-Engined Narrowbody Quadjet That Found Its Real Calling As A Freighter

Some of aviation's most successful innovations have been driven by unexpected challenges. Interestingly, one of the industry's most successful jet engine programs owes part of its early commercial success to an aircraft designed in the 1950s. The Douglas DC-8, which made its final flight in November 2025, remained in service far longer than originally anticipated. A decision to replace its aging engines not only extended its operational life but also helped secure the future of an entirely new engine family.

By the late 1970s, the Douglas DC-8 was becoming increasingly difficult to operate under tightening noise regulations, even though many aircraft still had substantial structural life remaining. Rather than retiring these aircraft, an ambitious re-engining program involving Cammacorp, United Airlines, and CFM International gave them a second lease on life. But how exactly did an aging four-engine jetliner become instrumental in launching one of aviation's most successful engine families while securing its own operational future?

To understand what was happening to the DC-8 Super 60 fleet, we first need to go back in time. Developed by the Douglas Aircraft Company in the mid-1950s, the DC-8 was one of the first American long-range commercial jetliners. The project grew out of Douglas's efforts to compete for a US Air Force (USAF) jet-powered aerial refueling tanker contract, which it ultimately lost to the rival Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker. The DC-8 subsequently entered commercial service with Delta Air Lines in September 1959. As demand for air travel grew, Douglas introduced the improved Super 60 series in 1965, comprising three variants. The DC-8-61 featured a fuselage stretched by 36 feet (10.97 meters) and accommodated up to 220 passengers, while the DC-8-62 prioritized range through aerodynamic refinements and a smaller fuselage extension. The DC-8-63 combined the stretched fuselage of the -61 with the performance improvements of the -62. All three variants were powered by four Pratt & Whitney JT3D turbofan engines.

By the 1970s, however, the world was changing. The Boeing 747 entered commercial service in 1970, ushering in a new era of widebody aviation and supporting the growth of international air travel. At the same time, environmental concerns were gaining political attention, with the first Earth Day taking place on April 22, 1970. Increasing aircraft movements brought growing concerns about noise pollution in communities surrounding major airports. Meanwhile, the 1973 oil crisis sent fuel prices soaring, placing additional financial pressure on airlines operating older, less fuel-efficient aircraft.

Against this backdrop, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) introduced aircraft noise certification standards under Annex 16, Volume I, with more stringent Chapter 3 standards adopted in 1977. Although ICAO established international standards, individual countries and airports determined how to implement restrictions on existing aircraft. In March 1977, the US Congress outlined new regulations for compliance with Stage 3 by 1985. Therefore, for the DC-8 Super 60, the problem was its increasingly outdated and noisy engines. Many aircraft still had years of useful life remaining, yet tightening noise requirements threatened their commercial viability. With so much potential life left in these aircraft, was retirement really the only option?

In response to the new ICAO noise standards and subsequent US regulations, a solution emerged that could keep the DC-8 Super 60 fleet in service. Jackson McGowan, who had retired as president of McDonnell Douglas' Douglas Aircraft Division, established a company called Cammacorp in March 1977 to manage a program to equip existing DC-8s with new engines. Acting as a management contractor for the re-engining project, Cammacorp began exploring the feasibility of modifying the aircraft rather than replacing them. Just a few months later, in May 1977, discussions were already underway with DC-8 operators about potential conversions.

The economic logic behind the proposal was relatively straightforward. Although replacing four engines would still be a substantial investment for airlines, it could let them keep their existing aircraft while reducing noise emissions and fuel consumption. More importantly, it offered an alternative to purchasing entirely new aircraft at a time when many DC-8s still had considerable structural life remaining. For operators, the potential savings extended beyond fuel efficiency, as re-engining could also help preserve access to airports facing increasingly stringent noise restrictions.

However, the success of the project depended on finding a suitable replacement engine. Discussions with General Electric began early in the program, with particular attention turning to the CFM56, a new turbofan being developed through its partnership with France's Snecma. The engine promised improvements in both noise performance and fuel efficiency, but its commercial future was still uncertain.

The design of the Douglas DC-8 was a masterpiece of early jet-age engineering, blending functionality with elegance.

On March 29, 1979, United Airlines announced that it would re-engine 29 of its DC-8-61 aircraft with CFM56-2 engines. This marked the first commercial order for the CFM56, which General Electric and France's Snecma spent approximately five years and more than $500 million developing through their joint venture, CFM International. The order provided a crucial commercial breakthrough for the engine program, which would eventually become one of the best-selling jet engine families in aviation history.

The project quickly gained momentum. By May 1979, McGowan announced that Cammacorp had secured 78 orders from seven airlines for the CFM56-powered Super 70 series. To support the conversions, Cammacorp contracted McDonnell Douglas' Long Beach facility for engineering assistance, while modification work was undertaken at several facilities, including McDonnell Douglas' Tulsa plant, Delta Air Lines, Air Canada, and UTA Industries. The growing number of commitments demonstrated that airlines were increasingly willing to invest in extending the operational lives of their existing DC-8 fleets.

Interestingly, Boeing also explored a similar approach for its rival 707. In 1979, the manufacturer flight-tested a modified aircraft known as the 707-700, equipped with CFM56 high-bypass turbofan engines. Although the tests demonstrated the technical feasibility of re-engining the aircraft, Boeing ultimately decided against commercializing the program. The DC-8 was a better candidate because it had greater engine ground clearance, making it more practical to accommodate the larger-diameter CFM56 engines.

Each re-engined DC-8 received four CFM56-2 turbofan engines, each rated at approximately 22,000 pounds (9,979 kg) of thrust. The modifications went beyond simply replacing the original Pratt & Whitney JT3D engines, requiring new mounting structures and associated systems to accommodate the larger, more modern turbofans.

The improvements were substantial. The re-engined DC-8 Super 70 series was approximately 70% quieter than the original Super 60 aircraft, while fuel consumption was reduced by up to 23%. Some estimates put the improvement in fuel efficiency at between 18% and 25%, depending on the aircraft variant and operating conditions. These improvements helped airlines reduce operating costs while meeting increasingly stringent aircraft noise requirements.

Approx. 150–156 feet (45.72–47.55 meters)

The conversion program produced three new variants: the DC-8-71, DC-8-72, and DC-8-73, corresponding to the original -61, -62, and -63 models. By 1986, 110 DC-8s had undergone the transformation. Although the program was initially intended to extend the aircraft's useful life in passenger service, the Super 70s' improved operating characteristics proved particularly valuable in the cargo sector.

The test flight showed that changing the engines could address some of the early performance issues without replacing the airframe.

Although the re-engining program was initially intended to extend the DC-8's operational life, it was in the freight sector that the Super 70 found its greatest success. As passenger airlines transitioned to newer, more efficient aircraft, cargo operators recognized the value of the DC-8's long fuselage, substantial cargo capacity, and durable airframe. The stretched Series 60 variants were particularly attractive, offering considerable cargo volume, while the upgraded CFM56 engines helped keep fuel consumption and noise emissions manageable. For freight operators, acquiring and converting older DC-8s was often considerably cheaper than purchasing brand-new aircraft.

The aircraft's robust construction became another major advantage later in its life. Cargo operations can place considerable demands on aircraft through repeated loading and unloading, high utilization rates, and frequent takeoffs and landings. The DC-8's durable structure made it well suited to these operations, allowing carriers to keep the aircraft in service long after many passenger airlines had retired theirs. This was particularly valuable to UPS, which acquired a substantial fleet of re-engined DC-8 freighters and continued operating them for decades.

The DC-8's cargo career extended beyond commercial freight operations. Humanitarian organization Samaritan's Purse gave the aircraft one of its final chapters when it acquired a DC-8-72CF, registered N782SP, from storage in Roswell, New Mexico, in 2015. The aircraft subsequently completed more than 200 humanitarian missions, transporting millions of pounds of relief supplies to disaster zones and crisis-affected regions worldwide.

As late as 2004, 159 Douglas DC-8s, mostly Super 60s and Super 70s, were still operating worldwide. However, the 2008 global financial crisis and rising fuel prices accelerated the retirement of older, less fuel-efficient aircraft. By 2017, only a handful of DC-8s remained in active service, primarily with organizations such as NASA and humanitarian operators. By the 2020s, the aircraft had become a true aviation rarity, with most surviving examples either retired, dismantled, or preserved in museums.

One of the last remaining examples was operated by Samaritan's Purse. Following a final humanitarian mission to Jamaica, the organization retired the aircraft on November 14, 2025, bringing an end to more than six decades of DC-8 operations. Its longevity showed how a durable airframe and the CFM56 re-engining program extended the aircraft's useful life far beyond what might otherwise have been possible.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Interestingly, the DC-8's retirement did not necessarily mark the end of its closest rival, the Boeing 707. Two civilian-built Boeing 707s, registered N707GF and N707MQ, have been associated with Omega Aerial Refueling Services and converted into aerial refueling tankers. Their continued existence shows how some early-generation jetliners found highly specialized roles long after they disappeared from scheduled passenger service.

We only recommend transferring points or miles if you have a short-term plan to use them. Transfers are irreversible, and you don’t want to be stuck with thousands of points or miles in a program you have little use for.

If you don’t have a specific redemption in mind but still want to earn points or miles, you’re likely better off earning rewards through card welcome bonuses and everyday spending.

We always recommend verifying award availability before transferring your rewards.

When a program with a transferable currency offers a transfer bonus, it’s important to run the numbers to determine whether it is worthwhile.

Generally, you won’t want to transfer your points or miles unless you have a specific redemption in mind. After all, a large part of the value of transferable points and miles comes from their flexibility, which you’ll give up when you convert them to a partner’s currency. However, a transfer bonus can help you get more value from your points and miles if you frequently use a partner program or plan to redeem them soon.

#6216. Are Authorized Users Eligible For Credit Card Bonuses?

Here’s a topic that seems to cause confusion among some people. If you’re an authorized user on someone else’s credit card, are you eligible for the bonus on that card if you apply outright? The answer is actually pretty straightforward, so let me explain…

Credit cards frequently offer huge upfront welcome offers, whereby you can earn a lot of bonus points for spending a certain amount within a limited timeframe. While there are different credit card application rules for each bank, there are generally restrictions whereby an existing cardmember can’t apply for a card they already have, while also receiving the bonus.

How does that work in the context of authorized users? If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s credit card, can you apply for the card as the primary cardmember and earn the bonus? The answer is universally yes — being an authorized user on someone else’s credit card doesn’t preclude you from applying for that card yourself, and earning the bonus.

When welcome bonus rules talk about existing cardmembers, they’re specifically talking about primary cardmembers, and not authorized users.

You don’t even need to cancel your authorized user card to be able to do this. For example, say you’re an authorized user on your spouse’s Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more), or Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more). You could remain an authorized user, and still apply outright and earn the welcome bonus on the card.

For those in relationships, it can sometimes be difficult to decide under which circumstances it makes sense to apply for a card outright, rather than being an authorized user on a spouse’s card (and vice versa). There are pros and cons to each.

The advantage of adding someone as an authorized user is that it minimizes annual fees, since many cards have lower (or no) annual fees for authorized users, compared to the primary cardmembers. Meanwhile the advantages of having both people in a relationship apply for a card outright is that many cards have big welcome bonuses, and on top of that some cards pay for themselves on an ongoing basis.

For more on this topic, see my post on the best credit card strategy for families.

Many credit cards have amazing welcome bonuses, though you’re generally only eligible for them if you don’t already have that card. The good news is that across the board, being an authorized user on someone else’s card still makes you eligible to apply for that card outright and receive the bonus (assuming you’re otherwise eligible for the card).

Therefore this really comes down to deciding for each card whether the economics of applying outright make sense.

Have you ever applied for a credit card on which you’re already an authorized user?

#6215. Buy Choice Privileges Points With 40% Bonus (0.74 Cents Each): Worth It?

Choice Privileges is currently offering a promotion on purchased points, offering up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While this isn’t among the best promotions we’ve seen from the program, it’s still better than no bonus, and there are many situations where you could come out ahead.

Let’s take a look at everything you need to know about this deal, and talk about under what circumstances it makes sense to buy Choice Privileges points. I generally recommend buying points only if you have a short term use in mind, and are sure the math checks out.

Link: Buy Choice Privileges points with a bonus

Between 12AM EDT on November 2 and 11:59PM EDT on November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is offering a sale on purchased points. The accounts I manage show a bonus of up to 40%, which is structured as follows:

Different accounts may very well show different offers, so you’ll want to log into your Choice Privileges account to see what you’re eligible for.

Choice Privileges’ pricing when buying points isn’t linear, and you get a lower cost the more points you purchase, not even factoring in any promotional bonuses or discounts. Before factoring in any bonuses or discounts, the cost to purchase points ranges from 1.28 cents per point (if buying just 1,000 points) to 1.03 cents per point (if buying 180,000 points), and that’s inclusive of taxes and fees.

If you maxed out this promotion, you could purchase a total of 252,000 points (180,000 base points, plus 72,000 bonus points) for $1,854, which is a rate of 0.74 cents per Choice Privileges point.

Note that purchased points will post within 24 hours of completing the transaction, and the points earned don’t count toward Choice Privileges elite status.

Choice Privileges lets you purchase up to 180,000 points per account per calendar year, not factoring in any bonus points.

When Choice offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically either a 30-45% discount or a 35-50% bonus. So this 40% bonus is toward the bottom end of that range. Personally, I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Choice Privileges on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Choice Privileges points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t generally count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. There is one exception — if you use a co-branded Choice Privileges credit card, then these purchases are rewarded in the same way as hotel spending.

Otherwise, I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

While it doesn’t get much attention in the miles & points world, Choice is a huge hotel group, with over 7,000 properties in 40 countries, representing roughly 570,000 hotel rooms. Choice hotel brands include (among others) Ascend, Cambria, Comfort Inn, Sleep Inn, Quality Inn, Clarion, Rodeway Inn, and more.

The catch is that Choice doesn’t have that many aspirational properties. In general there’s the most value outright purchasing points if you have a premium redemption in mind, given that this is the best way to get outsized value compared to the cost of a stay if paying cash.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have a formal award chart, but award pricing usually ranges from 6,000 to 45,000 points per night. In Asia-Pacific, some properties cost up to 75,000 points per night.

There are definitely some properties where you’ll get outsized value acquiring Choice Privileges points at a discount. For example, Choice has an impressive footprint in Northern Europe, where hotels can otherwise be expensive when paying cash, especially in summer.

Let me just give some examples, and let’s just keep the math easy, to show redemptions where you’re getting well over one cent of value per point (which is way higher than the acquisition cost here). Generally the key is to travel during peak periods, since that’s when you’ll get the most outsized value from your points.

For example, if you wanted to travel to Tromso, Norway, in December (to see the Northern Lights), I see two properties charging $560-620 per night, when you could book them for 40,000-45,000 points per night, getting you very nicely outsized value.

If you wanted to travel to Stockholm, Sweden, in July (summer is popular!), I see two properties charging $420-580 per night, when you could book them for 25,000-30,000 points per night, getting you excellent value.

For an example closer to home, say you wanted to go to Dunedin, Florida, in March. I see a property charging $730 per night, when you could book it for 40,000 points per night, also getting you hugely outsized value.

Let me be clear — you won’t always find outsized value in this way. For example, say you need to spend a night near LAX, where you’ll see properties charging $102-149 per night, when a points redemption requires 20,000-30,000 points per night. Paying cash is the much better value there.

The key is to travel places during peak periods, where the cash rate would be significantly higher than usual, while the points rate isn’t as elevated.

Here’s a fun redemption option with Choice Privileges points. While Choice doesn’t manage these properties, Choice Privileges has a partnership with Preferred Hotels & Resorts, which is a group of over 500 luxury independent properties around the globe.

You can redeem Choice Privileges points for stays here, and the hotels cost anywhere from 25,000 to 118,000 points per night. You can find participating hotels and award costs here, and nowadays you can even book these awards online. There are some participating hotels where you can get significant value redeeming this way, though the recent devaluation sure doesn’t help.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have blackout dates, and points can be redeemed for stays up to 50 weeks in advance, as long as a standard room is available.

Choice Privileges points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Virtually any activity that involves earning or redeeming points would be considered qualifying for these purposes.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Choice Privileges points to be worth ~0.6 cents each. That’s a conservative valuation, though if you’re strategic you should be able to get lots more value out of your points than that.

Several transferable points currencies have Choice Privileges as a partner:

As you can see, of those transfer partners, Wells Fargo is going to be the most lucrative, followed by Citi, followed by Amex and Capital One.

Through November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is selling points with up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While I wouldn’t recommend speculatively picking up Choice Privileges points at that cost, with a specific and short term use in mind, there could be value with this offer.

With the Rosewood Beyond promotion, guests can save 30% off the best available rate when booking a Rosewood property through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. To cover the basics:

In order to take advantage of the Rosewood Beyond sale, you need to book through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. Ford’s team is happy to help with this, and can be reached at [email protected]. Other travel advisors are welcome to leave their contact details in the comments as well.

Let me emphasize that the 30% discount is off the best available rate, otherwise known as the flexible rate. So you couldn’t get this discount on an advance purchase rate, third or fourth night free rate, etc. So in some situations the savings here won’t be that significant, while in other cases they are huge.

While there are of course some restrictions and blackout dates, this is about as no strings attached as promotions get.

#6213. Ex-Chicago FBI chief sues DOJ, claims he was ousted over failed anti-ICE prosecutions

‘The Five’ co-hosts discuss who or what is responsible for a reduction in crime in the second Trump administration.

The former chief of the FBI's Chicago Field Office said he was forced out of his job after he said he was wrongly blamed for the failed prosecution of six people who protested against the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in the Windy City, according to a lawsuit he filed on Monday.

Douglas DePodesta sued top Justice Department officials, alleging that federal prosecutors pushed "politically motivated prosecutions" against Chicago demonstrators before gathering evidence, according to the lawsuit. He said his superiors notified him that FBI Director Kash Patel pushed for his ouster before he was forced to resign over the summer.

"I saw the writing on the wall," DePodesta told The Associated Press.

DePodesta accused the top federal prosecutor in Illinois, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros, of launching a "campaign" within the DOJ to blame him after the so-called "Broadview Six" case fell apart earlier this year.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT

Douglas DePodesta sued top Justice Department officials, alleging that federal prosecutors pushed "politically motivated prosecutions" against Chicago demonstrators before gathering evidence. (Anthony Vazquez/Chicago Sun-Times via AP)

Hours after the lawsuit was filed, U.S. District Judge April Perry ordered Boutros and three of his assistant attorneys to testify under oath on Nov. 16 in the failed "Broadview Six" case.

"There is more than an adequate factual basis for the Court to pursue an inquiry as to whether willful false statements were made to the court," Perry wrote in the order.

Federal prosecutors brought charges against roughly 30 protesters during the federal immigration enforcement operation in Chicago, dubbed Operation Midway Blitz, but many of those charges have since been dropped or dismissed.

DePodesta’s lawsuit alleges that Boutros faced pressure from the DOJ throughout the immigration crackdown to slap protesters with felony charges.

"Boutros sent DePodesta emails demanding that DePodesta open FBI investigations into individuals with political views or affiliations in opposition to the Trump administration," DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the complaint.

Boutros often pressured assistant U.S. attorneys to press charges "before investigating the objective evidence," according to the lawsuit, which says he wanted felony charges when assistant U.S. attorneys "favored misdemeanors or no charges at all."

Douglas DePodesta accused U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros of launching a "campaign" within the DOJ to blame him after the so-called "Broadview Six" case fell apart earlier this year. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta)

Last October, Boutros charged six people with conspiring to obstruct a federal officer, a felony, in connection with their actions during a protest at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview.

Grand jury transcripts later turned over to the court showed that grand jurors twice declined to indict the six people as prosecutors sought charges, according to The Associated Press. Boutros dropped all charges against the six people in May as the court moved to investigate possible prosecutorial misconduct.

Boutros "repeatedly complained to his superiors in Washington" that the failure was DePodesta's fault "to deflect attention from his own malfeasance," DePodesta's attorneys wrote in the lawsuit.

DePodesta denied Boutros’ claims to his superiors at the FBI, and they conceded that he was only being forced out of his job due to the "political pressure Boutros created," according to the suit.

The complaint alleges Boutros told DOJ leadership that DePodesta and his sister-in-law, Nancy DePodesta, who is an attorney representing one of the six former defendants, "conspired to destroy" the case.

PRITZKER CALLS FOR CRIMINAL INVESTIGATIONS INTO ICE AGENTS OVER ‘MIDWAY BLITZ’ CONDUCT

Douglas DePodesta said his superiors notified him that FBI Director Kash Patel pushed for his ouster before he was forced to resign over the summer. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"There is no one at the FBI who took their oath of office and their ethical and moral responsibilities more seriously than Doug," Nancy DePodesta said in a statement to The Associated Press, adding that it is "both heartbreaking and shameful that he was forced out of his position based on what appear to be utterly false rumors spread by" Boutros.

In September, one of the prosecutors on the "Broadview Six" case abruptly resigned, writing in a resignation letter that Boutros had "scapegoated and publicly vilified" her. She filed a motion asking the court to treat her as an independent party moving forward.

The former defendants have asked the judge to appoint a special counsel to probe possible misconduct by prosecutors. At an Oct. 1 hearing, Perry ordered further "fact-finding" about communications between Boutros’ office and DOJ leadership.

Boutros has previously denied that politics played a role in charging decisions.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DOJ for comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Delta Air Lines is adding another route from its fastest-growing “focus city.”

Over the weekend, the Atlanta-based carrier filed plans to launch nonstop service from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) outside Bentonville.

Flights will begin in March 2027, with Delta offering service on board a Delta Connection regional jet.

The service will give the Texas capital a nonstop link to northwest Arkansas — not to mention parts of Oklahoma, Missouri and Kansas, which are all a relatively short drive from XNA.

SkyMiles news: Delta announces Medallion qualification requirements for 2027

The airport is also the closest option for travelers heading to the University of Arkansas.

For Delta, it’s the latest in a series of expansions in Austin.

The carrier has grown its flight offerings at AUS at a fast pace over the last couple of years, targeting the airport as one of its top non-hub “focus cities.”

That growth included the airline’s first nonstop service from Austin to Europe, which Delta revealed in August. Those flights to Paris will begin in April.

That’s on top of new routes to major tech hubs like San Jose in California's Silicon Valley and popular leisure destinations like Bozeman, Montana, and Cancun in Mexico.

All told, the airline plans to operate up to 70 daily departures by March, Delta chief commercial officer Joe Esposito told me this summer.

In 2019, it had 28 peak daily departures from AUS.

“The boom is incredible,” Esposito told me in August, noting that a growing number of Delta flyers will also start seeing itineraries with connections in the Lone Star State. That said, Delta has stopped short of saying it will ever make Austin a hub.

“We want to be the business carrier of Austin — we’re quickly moving in on the leading corporate carrier for Austin,” he said. “Then you wind up connecting people.”

It's likely no coincidence, then, that Delta would be interested in service to Bentonville: the region is home to Walmart's corporate headquarters.

As for this latest route, Delta’s service from AUS to Northwest Arkansas will launch on March 7.

It’ll be a late-night departure, with flights taking off just before 9 p.m. The return flight from XNA to AUS will launch the next morning, on March 8.

The service will be on board an Embraer 175 regional jet operated by regional partner SkyWest.

“This new direct route is another example of Delta’s continued investment in Austin and our commitment to making it easier for Austinites to get where they want to go as we continue growing alongside this important community,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement to TPG Monday.

While Delta has grown its flight offerings in Austin rapidly over the past couple of years, Southwest Airlines remains the market leader at the airport.

Southwest, like Delta, plans to offer its biggest schedule ever from AUS in 2027.

The airport will also be home to one of its inaugural airport lounges.

Delta, for its part, is planning a second — larger — Sky Club at AUS for the coming years.

By the way, Delta's new route to Northwest Arkansas will add to a strong run of air service growth for that region, too.

This year, the airport will see 28% more total flights than it did just two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Beyond its future route to Austin, Delta serves Bentonville from five other airports — all hubs: Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City and New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA).

#6211. New Cathay Pacific “Halo Suites” First Class For Boeing 777-9s

In late 2024, Cathay Pacific unveiled its new Aria Suites business class, which is progressively being introduced on the carrier’s Boeing 777-300ER fleet. While we know Cathay Pacific is introducing a new first class product, it’ll take some time before we see that in service.

In light of everything going on — the introduction of Cathay Pacific’s new business class, the delays to the Boeing 777X, the products being introduced by competitors, etc. — I’d like to cover the latest when it comes to Cathay Pacific’s new first class.

We’ve known for years that Cathay Pacific plans to introduce new first and business class products on its Boeing 777-9s. The airline has 35 of these aircraft on order, and they’re expected to become the carrier’s flagship aircraft.

Note that not all Cathay Pacific 777-9s are expected to get first class. The expectation is that somewhere around 20 of them will feature the cabin, while the remaining will feature business class, premium economy, and economy.

Initially the aircraft was supposed to enter service as of 2020, though due to delays stemming from a variety of reasons, the plane is now slated to be delivered in 2027 at the earliest.

Many airlines were planning on introducing new “flagship” products on their 777-9s, though the seven year delay has obviously not been ideal for that, and has caused many airlines to fall behind with their premium products. I would imagine that Cathay Pacific was planning on debuting its new business class on 777-9s, but now decided to install it on 777-300ERs.

While Cathay Pacific has moved forward with introducing its new business class, the airline only plans to introduce a new first class as of 2027, on Boeing 777-9s. Understandably, one major concern here is when 777-9s will actually enter service for Cathay Pacific.

At this point, the aircraft will enter commercial service in the second half of 2027 at the absolute earliest, and Cathay Pacific isn’t even the launch customer. So it could very well be 2028 before we see the first Cathay Pacific 777-9.

In 2023, Cathay Pacific applied for a trademark for “The Aria Suites,” which is the carrier’s new business class. The airline also applied for a trademark for “The Halo Suites,” and this is specifically intended to cover “luxury and first class air transportation services.”

For what it’s worth, the two patents were filed just a few weeks apart. While we can’t say anything with certainty, I’d be willing to bet with that this will in fact be the name of Cathay Pacific’s new first class product.

We know that Cathay Pacific has been working on developing its new first class product for many years (it was supposed to be ready in 2020, based on the initial Boeing 777-9 delivery timeline). We also know that Cathay Pacific is planning something truly spectacular. However, there hasn’t been any official indication as to what we can expect (though rumor has it that we could get a “tease” in the coming months).

Back in 2019, Cathay Pacific applied for a patent for a new first class product, and… wow! Let me emphasize that I can’t guarantee this will be Cathay Pacific’s new first class, though I think it’s very possible. I’d highly recommend reading the whole application, as it actually contains a couple of different concepts.

Below is the diagram that’s displayed, and if I’m understanding this correctly, the plan is that figures five through eight reflect what Cathay Pacific is hoping to offer.

This appears to be based on Paperclip Design’s Peacock Suites concept. The below pictures should give you a sense of just how spectacular this product might be (though I’d expect Cathay Pacific to have a customized version of this, so don’t expect it to be exactly like this).

This product looks absolutely wild, and I’m in disbelief that we could see anything like this introduced. It almost looks more like The Etihad Residence than a standard first class product. Heck, it almost looks more like what you’d expect on a private jet.

A couple of years back, former Cathay Pacific Chairman Patrick Healy has called the new product “mindblowing,” and “a really, really special product and very impressive.”

This would likely blow away the best first class products in the world, like Air France’s 777 first class, Emirates’ 777 first class, and Japan Airlines’ A350 first class. In terms of other first class products on the horizon, we know that Singapore Airlines will be unveiling a new first class shortly, and Qatar Airways is working on a new first class, but it’s not a sure bet yet.

Due to ongoing delivery delays with the Boeing 777-9, the carrier’s plan to transition its fleet is proving to be anything but straightforward.

Cathay Pacific is currently retrofitting its 777-300ER fleet with the new Aria Suites business class. As the airline retrofits its 777-300ERs, it’s also removing first class from those planes (assuming they have them). We’re seeing a combination of three-cabin aircraft reconfigured (with business class, premium economy, and economy), along with some four-cabin aircraft (with first class).

At this point, Cathay Pacific has just six planes remaining with first class. In the past, the airline has acknowledged that it may hold off on reconfiguring some jets, so that it can maintain even a small fleet with first class seats, for markets where it’s really needed. However, with the extent of the delays, one wonders if Cathay Pacific really wants to put the fleet retrofit project on hold, just to preserve a few dozen first class seats.

Cathay Pacific’s first class is an excellent, spacious product. While this isn’t the world’s most private first class, it is one of my favorites. On top of that, the soft product is very good.

Cathay Pacific plans to introduce a new first class product, though only on the 777-9, and not on the 777-300ER. You can expect this product to be introduced as of late 2027 at the earliest, assuming the Boeing 777X actually gets certified (that’s a big “if”).

Based on some filings, it would appear that Cathay Pacific will name its new first class “The Halo Suites,” and some diagrams suggest that this will be an unbelievably good product. I can’t wait to learn more. Rumor has it that we could get our first official tease of this product in the coming months, though who knows, that may be delayed yet again.

What do you make of what we know about Cathay Pacific’s new first class?

#6210. Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card Amex Offers Deal: Save $200 On $900+ Flight

The Amex Offers program frequently offers promotions that can save you money on flights, hotel stays, etc. There’s a new Amex Offers deal that seems to be specific to one co-branded Marriott card, and it’s incredibly lucrative.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more) seems to have a new targeted Amex Offers deal whereby you can earn $200 back when you spend $900+ on airfare.

This is really straightforward — targeted members just need to register for the Amex Offers deal, and then spend $900+ across one or more transactions by February 28, 2027.

You can reach that spending threshold through one or more qualifying purchases, and the flights need to be booked directly with airlines (so not through a third party). There are no restrictions as to which airline you can book through, so you can use this both for US and foreign carriers, which is awesome.

Officially Amex Offers deals are all targeted, though this one at least seems to be pretty widely targeted. It seems that it’s specific to this card, and that most people with the card are eligible for the offer.

The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card has a steep annual fee. Personally, it’s a card that I have, and one that I find to represent a good value, thanks to the variety of perks it offers. However, an easy $200 in savings beyond the expected value sure helps even more with making the math work!

The card ordinarily earns 3x Bonvoy points per dollar spent on airfare, and I value those points at 0.7 cents each, for a 2.1% return. So if you spent exactly $900 on a ticket, you’d get a $200 statement credit plus 2,700 Bonvoy points, which I value at an extra $19 return, for a total return of around 24%. That’s excellent.

Even if you don’t have an immediate ticket you want to book, most major US airlines let you bank credit if you buy a ticket and then decide that you no longer want to travel. So you could typically buy a $900 (non-basic) ticket, and essentially pick up that much credit with an airline for around $700. That’s a great value, assuming you can use the credit before it expires.

Amex Offers has a new deal that can save you $200+ on the cost of an airfare purchase of $900+. This seems to be specific to the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card, and it’s widely targeted. This is an easy opportunity to save well over 20% on the cost of an airline ticket with few strings attached, so it’s worth taking advantage of, if eligible.

Are you eligible for this Amex Offers deal, and do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6209. Breeze Airways Launches Nonstop Flights To 6 New Destinations: See Map Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Breeze Airways continues to develop its niche network of point-to-point flights between secondary airports or unserved markets. The airline will add services to six new destinations in the coming months, with the airline replacing Spirit on a number of routes, while also adding new international destinations in Jamaica and the Dominican Republic.

Utah-based Breeze Airways is another airline developed by aviation entrepreneur David Neeleman, who also supported the establishment of Azul Linhas Aereas, JetBlue, and WestJet. Breeze operates a fleet of 66 Airbus A220-300 aircraft.

As US ultra-low-cost carrier Spirit Airlines collapsed earlier this year, a number of popular leisure routes were left unserved. While some airlines, like JetBlue, were able to establish an extensive network in Fort Lauderdale after Spirit's exit, other carriers have been slowly picking up the pieces left behind by the Florida-based budget airline.

A major gap was left at Myrtle Beach International Airport (MYR). Breeze has been one airline stepping up here, and is now one of the largest carriers at the airport by destinations served. This coming February, Breeze will reconnect the South Carolina tourist hotspot of Myrtle Beach and Latrobe (LBE) and Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) with regular nonstop flights.

Adding to the airline's network will be a nonstop flight from Latrobe to Orlando International Airport (MCO). The airline's reintroduction of flights to Latrobe reestablishes commercial air service at the Pennsylvania airport that otherwise was left abandoned by Spirit.

Montego Bay (MBJ) and Santo Domingo (SDQ) will become the airline's latest international destinations when the airline adds services to these popular vacation hotspots. Breeze will add the nonstop flight from Tampa to Montego Bay in December, followed by Santo Domingo the following June.

These routes from Tampa join the airline's growing international network from the airport, which will see Cancun International Airport (CUN) also join the list this December 18 (not counted in this analysis). A full breakdown of Breeze's international services from Tampa can be seen in the table below.

From December 18 - Previously announced and not counted in this analysis

A notable mention is Breeze's upcoming new service that will connect Tampa to St. Thomas (STT) in the US Virgin Islands. This is not classed as an international flight. Travelers between these two cities can travel without a passport. Breeze will add the new flights to St. Thomas on December 16.

Four cities will join Breeze's network, including another international destination. Find out more here!

Buffalo Niagara International Airport (BUF) is set to gain three new Breeze Airways routes next June/July, as the airline connects the upstate New York city to Charleston (CHS), Myrtle Beach and Raleigh–Durham International Airport (RDU). All services will begin in time for the peak of summer.

Of these new services from Buffalo, just one will face direct competition. Denver-based Frontier Airlines maintains a seasonal service from Buffalo to Raleigh.
