#6208. Condor Plans To Open First-Ever Lounge At Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3

Germany’s second largest airline, Condor, plans to open its own lounge for the first time ever. However, some more patience will be required, and details are also still quite limited.

Earlier this year, we saw Frankfurt Airport (FRA) open its new Terminal 3, which is the airport’s first new terminal in decades. We’ve already seen all airlines that previously occupied Terminal 2 move to Terminal 3.

The long term plan is that Terminal 1 will be exclusively for Lufthansa and its Star Alliance partners, while Terminal 3 will be for all other airlines. Meanwhile Terminal 2 may eventually be rebuilt, as Lufthansa hopes to take it over as well, but that’s a very long term vision.

As of now, the only airline that hasn’t yet completed the move to Terminal 3 is Condor, which is Germany’s second largest airline. The carrier still operates out of Terminal 1, and uses Lufthansa lounges for its customers, despite Lufthansa’s disdain for the carrier.

The expectation is that Condor will make the move to Frankfurt Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027. As part of that, the airline also plans to open two lounges in the terminal, as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. The expectation is that one will be a Schengen lounge, while the other will be a non-Schengen lounge.

The catch is that the lounges will only open later in 2027, due to the pace of construction. While the company’s CEO confirmed these plans in a meeting with employees, publicly the airline has only confirmed that “we are currently in discussions with our partners at Terminal 3 of Frankfurt Airport to explore the possibilities for Condor’s own lounge offering.”

No details are yet known about what kind of amenities the lounges will offer… I’m definitely curious to see what they come up with, as it’s always interesting when an airline opens a lounge for the first time!

Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 is getting quite a nice selection of lounges. As things currently stand:

On top of that, we know that Qatar Airways is opening two lounges in the non-Schengen area of the terminal, which will be for passengers traveling on oneworld airlines.

Condor is expected to move to Frankfurt Airport Terminal 3 in the spring of 2027, as it’s the last (and largest) airline to make the move to the terminal. We now officially know that Condor is planning on opening two lounges in the terminal, though they’ll likely only open in late 2027.

It’s exciting to see the airline open lounges for the first time, and only time will tell how this plays out…

What do you make of Condor opening lounges for the first time?

#6207. Park Hyatt Phu Quoc, Vietnam, Opening Soon, And I’m Intrigued!

Back in 2019, plans were announced for an exciting new Park Hyatt resort in Vietnam. The property has been massively behind schedule on its planned 2022 opening. Several months ago, the hotel started accepting reservations for stays as of March 2027. There’s now a positive update, as the timeline has been moved forward to December 2026, so it’s just weeks away.

The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 8, 2026. The delays on this property have been endless, so it’s nice to see the timeline moved forward for once. Here’s to hoping that there are no last minute delays.

For those not familiar with Phu Quoc, it’s Vietnam’s largest island, and half of the island is in a national park and UNESCO site. The Park Hyatt Phu Quoc is expected to feature a total of 168 keys, including 114 rooms and suites, and 54 private pool villas. This is Park Hyatt’s first resort in Vietnam, and second property in the country, after the Park Hyatt Saigon.

The resort is located on the southwestern tip of Phu Quoc Island, and is developed on 160 acres of land, bordered by a mile-long white sand beach on one side, and lush hills on the other side. The Park Hyatt is a 30-minute drive from Phu Quoc International Airport (PQC).

Details about the property are fairly limited, though here are some things we do know:

Below are some renderings of the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc. Given that we’ve had the same renderings for years and the property has been delayed year after year, I can’t help but wonder if the actual property looks anything like the renderings.

With the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc bookable, what are rates like? If you’re looking to redeem World of Hyatt points, this is a Category 7 property, meaning that a free night redemption will cost anywhere from 25,000 to 55,000 points per night, assuming a standard room is available. I value World of Hyatt points at around 1.4 cents each, so that puts the “cost” of a redemption at $350-770 per night.

When it comes to cash rates, they seem to start at just over $700 per night, and that’s before the 13.4% in taxes and service charges, so we’re talking about entry level rates of over $800 per night all-in.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

Depending on the award pricing for the nights you’re looking at, redeeming points here could potentially be a very good value.

While I’ve visited major cities in Vietnam several times before, I’ve never gone there for a beach vacation, so I’m intrigued by this property, especially given the value of World of Hyatt points, plus of World of Hyatt Globalist status.

Based on what I’ve heard, currently the top properties on the island are the JW Marriott Phu Quoc, the InterContinental Phu Quoc, and the Regent Phu Quoc. Many people have told me that these properties are among the best of their respective portfolios.

I’m curious, though, for those who have been to Phu Quoc, is it worth a trek from the United States? I’m sure it’s gorgeous and I’ll certainly take Vietnamese food over Caribbean food, but is it otherwise worth traveling that far out of the way?

It’s funny how my preferences in that regard have changed over the years. 15 years ago, I’d almost exclusively take beach vacations in Southeast Asia, given the generally higher standard of everything (service, hotels, etc.), plus the more reasonable prices.

However, as I’ve gotten older, my opinion has changed. For one, the jet lag becomes more challenging the older I get, and can take away from relaxation. Furthermore, flight award options just aren’t as exciting as they were over a decade ago. Like, easily being able to always snag Cathay Pacific first class awards was a great reason to vacation in Asia, as far as I’m concerned. 😉 But that’s no longer so easy.

But I also have another motive here. I’m intrigued by airline startup Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is just taking delivery of some Airbus A330s. So if I can fly an ex-American A330 directly to here, I’d sure find that to be amusing! For that matter, I really love the Capella hotel brand, and I’ve heard the Capella Hanoi is among the best in the portfolio, so I’d really love to visit that, and pair it with a visit here.

A Park Hyatt property is expected to open in Phu Quoc, Vietnam, and it’s now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. This property has been under development for eons, and it’s over four years behind schedule on opening. With the opening being just weeks away, here’s to hoping that the timeline finally actually sticks.

Do you plan on checking out the Park Hyatt Phu Quoc?

Agoda is the usual spot in this part of the world to scroll glossy villa photos. FWIW the JW, the InterContinental and the Park Hyatt itself can show diff prices depending on the country you search from, since inventory and rates vary by market. A free tool like Arbitrica runs the same hotel through 195 countries or something like that and finds the lowest price in the world for it, handy at $800 all-in. Then it’s points vs cash. At 25-55k a night the Cat 7 award probably wins on peak dates

Vietnam is really one of those up and coming countries. They should have the recipe for success, great food and vibrant culture. Honestly, way more interesting to me than the overcrowded tourist spots in Thailand. Every time I return to PH Saigon, it impresses me how much more infrastructure and stuff there is around it. Same for Hanoi. I look forward to visiting this soon.

Phu Quoc has become like Bali, Phuket, Ao Nang/Krabi, Koh Samui, and Nha Trang: once sleepy, stunningly beautiful, and otherworldly lush, but now completely overdeveloped, overtouristed; and hiding places for Russians (and others) who don't want to get drafted.

In Feb 2025, we stayed 2n at IC and 5n at Regent. The former is a weak IC property , while the latter is simply phenomenal high end property, top 3 of the best beach resorts I have been to …

I went in 2018 and stayed at the jw and it was very nice but like most might already be saying it's not worth a trip just to go to that one Island. Go to da nang, hanoi, other places. Da nang has hai van pass (anyone remember the top gear Vietnam special) and hoi an, as well as hue close by. Mai son is close enough too and there's a nice fishing spot called lang co. All these examples are within a day trip from Da Nang. I doubt there's much to do on the island like that. I had rented a scooter on the island and rode around it. I did buy some pearls and go to a local market.... But I thought the island was weird. Parts of it were over, developed and looked silly. Other parts were extremely underdeveloped and there's really not much there on the island.

#6206. What Is A Lifestyle Hotel? The “Cool” Hotel Trend That Means Nothing

It goes without saying that the hospitality industry has a lot of trends. At times there might not actually be much substance to these trends, but the idea is that executives in the industry think certain things are “hot,” and they perceive it to reflect consumer demand.

Along those lines, if you look at trends among the major hotel groups, the concept of “lifestyle hotels” has become incredibly popular. There are an endless number of brands like these that have emerged. I think one logical question is what the term actually means. What makes a property a lifestyle hotel, rather than an… umm, not lifestyle hotel?

I know I’m generally pretty verbose and use a fairly limited vocabulary when it comes to describing things, but that’s intentional. In part, my issue is that many of the descriptors used in marketing, particularly in the travel industry, are so beyond meaningless:

My point is, we’re completely desensitized to useless descriptions of every aspect of the travel experience… unless you’re currently enjoying a seasonal fruit plate served by a private Michelin star chef on a plane, in which case I can’t save you. 😉

Anyway, that brings us to lifestyle hotels, one of the hottest trends in the hotel industry. It’s easy to name brands that claim to be lifestyle hotels — we’re talking Hilton’s Canopy and Curio Collection, Hyatt’s Andaz and Thompson, IHG’s Kimpton and voco, Marriott’s W Hotels and Autograph Collection, etc.

I guess the best way to define a lifestyle hotel would be to step back for a moment, and separate out the two words. Generally a lifestyle brand is a company that sells products by associating them with a specific way of living, set of values, or identities, that customers want to adopt.

A lifestyle hotel is generally defined as a property offering the personalization of an independent boutique hotel, with the attributes of a chain hotel (meaning loyalty, distribution power, etc.). Generally (but not always) these properties have a strong food & beverage or social concept as a core pillar, since that’s a large attribute that can make a hotel popular with a certain guest profile.

The issue with the concept of lifestyle hotels is that hotels can choose how they want to market themselves, and I think some hotels take a “fake it till you make it” approach. If you ask me, the concept of a lifestyle hotel should come down to two factors:

We can of course create all kinds of more specific distinctions, but I think it’s unnecessary. I’ve already written in the past about the concept of “boutique” hotels, another term that means so little. As far as I’m concerned, a lifestyle hotel could be small or big, as the big question is how bustling it is relative to its size.

But this also gets at the issue of how hotel groups choose to label their brands. For example, Marriott labels AC Hotels, Aloft, Autograph Collection, Element, Moxy, Tribute Portfolio, and W Hotels, all as lifestyle brands. From my perspective:

I mean, I live pretty close to a Moxy, and I’ve never thought to myself “hey family, maybe we should go to the Moxy for dinner tonight” (as much as my older son would probably love going somewhere and being able to microwave his own dinner).

So to me, these are the hotels that very much fit into the “fake it until you make it” camp. Like, the major hotel groups want to convince investors and customers that these are somehow something they aren’t. I mean, I’ve also had pleasant stays at AC Hotels properties, and that’s described as “a lifestyle brand that celebrates a new modern aesthetic complemented by a European soul and Spanish roots.” I mean… really?

Hotel groups love to grow and market their lifestyle hotel brands, but I feel like they take a lot of liberties with how they define these. On the most basic level, the idea is supposed to be that lifestyle hotels offer a boutique hotel-style experience, while being associated with one of the major brands.

However, I’d say more accurately, it’s about how much of a “destination” a property is, as that also determines the vibe of the place. I’d love if someone could help me understand just how hotel groups can in good conscience categorize some brands as being lifestyle hotels. Like, how does Marriott include AC Hotels, Autograph Collection, EDITION, and Moxy, all under that same umbrella?

How do you define the lifestyle hotel concept?

Never mind that "lifestyle" has an older, sexier meaning. Maybe they have their "meetings" in those coded hotels.

Looking for a lifestyle? Try traveling on Amtrak cross country. The rooms offer something like a survival event combined with a skill search for foraging enough edibles to sustain you for a few days. And I love Amtrak.

Ben, you said it perfectly in the intro - it's all horsechit. What really grinds my gears is when the marketing speak is used to mask outrageous price-gouging, where nothing is fundamentally different, but the room is 2X as it should because, in this case, "lifestyle". BTW, I used to do a little private cheffing on the side, and those guys in TK J ain't it. Although the show looks good.

To me it's like... "make it distinctive from a standard template for our bread-and-butter brands." For entry-level brands like AC, Aloft, Moxy, Tru, it may just be "use a different template and give it different aesthetics to make more appealing and interesting." For more upscale brands like Autograph Collection, Tribute Portfolio, Curio, and maybe Andaz, it is more like taking a collection of distinct or boutique hotels and putting them under a "brand umbrella." For other upscale brands like LXR, Edition, it is back to "use a different template and give it different aesthetics to make more appealing and interesting." Maybe pump up the marketing budget and language used to promote certain features of the hotel or add in an extra feature to make it "lifestyle." Is it a "lifestyle"? Not really. To me it was usually "do you like the different aesthetic that the hotel has to offer to pay the price difference or to stay there?" Sometimes it is worth it for the distinctiveness. Sometimes not.

#6205. Capital One Adds New Airline Partner With 30% Bonus—Book Emirates Business Class Without Fuel Surcharges

All of a sudden Panamanian airline Copa is taking U.S. points transfer programs by storm. Did not have that on my 2026 bingo card! Capital One has added Copa Airlines ConnectMiles as a transfer partner, opening another way to book Emirates business class without fuel surcharges. They’re offering a 30% transfer bonus to launch the partnership, too. But even with that bonus, you’ll get fewer Copa miles than Citi and Rove offer at their regular rates. Beginning November 2, Capital One miles transfer to Copa at 2:1.5. That’s 750 ConnectMiles for every 1,000 Capital One miles. The 30% bonus runs through December 1, 2026, bringing the effective rate to 975 ConnectMiles per 1,000 miles transferred. I like seeing Capital One expand its partner list again. They haven’t done so in a year! I just wish they weren’t quite so tight with the transfer ratio. Citi Added Copa Last Week, Following Rove I covered Rove adding Copa on September 1. Their regular transfer rate is 1:1, and they launched with a 40% bonus through September 30. That meant 1,000 Rove miles became 1,400 Copa miles. Then Citi added ConnectMiles on October 25: Citi Strata Elite, Strata Premier, Prestige and AT&T Access More cardholders receive 1,000 Copa miles per 1,000 ThankYou points. Other eligible ThankYou cards, including the no annual fee Citi Strata, Double Cash and Custom Cash cards, transfer 1,000 points to 700 Copa miles. Here’s how the three programs compare today: Transfer From Copa Miles Per 1,000 Points Rove 1,000 Citi, with an eligible premium card 1,000 Citi, other eligible cards 700 Capital One, regular rate 750 Capital One, with 30% bonus through December 1 975 Capital One’s bonus nearly gets you to 1:1. Transfer 10,000 Capital One miles and receive 9,750 Copa miles during the promotion. Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Copa at 3:1, with the usual 5,000-mile bonus for transferring 60,000 points. That’s 25,000 Copa miles for 60,000 Marriott points. When Rove added Copa, I liked having access to a program that the big U.S. bank currencies didn’t offer. Two months later, Citi and Capital One have followed. Rove’s 40% launch bonus is over, but their ordinary rate still beats Capital One’s promotional rate. The Value In Copa Miles Transfers Copa is a Star Alliance airline based in Panama. Its miles can book United Airlines and other alliance partners, but the redemption I flagged in September was Emirates. Emirates business class from the U.S. to Dubai for 80,000 miles one way, without carrier-imposed surcharges. Taxes and other applicable fees apply. United Airlines premium transcontinental business class for 25,000 miles one way when saver award space is available to Copa. Copa economy awards starting at 15,000 miles one way from its North America 1 region to Panama, Central America, parts of the Caribbean and northern South America. Capital One Now Has 23 Transfer Partners Capital One’s last additions were Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and I Prefer Hotel Rewards on September 23, 2025. It’s been more than a year, so it’s good to see them adding another option. Here’s the complete current list. These are the standard transfer ratios, before temporary bonuses, expressed as Capital One miles to partner miles or points. Transfer Partner Standard Ratio Aeromexico Rewards 1:1 Air Canada Aeroplan 1:1 Air France-KLM Flying Blue 1:1 Avianca LifeMiles 1:1 British Airways Club 1:1 Cathay Pacific Asia Miles 1:1 Copa Airlines ConnectMiles 2:1.5 Emirates Skywards 2:1.5 Etihad Guest 1:1 EVA Air Infinity MileageLands 2:1.5 Finnair Plus 1:1 Japan Airlines Mileage Bank 2:1.5 JetBlue TrueBlue 5:3 Qantas Frequent Flyer 1:1 Qatar Airways Privilege Club 1:1 Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer 1:1 TAP Air Portugal Miles&Go 1:1 Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles 1:1 Virgin Red 1:1 Accor Live Limitless 2:1 Choice Privileges 1:1 I Prefer Hotel Rewards 1:2 Wyndham Rewards 1:1 Capital One manages the economics of its rewards program tightly. They give you 750 Japan Airlines miles per 1,000 Capital One miles, and half as many I Prefer points as Citi offers with its premium cards. Copa is another useful partner, but with a less generous conversion rate. At the regular Copa ratio, earning 2 Capital One miles per dollar on Venture X spending means earning 1.5 Copa miles per dollar. Citi Double Cash earns 2 ThankYou points per dollar on purchases as you buy and pay, and pairing it with an eligible premium ThankYou card gets you 2 Copa miles per dollar. Sometimes, simplicity is king. And that's certainly the case with the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

The Venture Rewards is a card I frequently recommend to beginners who want to earn rewards they can maximize for travel.

Why? Because for a reasonable $95 annual fee, the card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, making it easy to build a rewards balance without keeping track of bonus categories. Plus, it offers valuable travel perks and flexible redemption options, whether you want to keep things simple or explore more advanced strategies.

Whether you're new to earning travel rewards or recently picked up the card yourself, here are six beginner-friendly ways to make the most of the Venture Rewards.

Earning a welcome bonus is one of the easiest ways for beginners to kick-start their points and miles journey.

Currently, new Venture Rewards cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, they'll also receive a $300 credit for Capital One Travel hotel and vacation rentals upon account opening.

According to TPG's October 2026 valuations, Capital One miles are worth 1.85 cents per mile. When including the credit, the total value of this welcome offer comes to $1,688. That makes this offer the most valuable we've seen in over two years.

Those 75,000 Capital One miles can be a great starting point for anyone new to maximizing points and miles.

And as for the $300 Capital One Travel credit, it's a great way to dip your toe into the world of travel portals. You could use it to cover a weekend hotel stay, save on a vacation rental or offset the cost of a more expensive trip.

Just remember that the credit must be used toward eligible hotel or vacation rental bookings through Capital One Travel within your first cardholder year.

Related: Credit cards 101: The beginner’s guide

One of the Venture Rewards' best perks is that it earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase.

With some travel rewards cards, you earn more points when spending in certain everyday categories. But with the Venture Rewards, you'll earn 2 miles per dollar whether you're filling up your tank, furnishing your apartment or stocking your fridge.

The card also earns 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel.

TPG lead writer Katie Genter has held the Venture Rewards for more than a decade and still finds it useful for everyday purchases: "I like the Venture's straightforward earning structure and the fact that it earns versatile yet valuable Capital One miles."

She often uses her Venture Rewards for purchases that would earn just 1 point or mile per dollar with another rewards card.

If you're new to the world of points and miles, the Venture Rewards can be a great place to start, given how simple it is to earn rewards that can then be used for travel, which we'll cover below.

Related: The best credit cards for everyday spending

Another way to maximize your Venture Rewards as a beginner is to book eligible travel through Capital One Travel, the issuer's online travel booking platform.

As mentioned above, Venture Rewards cardholders earn 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through the portal, compared to the standard 2 miles per dollar on other purchases.

For example, booking a $1,000 hotel stay through Capital One Travel would earn you 5,000 miles (compared to 2,000 miles if you booked directly with the hotel). That's an additional 3,000 miles, worth approximately $56 according to TPG's valuations.

Plus, Venture Rewards cardholders can access Capital One's Lifestyle Collection, which offers benefits such as a $50 experience credit for each eligible hotel stay and potential room upgrades (when available).

However, I don't recommend using the portal as your default method of booking travel. You usually won't earn hotel loyalty points or receive elite status benefits when booking through a third party, so it's worth comparing prices and benefits before making a reservation.

Still, for beginners looking to earn more miles without changing their spending habits, Capital One Travel can be a useful tool.

Related: Should I book flights through a travel portal?

Beyond earning miles, the Venture Rewards comes with several travel perks that can help you save money and make your trips a little easier.

One of the most useful is a statement credit of up to $120 (every four years) for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee. All you need to do is pay the application fee with your card, and you'll receive a statement credit for the eligible charge.

Both programs can help you save time at the airport, but Global Entry also includes TSA PreCheck benefits, so I recommend it for international travelers.

Another perk for international travelers is that the Venture Rewards charges no foreign transaction fees. This means you can use your card abroad without worrying about the additional fees some credit cards charge on international purchases.

The card also offers several travel protections, including an auto rental collision damage waiver and travel accident insurance, which can provide some added peace of mind when you're away from home.

You can also enroll in complimentary Hertz Five Star status, which comes with benefits like a wider selection of rental vehicles and the ability to skip the rental counter (at certain locations).

For a card with a $95 annual fee, these perks can offer strong ongoing value, especially if you travel a few times a year.

Related: 7 of the best starter travel credit cards

If you aren't ready to transfer your miles to travel partners but still want to redeem your rewards for travel, another option is to use your miles to cover eligible travel purchases.

Rather than searching for award availability or navigating airline loyalty programs, you can book an eligible travel purchase with your card and redeem miles to offset the charge within 90 days of the purchase.

When you redeem miles this way, each mile is worth 1 cent. That's less than TPG's valuation of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents per mile, but it offers a straightforward way to use your rewards.

For example, if you book a $300 flight with your Venture Rewards, you can redeem 30,000 miles to cover the purchase. You can also use this feature for other eligible travel expenses, including hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars.

TPG director of site strategy Carly Helfand has relied on this method before, redeeming 100,000 Capital One miles to cover a last-minute Airbnb purchase.

While transferring miles to travel partners can yield higher redemption values, covering travel purchases is a useful alternative when you want to book directly or can't find award availability that works for your dates.

For potentially higher-value redemptions, consider transferring your Capital One miles to the issuer's airline and hotel partners.

If you're new to the world of travel rewards, transferring miles simply means moving your Capital One miles into another travel loyalty program, where you can then redeem them for flights or hotel stays.

Capital One has more than 15 travel partners, including Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club and Wyndham Rewards.

Most of Capital One's airline partners offer a 1:1 transfer ratio, meaning 1,000 Capital One miles become 1,000 miles in the partner program. However, some partners have different ratios, so be sure to check before transferring.

Personally, I love transferring my Capital One miles to airline partners to book flights to and around Europe.

For example, I recently transferred about 6,000 Capital One miles to Air France-KLM Flying Blue to book a Scandinavian Airlines flight from Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) to Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN). I paid just $11 in taxes and fees for a flight that would have otherwise cost about $450 in cash, giving me 7.3 cents per mile in value — well above TPG's valuation of 1.85 cents per mile.

If you're just getting started, don't feel like you need to master transfer partners right away. You can begin by redeeming miles for travel purchases and explore transfers as you become more comfortable.

Related: How to transfer Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners

The Capital One Venture Rewards stands out as a beginner-friendly travel rewards card thanks to its simple earning structure, valuable travel perks and flexible redemption options.

If you're new to the world of points and miles, start by using the card for everyday spending and exploring simple travel redemptions. As you become more comfortable, you can transfer miles to travel partners to unlock even greater value.

And even as you become more experienced with points and miles, the Venture Rewards' simplicity and flexibility make it a card worth keeping in your wallet long term.

For more details, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Rewards.

Learn more: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

#6203. Southwest Premier Business Card Review: Is The $149 Annual Fee Worth It?

The Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card is the more basic of the two Southwest business cards. This card has a $149 annual fee, and gets you a handful of valuable benefits when you fly Southwest, including complimentary upgrades to Preferred seating within 48 hours of departure and a free checked bag, among other things.

If you fly Southwest at least a few times a year and you qualify for a small business credit card, the Southwest Premier Business Card is worth considering. It’s worth an extra close look right now, because now is your last chance to earn a Southwest credit card welcome bonus that counts toward the airline’s valuable Companion Pass benefit. I’ll get into all that and more below in my comprehensive Southwest Premier Business Card review.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Premier Business Credit Card

Before getting into the Southwest Premier Business Card in detail, let’s take a broader look at the card’s main features:

I also put together my pros and cons for the Southwest Premier Business Card:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is Southwest’s entry-level business credit card. Let’s take a look at the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and annual fee, given that these are factors that many people consider when applying for a card.

The Southwest Premier Business Card currently has a welcome bonus where you can earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 within the first three months.

Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each, as that’s roughly the rate at which you can redeem points toward flights. So by my valuation, 60,000 Rapid Rewards points are worth ~$720.

While this is a decent welcome offer, let me note that we’ve seen bigger limited time welcome offers in the past. So if you’re primarily after the best welcome offer, it could make sense to wait to apply.

The welcome bonus on the Southwest Premier Business Card isn’t available to those who currently have this card, or those who have received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible for this card (including the welcome bonus) if you have the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more), or any personal Southwest credit card.

Also remember Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, apply. With the 5/24 rule, you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the last 24 months. However, business credit cards aren’t always included on your credit report, so they often don’t count toward 5/24.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a $149 annual fee. There’s no cost to add additional users to the card. You can set individual spending limits for additional cards, and you can earn points on their spending.

The Southwest Premier Business Card doesn’t charge any foreign transaction fees, so you can use it abroad without worrying about racking up extra charges.

Obviously the rewards structure is an important factor to consider when applying for a credit card. So how does the Southwest Premier Business Card do on that front? In addition to offering bonus points in select spending categories, the card also offers the ability to earn status through spending, so let’s cover those details.

As far as the rewards structure goes, the Southwest Premier Business Card offers:

While these are some good bonus categories, I wouldn’t consider this to be an industry-leading rewards structure — there are better cards for airfare spending, and better cards for everyday spending.

Based on my valuation of Southwest points at 1.2 cents each, using the Southwest Premier Business Card to book Southwest flights gets you a 3.6% return on spending, while the 2x and 1x categories get you 2.4% and 1.2% returns on spending, respectively.

Spending on the Southwest Premier Business Card can count toward A-List elite status. Specifically, through the end of 2026 you can earn 2,000 Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward A-List for every $5,000 you spend on the card. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on the card will earn one TQP.

A-List status ordinarily requires 35,000 TQPs per year, and offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number.

However, Southwest has announced some big changes to its loyalty program, including new status level names and the introduction of a third tier called Platinum. Starting in 2027, A-List status will become Silver status. Earning it will require 35,000 TQPs (unchanged) or 25 qualifying flights (up from 20 today).

Personally I probably wouldn’t spend that much money on a credit card to earn A-List status, but for some people this could prove to be worthwhile, especially if you’re close to earning A-List status otherwise.

One of the very best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. With Southwest Companion Pass, you can have someone travel with you for the entire year (whether on a cash ticket or award ticket), and just pay taxes and fees for them. This is such an incredible deal, and basically doubles the value you can get from flying Southwest. The pass is valid for the rest of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the following full year, so the earlier in the year you earn it, the more it’s worth.

Historically, you’ve been able to get the Companion Pass by earning 135,000 Rapid Rewards points in a calendar year — and Southwest credit card welcome bonuses counted toward this, along with referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending on the card, and more. Starting January 1, 2027, though, this will no longer be the case.

Southwest is updating its elite status program to have three tiers, the highest of which is called Platinum and gets you unlimited Companion Pass trips. At that time, credit card welcome bonuses and all the other points earning mentioned above will no longer count toward qualifying for the Companion Pass (or any level of status).

To earn Platinum, and therefore the Companion Pass, you’ll instead need to earn 140,000 TQPs or take 100 qualifying flights. This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Premier Business Card; it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that points from the current welcome bonus offer do count toward Companion Pass qualification for the rest of 2026 and through 2027, per Chase’s offer details, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity is closed.

I have an entire post on how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work and how to get the most value out of your points here.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, with Basic awards usually offering the highest redemption value.

In my experience, the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. Southwest also flies to Hawaii, which can be a good use of points, but I’ve found that the redemption value is often a bit lower on these in-demand routes. And of course, if you have the Companion Pass your points become twice as valuable because a friend can travel for free minus taxes and fees.

There are no change or cancellation fees on Southwest award bookings, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d want to cancel and rebook rather than change your existing itinerary.

The Southwest Premier Business Card has a solid welcome bonus that’s especially valuable now that it’s your last chance to earn it and have it count toward the Companion Pass, but that’s not the only reason to consider this card. There are also several ongoing perks that can make your experience flying Southwest a little more comfortable.

One major ongoing perk of the Southwest Premier Business Card is that you earn 6,000 Rapid Rewards bonus points on your account anniversary every year. As mentioned above, I value Rapid Rewards points at around 1.2 cents each, so to me, that’s like $72 worth of value annually.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a free first checked bag for you and up to eight additional passengers on your same reservation.

If you usually check bags on Southwest — especially if you don’t have Southwest status, which gets you a free first checked bag — this benefit alone can help you recoup the annual fee. For non-elite Southwest travelers, a checked bag costs $45 one-way, so you could save $90 on a roundtrip flight. With two roundtrip flights with checked bags in a year, that already cancels out the $149 annual fee.

As a Southwest Premier Business cardholder, you can select a Preferred or Standard seat within 48 hours prior to departure, if they’re available. This benefit also extends to eight travelers on your same reservation. The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight.

The Southwest Premier Business Card also gets you a 15% promo code each year on your account anniversary. You can use this to score a 15% discount on a Southwest flight, excluding Basic fares. This perk is another nice way the card can save you money when flying Southwest, especially if you book cash tickets in addition to award flights at least once a year.

Southwest Premier Business cardholders can board with Group 5, or earlier if they have status or a fare that entitles them to a higher boarding group. This perk extends to eight additional travelers on the same reservation.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers 25% savings on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases on Southwest. Just charge your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for 25% of the purchase total, which should appear within two billing cycles.

The Southwest Premier Business Card offers a great welcome bonus, and the $149 annual fee can be largely offset by the 6,000 anniversary bonus points and other benefits. The welcome bonus can also go a long way toward earning the Companion Pass, which is all the more reason to get the card now before this opportunity ends.

That said, I don’t necessarily think the Southwest Premier Business Card is a great pick for everyone. If you’re not loyal to Southwest or you split flying across multiple airlines, it’s probably not the best card for you. And if you want flexible points that you can redeem with a variety of airlines and hotels, it could also be best to skip this card.

First, let me compare it to the more premium Southwest Performance Business Card, then I’ll share the points currency I recommend earning instead if you’re mainly concerned with booking award flights on Southwest, not extra perks with the airline.

The Southwest Performance Business Card (learn more) is the more premium sibling of the Southwest Premier Business Card. Overall it comes with more benefits — and in some cases enhanced versions of the same perks on the Southwest Premier Business Card.

Here’s a quick overview of how the Southwest business credit cards compare:

The extra 3,000 anniversary points are worth $36 by my valuation, so you’d need roughly $9,500 in Southwest spending for the extra point per dollar to cover the rest of the $150 fee difference, before counting the seating and Global Entry perks.

If you fly Southwest several times a year and you want as many perks and points as possible, the Southwest Performance Business Card could be worth the higher annual fee.

If your goal is to earn Southwest Rapid Rewards points, but you don’t actually plan on earning the Companion Pass or Southwest status, there’s a much faster way to earn those points.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. You can earn points at a much faster rate with the following business cards:

The Southwest Premier Business Card is a good entry-level Southwest Airlines business credit card with a nice welcome bonus. The current bonus can earn you a lot of travel on Southwest, and can even help you earn Companion Pass — but only if you earn the bonus under the current offer, before the 2027 program changes take effect.

This card is definitely worth considering, though the only other consideration is that I think it could be worth paying the premium for the Southwest Performance Business Card, which has better ongoing perks. And earning Ultimate Rewards points with a Chase credit card could also make more sense unless you really value the Southwest-specific benefits.

#6202. American Airlines Philadelphia Flagship Lounge Expected To Double In Size, Taking Over The Admirals Club Next Door

American Airlines’ gorgeous Philadelphia Flagship Lounge may finally get the space it should have had from the start. Lounge staff are reportedly telling passengers it’ll take over the Admirals Club next door around March 2027, essentially doubling the size of the business class lounge before next summer’s transatlantic seasonal peak. That’s the change I called for when the lounge opened. But there’s a potential problem for Admirals Club members since there’s no announced replacement for the club they’d lose. A passenger reports being told by the employee managing Flagship lounge entry that it would expand into the adjoining A West Admirals Club “sometime around next March.” Another commenter says an agent separately told them about expanding to the whole floor (which is the same thing), after they gave up on finding a seat in Flagship and went next door. Officially, an American Airlines spokesperson tells me: Nothing set in stone right now, but we are always evaluating how we can best serve our customers during the summer peak next year. In my original review, I showed the connector behind the check-in desk. There’s already ‘swing space’ that can be opened to either lounge. During my visit it was part of Flagship. These are adjoining spaces with the same beautiful design, and they’re already connected. The dimensions of the spaces are: Flagship: 12,500 square feet, with 200 seats. Admirals Club: 11,000 square feet, with 181 seats. Additional flex space: 1,364 square feet. That’s nearly 25,000 square feet across the complex. Moving the Admirals Club space into Flagship would roughly double its footprint. I quite like this lounge. In the morning and early afternoon, it’s a lovely place to spend time. The trouble comes before the bank of transatlantic departures, when the passengers it’s supposed to serve all arrive at once. A business class lounge needs enough seats for people flying business class. And in the summer from Philadelphia that total grows quite a lot with American’s seasonal services. Things are even worse now that the A West terminal has lost the American Express Centurion Lounge for expansion into the British Airways lounge space, expecting to reopen by the end of 2027. I’ve covered the project taking over the British Airways lounge space below. The British Airways lounge is closed, too. I actually think Flagship was already better than both lounges. It’s just crowded (but not as cramped as Centurion was!). American has been investing more in lounge food. At Dallas recently, I found a better buffet, staffed charcuterie and food ordered by QR code that arrived at my table in four minutes. Philadelphia helped introduce that ordering system, coming after the Soho lounge at JFK which is shared with BA. Philadelphia wasn’t built with a separate Flagship Dining room. Those are operating in Dallas and Miami, and I broke the news that Los Angeles reopens this week. Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has talked about rethinking Flagship. Delta was the last of the big three to introduce a separate business class lounge, and I think Delta One lounges now offer the strongest overall product. American’s access rules are much more generous, including eligible elites flying coach on qualifying international trips and oneworld Sapphire and Emerald members from programs other than American and Alaska even on domestic itineraries. That makes having enough space especially important. American had an Admirals Club in A East. They closed it when these lounges opened in May 2025. I argued then that they should keep A East for Admirals Club members and dedicate A West entirely to Flagship. Under the reported plan, the nearest Admirals Club would instead be B/C. Someone paying for a membership, or carrying the Citi Executive card, would lose access to the beautiful A West club without gaining access to the larger Flagship Lounge. American should take back the A East space as well. Kennedy International AirportLos AngelesMiamiPhiladelphia+11 more More From View from the Wing

That’s the change I called for when the lounge opened. But there’s a potential problem for Admirals Club members since there’s no announced replacement for the club they’d lose.

A passenger reports being told by the employee managing Flagship lounge entry that it would expand into the adjoining A West Admirals Club “sometime around next March.” Another commenter says an agent separately told them about expanding to the whole floor (which is the same thing), after they gave up on finding a seat in Flagship and went next door.

Officially, an American Airlines spokesperson tells me:

Nothing set in stone right now, but we are always evaluating how we can best serve our customers during the summer peak next year.

In my original review, I showed the connector behind the check-in desk. There’s already ‘swing space’ that can be opened to either lounge. During my visit it was part of Flagship. These are adjoining spaces with the same beautiful design, and they’re already connected.

That’s nearly 25,000 square feet across the complex. Moving the Admirals Club space into Flagship would roughly double its footprint.

I quite like this lounge. In the morning and early afternoon, it’s a lovely place to spend time. The trouble comes before the bank of transatlantic departures, when the passengers it’s supposed to serve all arrive at once. A business class lounge needs enough seats for people flying business class. And in the summer from Philadelphia that total grows quite a lot with American’s seasonal services.

Things are even worse now that the A West terminal has lost the American Express Centurion Lounge for expansion into the British Airways lounge space, expecting to reopen by the end of 2027. I’ve covered the project taking over the British Airways lounge space below. The British Airways lounge is closed, too.

I actually think Flagship was already better than both lounges. It’s just crowded (but not as cramped as Centurion was!). American has been investing more in lounge food. At Dallas recently, I found a better buffet, staffed charcuterie and food ordered by QR code that arrived at my table in four minutes. Philadelphia helped introduce that ordering system, coming after the Soho lounge at JFK which is shared with BA.

Philadelphia wasn’t built with a separate Flagship Dining room. Those are operating in Dallas and Miami, and I broke the news that Los Angeles reopens this week.

Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has talked about rethinking Flagship. Delta was the last of the big three to introduce a separate business class lounge, and I think Delta One lounges now offer the strongest overall product. American’s access rules are much more generous, including eligible elites flying coach on qualifying international trips and oneworld Sapphire and Emerald members from programs other than American and Alaska even on domestic itineraries. That makes having enough space especially important.

American had an Admirals Club in A East. They closed it when these lounges opened in May 2025. I argued then that they should keep A East for Admirals Club members and dedicate A West entirely to Flagship.

Under the reported plan, the nearest Admirals Club would instead be B/C. Someone paying for a membership, or carrying the Citi Executive card, would lose access to the beautiful A West club without gaining access to the larger Flagship Lounge. American should take back the A East space as well.

#6201. Hyatt Dining & Spa Awards: Are They Worth Redeeming Points For?

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night award redemptions, there are some lesser known ways to redeem Hyatt points. One of those is the ability to use points for Dining & Spa awards, which can be a surprisingly good deal.

This doesn’t get a lot of attention, and it’s particularly useful if you want to minimize your out-of-pocket when staying at a Hyatt property, while still indulging in on-property experiences.

Most people don’t realize that you can redeem World of Hyatt points toward the cost of on-property dining and spa experiences, and the value proposition can be surprisingly good. Specifically, you can redeem a certain number of points for a certain amount of credit to use toward on-property spending, even if you’re not staying at a Hyatt property. Let’s take a closer look at how this works.

Below is a chart showing the various redemption opportunities available with Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards, along with how much value you can potentially get per point:

As you can see, you can redeem anywhere from 1,000 points for a $10 credit, to 65,000 points for a $1,000 credit. The value per point ranges anywhere from 1.0 cents per point, to 1.54 cents per point.

1.54 cents per World of Hyatt point sounds like a solid deal. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, World of Hyatt points are worth 1.4 cents each, so this actually offers solid value, at least on the surface. Is there a catch, though?

The exact redemptions that are allowed vary by hotel, but generally you can expect that these awards can be used for food and beverage purchases, spa and salon services, and spa and salon retail items.

On top of that, when charged to a member’s guest room, the following charges may be eligible:

laundry, dry cleaning, telephone charges, pay-per-view movies, parking, gift/retail shop, service charges, taxes (not including room taxes) and gratuities

Meanwhile the following charges are expressly prohibited from being eligible:

room rates, room taxes, alcoholic beverages (in certain jurisdictions), catering or banquet charges, and casino charges

If you’re staying at a Hyatt then you should be able to redeem these awards for cumulative charges over the course of your stay. However, I’d recommend confirming this with the front desk at check-in, including which outlets would be eligible for these redemptions, since individual hotels could have different policies.

Not all Hyatt hotels participate in this program. Miraval, Unscripted by Hyatt, Hyatt Select, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Vacation Club properties, Hyatt Vivid, Bahia Principe, Impression by Secrets, Secrets, Dreams, Breathless, Zoëtry, Alua, Sunscape, and other Legacy AMR Collection resorts, as well as some Dream properties, do not participate. Furthermore, redemption of these certificates is limited to registered guests at Hyatt Zilara, Hyatt Ziva, and Hyatt Studios properties.

To be positive, you can search participating properties at this page.

You don’t need to redeem for these certificates in advance, but rather the World of Hyatt member should just inform the Hyatt employee at the eligible outlet that they’d like to redeem points toward their purchase at the outset. You’ll need to have your membership information, and should then be asked how many points you want to redeem.

If you’re a registered guest at a hotel then you can apply one of these at check-out toward multiple purchases over the course of a stay. If you’re not a registered guest then you’ll have to settle your folio at the particular outlet you’re at.

There are a few other things to potentially be aware of:

On the surface, being able to redeem World of Hyatt points for up to ~1.54 cents toward the cost of a purchase is a solid deal. Is it exceptional? No. But as a way of essentially “cashing out” your points to offset cash costs I think it’s very good.

I do think it’s important to create a more realistic valuation of these redemptions, though. When you redeem these awards you’re forgoing the opportunity to earn points on these purchases:

As a Globalist member I earn 10.5x points per dollar spent, which I value at a return of ~15% (1.4 cents per point). That’s an opportunity cost that’s worth factoring in, so in reality, I’d adjust the maximum value from 1.54 cents to ~1.3 cents.

Personally, this isn’t how I’d redeem my World of Hyatt points, though I do think many people could find this to be worthwhile for a splurge:

World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, allowing members to redeem points for dining and spa experiences at most Hyatt properties. This has the potential to be a solid deal, as getting 1.54 cents per Hyatt point toward the cost of a purchase is a good redemption. However, do factor in the points you’re forgoing, which brings down the redemption value a bit.

While I wouldn’t say this is the best way to redeem Hyatt points, this could be worth it to lower how much cash you’ll pay for a Hyatt stay, especially at a secluded resort where you’re likely to spend most time on-property.

What do you make of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards? Could you see yourself redeeming points for them?

#6200. The battle for Congress is just the beginning. Here's what's at stake on Election Day

'Fox & Friends Weekend' co-host Griff Jenkins breaks down the latest Power Rankings ahead of the midterms, highlighting shifts in Kansas and Nebraska, seven toss-up Senate races and the battle for control of Congress.

It's Election Day in America, with voters heading to the polls to determine control of the U.S. House and Senate for the next two years.

Republicans are defending their slim congressional majorities, but President Donald Trump predicts the GOP will hold the House and Senate for the final two years of his presidency.

"We're going to win and let's make the next two years bigger and better and stronger than ever before," Trump told supporters Sunday night at a rally in Kansas.

But Republicans are fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. The GOP also faces a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation tied in part to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings.

DEMOCRACY 2026: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

President Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally at the Salina Regional Airport, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Salina, Kansas. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo)

The GOP is also facing a potential turnout deficit, with public opinion polls indicating Democrats are more energized than Republicans to cast ballots in the midterms.

Early voting in the midterms has shattered previous records, with more than 54 million people already casting ballots, according to The Associated Press. That's nearly 9 million more ballots cast in early voting than in 2022, the previous midterm elections.

With early voting traditionally favoring Democrats, Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters, pointing to Election Day turnout, recently told Fox News Digital, "If our voters turn out, we win."

A voter fills out their ballot at a polling location inside Wayne Community College Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The political climate has the GOP playing plenty of defense on the campaign trail, as the president tries to energize the GOP base.

Trump's event in red-leaning Kansas, which he touted as his 30th rally over the past month, came hours after the Fox News Power Rankings shifted the state's Senate race from Lean Republican to Toss-up. Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton, who is challenging GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, is aiming to become the first Democrat in nearly a century to win a Senate election in Kansas.

The Fox News Power Rankings, as well as many of the leading nonpartisan political handicappers, point to Democrats retaking control of the House, with the majority in the Senate a toss-up heading into Election Day.

"Think of what is possible tomorrow: Democrats can flip the House, take back the Senate, and stop Trump’s harmful agenda," Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin spotlighted in an Election Eve social media post.

Also up for grabs in this year's elections — governorships in 36 of the 50 states. Plus, all but four states are holding legislative elections. And voters will also weigh in on 145 statewide ballot measures in states from coast to coast.

The big question with Election Day upon us — have the public opinion polls that point to a potential blue wave undercounted Republican voters?

LEAVITT SAYS TRUMP DEFYING MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS HE BARNSTORMS COUNTRY

The Election Day sign outside town hall in Newfields, New Hampshire, ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Until then, here's a closer look at what's up for grabs on Election Day 2026.

Republicans currently control the chamber 53-47, which means Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority. The GOP needs to hold at least 50 seats to retain control of the chamber, since Republican Vice President JD Vance is the tie-breaking vote in the Senate.

Besides Kansas, Republicans are also playing defense in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, which are all rated toss-ups in the Power Rankings. They're also defending seats in competitive races in Kansas, which is rated Lean Republican, and Ohio, which is rated Lean Democrat.

Democrats are on defense in Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire.

The GOP is hanging on to a razor-thin majority in the House, with Democrats needing a net gain of just three seats to reach 218, which would hand them the majority.

A good night for the Democrats could see them ending up with as many as 240 seats in the 435-seat chamber, according to the Power Rankings. But if Republicans have a good night, they could end up with 212 seats. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party.

The earliest-closing district polls on election night will give some sense of the House’s future.

"Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th District, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle," Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings, said.

There are currently 26 Republican and 24 Democratic governors.

The Power Rankings list three states where the GOP controls the governor's office – Alaska, Nevada and Georgia – as toss-ups. Wisconsin, which has an open Democratic-controlled governor's office, is also rated a toss-up.

The gubernatorial races in red states Florida, Kansas and Texas are rated Lean Republican, according to the Power Rankings. Meanwhile, the showdowns in Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio and Oregon are rated Lean Democrat.

Referendums requiring voters to present identification when they show up at the polls, or bans on noncitizen voting, are on the ballot in 11 states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Kansas, Nevada, North Carolina, Ohio, South Dakota and West Virginia.

Voters in Alaska will also decide if they want to repeal the state’s ranked choice voting system, open primaries and a campaign finance disclosure rule. Voters approved the current system in 2020 and narrowly kept it in 2024.

But the voting system has come under fresh scrutiny amid the controversy over a potential spoiler candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race.

Voters in Virginia will decide whether the right to vote should be restored to convicted felons upon their release.

Roughly a dozen states are holding ballot measures on Election Day that are related to voting. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

California's Proposition 40 is making national headlines.

The measure, the first of its kind, would slap a one-time 5% tax on wealth for Californians worth over $1 billion, with the vast majority of the revenue generated going to pay for healthcare.

Also in the spotlight is a millionaires' tax in Washington state. If passed, the referendum would repeal a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million a year, which state lawmakers recently approved. Washington state currently does not have a personal income tax.

Voters in Maryland, Missouri and Colorado weigh in on ballot measures on congressional redistricting, as the mid-decade redistricting fight between Democrats and Republicans will be waged again in 2028.

Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington state have referendums on transgender students’ participation in sports. Colorado also has a referendum on blocking gender transition surgeries for minors and preventing state or federal funding from being used for those operations.

Voters in Missouri weigh in on repealing a right to abortion and banning gender transition medical care for children. Meanwhile, an Idaho initiative would overturn one of the nation's strictest abortion bans, while Virginia and Nevada voters decide on establishing a right to abortion in their state constitutions.

California, Colorado and Arizona hold ballot measures on policy around energy, transportation and development.

The first poll closings come at 6 p.m. ET, with the final poll closings happening at 1 a.m. ET.

6 p.m. ET: Polls close in parts of Kentucky and Indiana.

7 p.m. ET: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia. The final polls in Kentucky and Indiana close. And most polls in Florida and New Hampshire close.

7:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.

8 p.m. ET: Polls close in Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee and Washington, D.C. The remaining polls in Florida and New Hampshire close. Most polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota.

9 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. The final polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota.

10 p.m. ET: Polls close in Montana and Utah. Most polls also close in Idaho and Oregon.

11 p.m. ET: Polls close in California and Washington state, with the remaining polls in Idaho and Oregon also closing.

Midnight ET: Polls in all of Hawaii and most of Alaska close, with the remaining polls in Alaska closing at 1 a.m. ET.

#6199. Southwest’s New Credit Card Bonuses Offer Up To 90,000 Points Toward Companion Pass—Last Chance Before Rules Change

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Southwest’s Companion Pass lets someone fly with you for just taxes and fees, even when you redeem points for your own ticket. For someone who flies Southwest with a partner a few times a year, it’s the single best deal in domestic air travel. And the easiest way to earn it is about to disappear.

There’s still a final window to use an 80,000- or 90,000-point credit card initial bonus toward a pass valid through December 31, 2027. You need to apply by December 2, 2026 and get approved. Neither bonus gets you all the way there on its own, but both give you a huge head start.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. It has a $229 annual fee. This is the premium Southwest co-brand card, really designed for folks who fly the airline. It makes those trips better, and spending helps earn both elite status and Companion Pass®. The travel benefits cover the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation: First checked bag free. Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. Boarding with Group 5 or earlier if another benefit qualifies you for a better group. You earn 4 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, including flights, inflight purchases and Southwest gift cards; 2 points per dollar at gas stations and restaurants; and 1 point per dollar on other purchases. There are also 7,500 anniversary points each year. The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Its annual fee is $99. That’s a much lower spending requirement for a bonus that’s only 10,000 points smaller. First checked bag free for the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. Standard seat selection within 48 hours of departure, when available, for the same group of travelers. Group 5 boarding or earlier if you otherwise qualify. 3,000 anniversary points each year, plus a 10% anniversary flight discount code that excludes Basic fares. The Plus card earns 2 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, and 2 points per dollar at gas stations and grocery stores on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per anniversary year. Other purchases earn 1 point per dollar. I’d choose Plus for the lower cost of getting the bonus. Priority costs $130 more per year, but gives you better seat benefits, 4,500 more anniversary points and a larger initial bonus. For a family that flies Southwest regularly, those seating benefits can easily be worth the difference. How Close These Bonuses Get You To Companion Pass Under the 2026 rules, earning 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year gets you the pass for the rest of that year and the following year. Southwest credit card customers receive a 10,000-point qualifying boost, so they effectively need 125,000 more. Priority: 90,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 100,000. You need another 35,000 qualifying points. Plus: 80,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 90,000. You need another 45,000 qualifying points. The purchases you make to earn the bonus also earn points. Assuming those purchase points post in 2026, spending the minimum at 1 point per dollar reduces the remaining gap to 32,000 points with Priority or 44,000 with Plus. Bonus category spending and qualifying points you’ve already earned reduce it further. Qualifying flights and eligible partner activity can help fill the gap, too. Check your Companion Pass progress in your account. Once you have the pass, book your own Southwest flight with cash or points and add your designated companion, as long as there’s an available seat. Their taxes and fees start at $5.60 one-way. You can use the benefit repeatedly and change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. How Optimal Timing Of The Companion Pass Has Changed As I covered in Southwest’s 2027 Rapid Rewards overhaul, unlimited Companion Pass becomes a benefit of the new Platinum elite tier next year. Initial bonuses generally stop helping you qualify. Anniversary points, referral bonuses and extra points from card bonus categories stop counting, too. Southwest’s transition exception preserves the initial bonus for customers who apply by December 2, 2026, are approved, and meet the offer’s requirements. Even if you finish the required spending in early 2027, the bonus can count toward 2026 qualification for a pass ending December 31, 2027. So the old strategy of waiting until January to earn nearly two years of Companion Pass doesn’t work here. A bonus earned under this exception won’t get you a pass through the end of 2028. And Chase’s terms distinguish the initial bonus from ordinary purchase points. Those purchase points must post to your Rapid Rewards account in 2026 to count toward this pass. Spending after your December statement closes generally posts in January. You also want the 10,000-point qualifying boost credited in 2026; Southwest allows up to 30 days after account opening for it to arrive. You still have to meet the initial bonus spending requirement within the first 3 months from account opening. The transition rule doesn’t extend that deadline. I’m a former Companion Pass holder, and a promotional Companion Pass holder.Southwest still represents about 40% of the seats out of my home airport in Austin. Even with all the changes they’ve made, being able to bring someone along on those flights for just the taxes is huge. Before applying, you can’t currently hold a Southwest personal credit card, and you can’t have received an initial bonus on any Southwest personal card in the past 24 months. Southwest business and employee cards are excluded from that restriction. Chase’s usual 5/24 rule also applies: generally, you need fewer than 5 new credit card accounts on your credit report in the past 24 months. If you’re eligible, can handle the required spending, and have a path to the remaining qualifying points, I’d take advantage of this before December 2. The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. It has a $229 annual fee.

This is the premium Southwest co-brand card, really designed for folks who fly the airline. It makes those trips better, and spending helps earn both elite status and Companion Pass®. The travel benefits cover the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation:

First checked bag free. Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. Boarding with Group 5 or earlier if another benefit qualifies you for a better group.

You earn 4 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, including flights, inflight purchases and Southwest gift cards; 2 points per dollar at gas stations and restaurants; and 1 point per dollar on other purchases. There are also 7,500 anniversary points each year.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Its annual fee is $99. That’s a much lower spending requirement for a bonus that’s only 10,000 points smaller.

First checked bag free for the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. Standard seat selection within 48 hours of departure, when available, for the same group of travelers. Group 5 boarding or earlier if you otherwise qualify. 3,000 anniversary points each year, plus a 10% anniversary flight discount code that excludes Basic fares.

The Plus card earns 2 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, and 2 points per dollar at gas stations and grocery stores on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per anniversary year. Other purchases earn 1 point per dollar.

I’d choose Plus for the lower cost of getting the bonus. Priority costs $130 more per year, but gives you better seat benefits, 4,500 more anniversary points and a larger initial bonus. For a family that flies Southwest regularly, those seating benefits can easily be worth the difference.

Under the 2026 rules, earning 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year gets you the pass for the rest of that year and the following year. Southwest credit card customers receive a 10,000-point qualifying boost, so they effectively need 125,000 more. Priority: 90,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 100,000. You need another 35,000 qualifying points. Plus: 80,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 90,000. You need another 45,000 qualifying points. The purchases you make to earn the bonus also earn points. Assuming those purchase points post in 2026, spending the minimum at 1 point per dollar reduces the remaining gap to 32,000 points with Priority or 44,000 with Plus. Bonus category spending and qualifying points you’ve already earned reduce it further. Qualifying flights and eligible partner activity can help fill the gap, too. Check your Companion Pass progress in your account. Once you have the pass, book your own Southwest flight with cash or points and add your designated companion, as long as there’s an available seat. Their taxes and fees start at $5.60 one-way. You can use the benefit repeatedly and change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. How Optimal Timing Of The Companion Pass Has Changed As I covered in Southwest’s 2027 Rapid Rewards overhaul, unlimited Companion Pass becomes a benefit of the new Platinum elite tier next year. Initial bonuses generally stop helping you qualify. Anniversary points, referral bonuses and extra points from card bonus categories stop counting, too. Southwest’s transition exception preserves the initial bonus for customers who apply by December 2, 2026, are approved, and meet the offer’s requirements. Even if you finish the required spending in early 2027, the bonus can count toward 2026 qualification for a pass ending December 31, 2027. So the old strategy of waiting until January to earn nearly two years of Companion Pass doesn’t work here. A bonus earned under this exception won’t get you a pass through the end of 2028. And Chase’s terms distinguish the initial bonus from ordinary purchase points. Those purchase points must post to your Rapid Rewards account in 2026 to count toward this pass. Spending after your December statement closes generally posts in January. You also want the 10,000-point qualifying boost credited in 2026; Southwest allows up to 30 days after account opening for it to arrive.
