#6198. 59-Room Andaz Turks & Caicos At Grace Bay Opening April 2027, Now Bookable

The much delayed Andaz Turks & Caicos is getting closer to opening. The hotel has now moved forward the date as of which it’s accepting reservations, and we’ve also learned more details about the on-property amenities. Let’s cover all the details, as we’re potentially under five months from the opening…

The Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. This will mark Hyatt’s first hotel in Turks & Caicos, and the first Andaz property in the Caribbean. For that matter, it’s one of the only Andaz properties that’s currently in the pipeline outside of Asia, as the brand has really lost steam.

The 5.5-acre resort will offer four restaurants and bars, three outdoor pools, a spa, a kids club, a fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, and more. The Andaz will be comprised of 59 rooms and 73 branded residences, so at least the hotel portion of the property will be boutique. It’ll be located directly on Grace Bay, known for offering one of the most beautiful stretches of beach in the Caribbean.

As far as the culinary concepts go, the Andaz Turks & Caicos will feature the following:

Runa Spa & Wellness, the spa at the Andaz, will be around 7,000 square feet. It will have five treatment rooms, along with a sauna, cold plunge, relaxation area, and more.

The opening of this resort has been majorly delayed. It was initially announced in 2018 with a 2021 opening, but the timeline slipped by six years, presumably due to a combination of the pandemic, plus… well, how hotel construction projects often work out. Hopefully there are no additional delays beyond the current planned spring 2027 opening.

With the Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay bookable, what are rates like? For those redeeming points, this is a Category 8 World of Hyatt property, meaning a free night redemption in a standard room costs 35,000-75,000 points per night.

World of Hyatt’s new award chart sure makes top end redemptions expensive, unfortunately! As of now the hotel is primarily bookable between April and November of 2027, so this doesn’t really cover peak season. For most dates, I currently see rates of either 35,000 points, 45,000 points, or 55,000 points per night. So value here is highly dependent on which of those rates you can find.

When it comes to cash rates, those currently start at around $900-1,300 per night, and that depends on when you’re staying. That’s inclusive of the service charge, but exclusive of the taxes.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, and a hotel credit.

I suppose good options on Grace Bay are limited, and this hotel is boutique. But at these rates, they better offer something significantly better than the typical Andaz experience, in my opinion.

Turks & Caicos is absolutely beautiful, and it’s an easy getaway from the United States, given how close it is to Florida. Historically, the country hasn’t had that many points hotels, though that’s slowly starting to change.

Several years back, we saw the opening of the Ritz-Carlton Turks & Caicos. It has an amazing location on Grace Bay and the grounds of the property are beautiful, but it otherwise doesn’t feel very luxurious, and lacks personality.

So it’ll be nice to have another points property, and I look forward to learning more about the Andaz. Maybe I’m overly optimistic, but I think the Andaz might just end up offering a better experience than the Ritz-Carlton, at least based on the design renderings, and also the more boutique scale of the property. Andaz really is quite an inconsistent brand.

I of course should acknowledge that many people are understandably frustrated by the way that Grace Bay has developed over the years, given all the huge concrete towers that have taken shape along the beach. It has definitely lost its charm a bit, though the beach is still gorgeous.

Even beyond Grace Bay, we’re seeing some other great new options in Turks & Caicos. In 2025, we saw the opening of Salterra Turks & Caicos, a Marriott Luxury Collection property. This is great for those who want a bit more secluded of a trip, since South Caicos Island is a bit less crowded than the area around Providenciales. This is also where Sailrock Resort is located, which is an independent hotel affiliated with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH).

There’s also a Waldorf Astoria Turks & Caicos planned for a 2028 opening, located on Dellis Cay, a nearby island that’s not as developed, which can be reached by a 25-minute boat transfer from Providenciales. That should also be a great option, especially with how the Waldorf Astoria portfolio is developing. However, don’t count on that timeline sticking either.

The Andaz Turks & Caicos is accepting reservations for stays as of April 2027, and it will be located on the famous Grace Bay. The property will have just 59 hotel rooms, in addition to residences, so I like how it’s on a smaller scale than some other properties.

This should be a very nice addition to the Caribbean points hotel market. Hopefully we don’t see any additional delays with the opening…

What do you make of the upcoming Andaz Turks & Caicos?

Beyond welcome bonuses, points and miles aren't always the easiest to earn. That's why I advocate for stacking your card's earning rates with shopping portal bonuses and other promotions whenever you can.

That's exactly what I did recently when I purchased three tickets for my parents and me to see the Portland Timbers while they were visiting. The total charge was about $180; if I’d paid with a card earning just 1 point per dollar spent and skipped the other offers, I’d have earned only 180 points.

But by paying close attention to my Chase Freedom Flex®'s (see rates and fees) quarterly categories and promotions offered by Rove and Paze, I was able to walk away with just shy of 4,000 points (or over $75 in value back). Here's exactly how my earnings break down.

For Q3 2026, the Freedom Flex offered select live entertainment as one of its rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories (activation required; on up to $1,500 in combined quarterly category spending per quarter).

Despite being marketed as a cash-back card, the Freedom Flex actually earns Ultimate Rewards points. That means my earning rate for live entertainment purchases in Q3 was effectively 5 points per dollar spent, since I have an eligible card that allows me to convert my Freedom Flex rewards into fully transferable points.

On its own, this category earned me about 900 points, a solid haul considering I'd earn only 180 points during quarters when live entertainment isn't offered. Still, while planning my purchase, I knew I could do better.

I've been a big fan of Rove over the past several months, using it for a variety of events and travel bookings. Rove offers members the opportunity to earn Rove miles, which are transferable to over 20 airline and hotel partners. This includes partners that aren't offered by any credit card loyalty programs, such as Frontier Miles and Lufthansa Miles & More.

It's free to join. Rove has its own travel booking portal, but for this particular purchase, I focused solely on its shopping portal. At the time, Rove offered 6.5 miles per dollar spent on StubHub purchases.

By booking my tickets through StubHub, I earned over 1,100 Rove miles. An unfortunate downside to shopping through Rove is that your miles often take an extended amount of time to post, which isn't uncommon with shopping portals. I'm still waiting for my miles to land in my account, which Rove indicates could take until early December.

Don't forget to start your purchase in the Rove app, on Rove's website or via its browser extension. If you're using the browser extension or accessing Rove via desktop, make sure all other shopping portal browser extensions are disabled.

With my decision to book through StubHub, there was one more way I could make my purchase work for me: Paze.

Currently, eligible Chase cardholders can earn 10 additional Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent when checking out with Paze at select merchants (through Dec. 31). StubHub is among those eligible for this promotion, meaning I could triple-dip on my purchase.

Checking out with Paze instead of the standard StubHub checkout process earned me roughly 1,800 additional points.

Using Paze at checkout is easy. You should be able to select it as a payment method on your eligible merchant's checkout screen, just as you would with a digital wallet or credit card.

One technical snag to note: I wasn't able to get Paze to work on mobile, but it worked on the first try on desktop. My transaction didn't say anything about Paze, so don't fret if the same is true for you. My points posted with no problem after a few days, but I recommend screen recording your purchase as proof if you're worried.

To summarize, here's how my earnings and their value broke down in the end:

*Valuations are according to TPG's November 2026 valuations and are not provided by credit card or program issuers.

My Freedom Flex is one of my oldest cards, but I still pull it out regularly, thanks in large part to strategies like this. While Chase's Paze promotion isn't limited to this card, the Freedom Flex is the only Chase card currently open to applicants that offers rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories.

Live entertainment reliably appears as a quarterly category every year, so I expect I'll be able to replicate this strategy (or a similar one) in 2027.

The more credit cards you open, the harder it becomes to find new welcome bonuses to earn. With welcome offers being the main way to earn heaps of rewards at once, it's important to have other ways to earn points and miles when that well starts to dry up.

Knowing how to maximize your purchases, especially larger ones or those you're splitting with friends or family, will help you maintain a large rewards balance even when you're not actively applying for new credit cards.

If you're currently not a Freedom Flex cardholder, you can apply and, upon approval, have the chance to earn $250 cash back (or 25,000 bonus points) after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. That's one of the easiest welcome bonuses to earn right now, but this offer ends soon.

If you hold an eligible Ultimate Rewards card, such as the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see ), you can transfer the points you earn with your Freedom Flex to Chase's 14 transfer partners.

The Timbers weren't able to walk away with the win, but the more than 3,800 points and miles I earned from the tickets I purchased helped ease the sting of that loss.

You can create a strategy like this with virtually any card in your wallet. Consider the offers, limited-time earning rates and promotions that are available for your specific card; take a look at shopping portals like Rakuten and Rove to see what they offer; and use sites like Cashback Monitor to make sure you're getting the best deal.

Effectively maximizing your card's earning potential means thoroughly understanding which offers and deals are available to you and knowing how to combine them. It requires a little extra work on your part, but that effort will be worth it when those extra rewards help take you on your next dream trip.

To learn more, check out our full review of the Chase Freedom Flex.

#6196. Country Star Jessie James Decker Sprays Passenger’s Bare Foot That Invades Her Armrest

Country singer Jessie James Decker shared video of herself spraying the bare foot of a passenger that had invaded her plane armrest. She holds her nose, takes aim with a small mint-green bottle, and the foot quickly disappears. Then she covers her mouth and laughs. Her Instagram video says, “Someone’s foot smells so bad on the plane.” She asked her followers how they would have handled it. Several suspected she was just messing with her husband, former football player Eric Decker. She refuted that: “Have you seen Eric’s feet? Toeeeee UP.” Jessie James Decker’s airplane video Decker is a country pop singer whose 2017 album Southern Girl City Lights debuted at number one on Billboard’s country albums chart. Her sister is Sydney Rae Bass, whose husband Anthony Bass complained that United Airlines made his pregnant wife clean up their child’s spilled popcorn a few years ago. In April, an American Airlines first class passenger shoved a woman’s feet off their armrest, only to see her put them up on the window. The suggestions in that discussion included spraying cologne. Here Decker puts that into practice. Somehow though this keeps happening? I’d want that foot gone, too. I’d ask the passenger to move it, and get a flight attendant involved if they refused. Some Facebook commenters insist this isn’t the crew’s job. They shouldn’t have to deal with it, and neither should a passenger. Each of us is supposed to contain our bodies within the space of our assigned seats. Her Instagram video says, “Someone’s foot smells so bad on the plane.” She asked her followers how they would have handled it. Several suspected she was just messing with her husband, former football player Eric Decker. She refuted that: “Have you seen Eric’s feet? Toeeeee UP.”

Decker is a country pop singer whose 2017 album Southern Girl City Lights debuted at number one on Billboard’s country albums chart. Her sister is Sydney Rae Bass, whose husband Anthony Bass complained that United Airlines made his pregnant wife clean up their child’s spilled popcorn a few years ago.

In April, an American Airlines first class passenger shoved a woman’s feet off their armrest, only to see her put them up on the window. The suggestions in that discussion included spraying cologne. Here Decker puts that into practice. Somehow though this keeps happening?

I’d want that foot gone, too. I’d ask the passenger to move it, and get a flight attendant involved if they refused. Some Facebook commenters insist this isn’t the crew’s job. They shouldn’t have to deal with it, and neither should a passenger. Each of us is supposed to contain our bodies within the space of our assigned seats.

#6195. Marriott’s Fees Jump 14% as Hotel Owners Seek a Bigger Cut

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Aerial view of The Ritz Carlton Oahu Turtle Bay. Marriott

Marriott said that its talks with hotel owners who want a bigger cut of the pie have been "constructive." It's easier for everyone to stay polite about the fee math when profit growth has revived significantly.

Marriott’s fees are climbing just as some of its hotel owners push for a bigger share of them.

Gross fees rose 14% to $1.52 billion in the third quarter, helped by a larger hotel network and by co-branded credit card fees, which Chief Financial Officer Jen Mason said on a Monday earnings call were “expected to rise in the high 30% range” for the full year. A group of owners wrote to Marriott’s management earlier this year asking for a bigger share of loyalty income, citing the card fees in particular. Net income rose 17% to $790 million.

Strong results may also give Marriott more leverage in those talks. Worldwide revenue per available room (RevPAR) rose 6.5% year over year, far above the 3.5% to 4% the company had projected in August, and Mason cited “a solid improvement in hotel margins.”

The gains reached the hotels that had been struggling most. Limited-service hotels posted a third consecutive quarter of RevPAR gains, up more than 6%.

Marriott beat expectations in the third quarter, with worldwide RevPAR up 6.5% year over year against August guidance of 3.5% to 4%, gross fees up 14% to $1.52 billion, and net income up 17% to $790 million. The company raised its full-year RevPAR outlook to 4.5% to 5%, up from the 1.5% to 2.5% it forecast in February, and offered an early view that 2027 worldwide RevPAR could grow 3.5% to 4.5%. The results land in the middle of a negotiation with a group of owners who wrote to management earlier this year asking for a bigger share of loyalty income, citing co-branded credit card fees, which CFO Jen Mason said are expected to rise in the high 30% range for the full year. CEO Anthony Capuano described Marriott's approach to owners as incremental, pointing to concessions already announced — a lower owner contribution rate on loyalty spending, better reimbursement for redemption stays on high-demand nights, relaxed operating and renovation rules, and a rebate for some well-reviewed hotels — and did not rule out more. Incentive management fees rose 22% to $181 million, which Marriott cites as evidence that owner and brand economics move together. Meanwhile, net room growth held at 4.6%, Capuano called key money the "weapon of choice" in winning development deals, and conversions made up more than a third of signings. The strong quarter arrived a week after Capuano told staff Marriott would eliminate some corporate roles while creating others; neither executives nor analysts raised the restructuring on the call.

#6194. Use Lyft For Work? How To Get 6%–8% Back, Plus Extra Airline Or Hotel Points

I have a personal preference for Lyft, as regular readers know. One of the things that I really like is that they have the best rewards in rideshare. But I didn’t realize things get even more lucrative for business travelers using a Lyft business profile. They have benefits, like:

keeping all of your regular rewards to use on personal or business rides. earning with Lyft’s airline or hotel partners goes up significantly for eligible business travelers. and pocketing 6% – 8% back in Lyft Credits on business profile rides, to use on your own rides later. That’s why it makes sense to sign up for a business account. Bonus, it lets you separate personal and business rides, which makes expense management easier (and you won’t mistakenly apply personal credits to reimbursable trips as I sometimes do by accident). Earn Lyft Credits On Top of Travel Rewards The original idea of a frequent flyer program was that you’d earn rewards on business travel. Your employer pays for a ticket, you benefit personally with your miles. That kept you loyal. This is really the same idea that the airlines pioneered about 45 years ago. When you ride for work, you can get Lyft Credits to use on your own trips later – 6% for standard rides taken with your business profile and 8% for premium, airport, and scheduled business profile rides. And you can do this even while earning with your preferred travel partner, and you earn those points or miles faster than you do with a personal account (where I’ve already been happy with the points-earning). How To Join I already use Lyft for business travel, so enrolling is a no-brainer since it’s fast and free and you accelerate your earnings. This also lets you bill a business card or directly to your employer and it integrates with popular expense tools. Lyft estimates that over half of business travelers forget to take advantage of automatic company expensing, leading to missed rewards and lack of visibility for organizations. Can We Just Appreciate Rideshare For A Moment? For most of my life there was no such thing as rideshare. For a brief time in Austin where I live, the city government chased it away, and I actually had to re-learn how to get to the airport. Now I pull up my Lyft app and I’m frustrated if I see that my driver is six minutes away. Six minutes. That’s my complaint. A stranger is coming to my exact location, in their personal car, because I touched glass. That’s sorcery with seatbelts. It used to be that you had to stand on the curb with your arm out like the Statue of Liberty, just waving at traffic. “Please! Someone! I have money and a destination!” And the taxis would just drive by. Sometimes they’d slow down just enough to let you experience hope before crushing it. You’d make eye contact with the driver. He’d look at you, look through you, and drive right past. And if it rained? You were done. Some cab would blast through a puddle and soak you like you’re Carrie Bradshaw in Sex and the City. Now you press a button and a tiny map shows you a little car cartoon coming toward you. You get in, you get out. Start to finish, it’s frictionless. And to top it off, you even get rewarded for it. Just by using a business profile, you can earn Lyft Credits and extra travel points or miles on rides your company is already paying for. George Clooney said it best in Up In The Air, “I don’t spend a nickel if I can help it unless it somehow benefits my mileage account.” Your company is spending the nickel. You might as well get the miles. CEO Dom Dragisich can claim a win in budget hotels, with Choice recently outperforming the industry average. But upscale brands grew at a much lower pace than the industry averages.

Choice Hotels' budget brands outpaced their U.S. industrywide benchmark in the summer, offering an early sign of progress for CEO Dominic Dragisich. But the company's higher-priced brands continued to lag.

U.S. revenue per available room (RevPAR) grew 3.8%, roughly a 1.5 percentage points above Wall Street's forecast. Dragisich said on a Monday earnings call that October's RevPAR was about 7%.

Dragisich's core problem in August was that Choice trailed in every price tier where it competes, from economy to upscale, according to CoStar data. The third quarter improved the picture without erasing it.

"We did narrow the gap," Dragisich said, referring to Choice's performance relative to industry averages.

Choice Hotels' third-quarter results gave CEO Dominic Dragisich an early sign of progress at the low end of the portfolio and little else. U.S. RevPAR rose 3.8%, about 1.5 percentage points ahead of Wall Street's forecast, and Dragisich said October RevPAR came in around 7%. But the gains were uneven: Choice's economy brands grew RevPAR 3.5% against an industry figure of about 2.5%, while its upscale and above brands grew just 1.1% against a roughly 4% industry average, and midscale and upper-midscale grew 3.6% against about 4.5%, according to Truist Securities citing CoStar data. Truist analysts C. Patrick Scholes and Gregory Miller wrote that the result implies Choice continues to lose market share, estimating fair share would have been closer to 5% to 6% growth. The U.S. hotel sector overall grew RevPAR 7% in the quarter, according to CBRE. Choice's room count is roughly flat year over year, and Dragisich said he wants net room growth of 2% to 4%. The company took a $24 million charge to terminate an option to acquire an unnamed European hospitality business after the option "eventually migrated to an obligation" and the target's growth became more lease-based. Choice said it is prioritizing organic growth, bought RV membership club Harvest Hosts for about $130 million on October 1, and sold two owned hotels for about $34 million in net proceeds while keeping the franchise agreements, leaving 17 owned hotels.

#6192. Marriott Earnings Call: New Upgrade List Encourages Elites To Pay For Better Rooms—But Puts Its Credit Card Cash Cow At Risk

Marriott earned $794 million in the third quarter, up from $728 million a year ago. They’re doing well. At the same time, I’ve been covering reports of layoffs in the customer service teams guests turn to when hotels won’t honor benefits. And on their earnings call, Marriott explained that its new elite upgrade list is being designed to preserve owners’ ability to sell upgrades. The company is getting better at monetizing Bonvoy. More than half its fee growth came from credit cards. But they’re spending down the trust that makes the program worth something in the first place. The hotel business has been good, outside of pockets like the Mideast. Marriott’s revenue per available room rose 6.5%. Adjusted earnings per share rose from $2.47 to $3.02, beating the $2.84 analysts expected. Marriott’s quarterly filing identifies $68 million in additional credit card fees compared with the same quarter last year. More than half of the increase in franchise fees comes from cards. Third Quarter Fee Growth   Increase   Share From Higher Card Fees Franchise fees   $131 million   52% Total gross fees   $184 million   37% I’ve covered owners’ unhappiness with these economics. Fifty-one owners representing about 1,000 hotels demanded better compensation for award stays. They’re supplying the rooms, Marriott sells them at a discount to Chase and American Express customers. The basic hotel loyalty bargain is a loop. Hotels pay into a program that rewards guests for stays. Those guests redeem points for more stays. Owners supply discounted award nights in exchange for a program that encourages customers to choose their hotels. A vacant room is cheap to give away. When an award guest doesn’t displace a paying customer, the hotel’s cost is mostly cleaning, utilities and whatever benefits it provides. Deep discounts make sense. But Marriott selling the points through Chase and American Express, using access to those discounted nights to monetize the owners’ inventory, infuriates some of them. As I’ve explained about bank payments for rewards, Marriott’s reported card fees aren’t everything the banks pay. Some money funds points and benefits. Some pays Marriott for licensing its brand and customer access. On the earnings call, Marriott pointed to the ways they’re appeasing owners: lower fees for Bonvoy higher reimbursement on high-demand award nights more flexible renovation requirements (letting owners allow the product to slip) a guest recommendation incentive. Marriott discussed its new upgrade lists. I covered the beta last month. Members can see their place in line and an estimate of upgrades matching their reservation. CEO Anthony Capuano told investors the feature would provide that visibility “while still preserving premium room upsell opportunities for our owners.” Showing you a position on a list doesn’t commit a room to you. A hotel can keep selling premium rooms while guests wait for complimentary upgrades. The later it commits the room, the longer it has to find someone willing to pay. Marriott hasn’t explained the beta’s inventory or clearance rules. They’re promising more visibility, but they aren’t saying hotels will release more rooms or confirm upgrades earlier. People who are lower on the list – and therefore less likely to get a free upgrade – become motivated to buy the upsell. Which, in turn, means fewer upgrade rooms available even at the top of the list. I’ve already described where Marriott’s technology investment is headed: selling room attributes and extras that guests used to receive as part of their stay or status. Better views, room locations and upgrades are going to become new opportunities for revenue generation. Selling a premium room is perfectly reasonable. But Bonvoy also encourages guests to concentrate their stays and spending to earn upgrades. And they’ll sell those same upgrades back to lower-tier elites for tens of dollars – prioritizing minor ducats over long-term value. Meanwhile, Capuano trumpeted 309 million Bonvoy members. I’m amazed anyone keeps repeating these enrollment numbers seriously. It means a guest signed up to get a lower (member) room rate. That tells us they wanted to pay less for the reservation they were already making. It says nothing about interest in Bonvoy or continued engagement. And the numbers are large because Marriott has a lot of hotels and rooms. I’ve reported on employees signing guests up who don’t even know about it, alongside hotel incentives worth as much as $10,000 a month for enrollment performance. Marriott intentionally does not share active members When I wrote about Chris Buckner taking over Bonvoy, I argued that his biggest opportunity was getting hotels to deliver the benefits members had already earned. Marriott’s business depends on guests starting their hotel search with Marriott. The brand is supposed to stand for a consistent product, and Bonvoy is supposed to make the brand sticky. That’s what lets Marriott deliver customers to owners as “leads” and charge for access to them. The reservation system doesn’t have value to sell to owners if guests stop trusting the hotels it displays. An individual owner can save money by denying breakfast or an upgrade. The damage gets spread across the whole portfolio. That hotel benefits from shirking on the program, while the program loses value. That’s why Marriott is supposed to enforce its promises. Yet they rarely seem to! I covered a breakfast dispute where the hotel closed the guest’s case seven times before finally paying the $100 benefit guarantee the guest was clearly due. In Marriott’s system, the hotel becomes the judge of complaints against it. . At the same time, I’ve been covering reports of layoffs in the customer service teams guests turn to when hotels won’t honor benefits. And on their earnings call, Marriott explained that its new elite upgrade list is being designed to preserve owners’ ability to sell upgrades.

The company is getting better at monetizing Bonvoy. More than half its fee growth came from credit cards. But they’re spending down the trust that makes the program worth something in the first place.

The hotel business has been good, outside of pockets like the Mideast. Marriott’s revenue per available room rose 6.5%. Adjusted earnings per share rose from $2.47 to $3.02, beating the $2.84 analysts expected.

Marriott’s quarterly filing identifies $68 million in additional credit card fees compared with the same quarter last year. More than half of the increase in franchise fees comes from cards.

I’ve covered owners’ unhappiness with these economics. Fifty-one owners representing about 1,000 hotels demanded better compensation for award stays. They’re supplying the rooms, Marriott sells them at a discount to Chase and American Express customers.

The basic hotel loyalty bargain is a loop. Hotels pay into a program that rewards guests for stays. Those guests redeem points for more stays. Owners supply discounted award nights in exchange for a program that encourages customers to choose their hotels.

A vacant room is cheap to give away. When an award guest doesn’t displace a paying customer, the hotel’s cost is mostly cleaning, utilities and whatever benefits it provides. Deep discounts make sense. But Marriott selling the points through Chase and American Express, using access to those discounted nights to monetize the owners’ inventory, infuriates some of them.

As I’ve explained about bank payments for rewards, Marriott’s reported card fees aren’t everything the banks pay. Some money funds points and benefits. Some pays Marriott for licensing its brand and customer access.

On the earnings call, Marriott pointed to the ways they’re appeasing owners: lower fees for Bonvoy higher reimbursement on high-demand award nights more flexible renovation requirements (letting owners allow the product to slip) a guest recommendation incentive. Marriott discussed its new upgrade lists. I covered the beta last month. Members can see their place in line and an estimate of upgrades matching their reservation. CEO Anthony Capuano told investors the feature would provide that visibility “while still preserving premium room upsell opportunities for our owners.” Showing you a position on a list doesn’t commit a room to you. A hotel can keep selling premium rooms while guests wait for complimentary upgrades. The later it commits the room, the longer it has to find someone willing to pay. Marriott hasn’t explained the beta’s inventory or clearance rules. They’re promising more visibility, but they aren’t saying hotels will release more rooms or confirm upgrades earlier. People who are lower on the list – and therefore less likely to get a free upgrade – become motivated to buy the upsell. Which, in turn, means fewer upgrade rooms available even at the top of the list. I’ve already described where Marriott’s technology investment is headed: selling room attributes and extras that guests used to receive as part of their stay or status. Better views, room locations and upgrades are going to become new opportunities for revenue generation. Selling a premium room is perfectly reasonable. But Bonvoy also encourages guests to concentrate their stays and spending to earn upgrades. And they’ll sell those same upgrades back to lower-tier elites for tens of dollars – prioritizing minor ducats over long-term value. Meanwhile, Capuano trumpeted 309 million Bonvoy members. I’m amazed anyone keeps repeating these enrollment numbers seriously. It means a guest signed up to get a lower (member) room rate. That tells us they wanted to pay less for the reservation they were already making. It says nothing about interest in Bonvoy or continued engagement. And the numbers are large because Marriott has a lot of hotels and rooms. I’ve reported on employees signing guests up who don’t even know about it, alongside hotel incentives worth as much as $10,000 a month for enrollment performance. Marriott intentionally does not share active members When I wrote about Chris Buckner taking over Bonvoy, I argued that his biggest opportunity was getting hotels to deliver the benefits members had already earned. Marriott’s business depends on guests starting their hotel search with Marriott. The brand is supposed to stand for a consistent product, and Bonvoy is supposed to make the brand sticky. That’s what lets Marriott deliver customers to owners as “leads” and charge for access to them. The reservation system doesn’t have value to sell to owners if guests stop trusting the hotels it displays. An individual owner can save money by denying breakfast or an upgrade. The damage gets spread across the whole portfolio. That hotel benefits from shirking on the program, while the program loses value. That’s why Marriott is supposed to enforce its promises. Yet they rarely seem to! I covered a breakfast dispute where the hotel closed the guest’s case seven times before finally paying the $100 benefit guarantee the guest was clearly due. In Marriott’s system, the hotel becomes the judge of complaints against it. . Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. More About Gary »

So, they learned from Delta’s earnings calls to not literally say the quiet part out loud and be explicitly evil. (“We’re gonna price-gouge the sh*t outta our customers!”) Huh. Wild.

At many properties, you need to have a Bonvoy number to get complimentary internet. There would be less Bonvoy members if they didn’t do this.

Also, always use a VPN, so that Bonvoy isn’t building a profile on your internet history.

I may be one of the most infrequent travelers, but I still remember the moments I signed on encouraged by desk staff to SPG when staying at the Sheraton Boston. I was immediately upgraded to a mini suite and got take out from the Kon TIki off the lobby and enjoyed every minute of my stay. What I lack in travel (due to work, caregiving, and health issues of my own) I make up for in loyalty and I never voted as the Shareholder I became based on my visits since a teen to the new (then) Sheraton Toronto. I am devastated by the ignorance of one of the most valued aspects imo of Marriott buying out Starwood, which I, as a tiny shareholder did not endorse. Heartbreaking that they have managed to destroy what was such a wonderful program. THe stupidity was obvious when they trashed all of our SPG numbers and did not provide new membership cards, not to mention how imo the related AMEX card art was well, I was going to say ugly, but I will say it is unappealing.

Unfortunately that is the norm in the US! Screw the customer! Let the hotel deny anything they want. I don’t expect any upgrade as a Platinum in the US. My number one complaint is breakfast in a High-end Marriott ! When you pay 800-1K or more? You don’t want continental breakfast! You don’t want them to act like they are doing you a favor giving you a donut! Most of all after you have spent all that money becoming so called the customer they want……then Marriot do as little as they can for that loyalty

I used to play a game called Roller Coaster Tycoon. One time I built an amusement park, where nobody could leave. At first it worked great. Then the customers became more and more unhappy, and no new people came to my amusement park.

More seriously, goodwill is an asset. Over the short run, you can increase profits by monetizing assets. However, over the long run, that will cause the goodwill to depreciate significantly. Famous brands that have no value any more are everywhere.

I am lifetime Platinum (Titanium currently). However, Marriott’s tricky app (in terms of pricing and cancellation date) (as I commented previously), removal of the ability to add guests, and other unfriendly acts are causing me to book elsewhere often.

For example, I am planning to meet my girlfriend near LAX. The LAX Marriott would normally be a good choice. However, we are flying in on different itineraries. If my plane is delayed, she won’t be able to check in. Going to book elsewhere.

As a Starwood transfer and current Marriott Lifetime Titanium (1700+ nights) I’m very disappointed with Marriott/Bonvoy. One problem might be that Marriott gives away upper tier status just by holding credit cards. When you can reach upper tier status basically just by holding credit cards, of course that status is going to be worthless.

I actually just reread Gary’s “Marriott Names A New Bonvoy Boss From JetBlue And The Points Guy—Will He Make Hotels Honor Your Benefits?” that he linked to above. It was a pretty good read. I am at the point where I do not expect any of the benefits to be honored. Enough said.

The whole craziness with Marriott and its ongoing process of nickel and diming its customers who buy into its “loyalty” program (Bonvoy) reminds me quite a bit of the “Master of the House” scene in the musical “Les Miserables” in which the innkeeper continually gouges and shortchanges his guests (with unexpected extra charges for everything) … and publicly brags about it. What Marriott does (and increasingly other so-called hospitality companies do) is at best shameful. Marriott and the others are selling you are for the most part illusions and wishful thinking for your blind “loyalty.”

#6191. AI Is a Choice

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

The Narrow but Feasible Path to Collective Good

Alex Imas, Mohamed A. El-Erian, and James Manyika

Few technologies in history have matched the potential of artificial intelligence to transform the economic landscape in which they emerged. Deployed broadly and effectively, AI can make workers more efficient, enable more dynamic entrepreneurship, and lift economic growth, all of which could be necessary bulwarks against the powerful economic headwinds brought on by aging populations and mounting public debt. AI can also make possible revolutionary new advances in science and medicine and democratize access to knowledge once reserved for the select few.

But the acceleration of AI also carries risks. It could be applied in ways that displace workers, disrupt how students learn, create new bioweapons and cyberweapons, and strain current supplies of energy, water, and land. Compounding these challenges is a mismatch: the benefits of this new technology may take a long time to become visible and widespread. As with earlier transformations, such as the Industrial Revolution, people are likely to experience the disruptions that come from adopting AI before they feel its benefits. And whereas users directly feel the effects of tools like chatbots, some benefits that AI is indirectly making possible, including more accurate predictions of natural disasters and improved medical diagnoses, may not be perceived as owing to the technology at all.

Public opinion has already begun to turn against AI, especially in the United States. One of the main targets has been data centers, with polls showing that a significant majority of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. Opposition to data centers needed for the new AI economy now cuts across party lines and age groups. Numerous surveys have found that residents worry about data centers using too many resources, creating endless noise, and raising their utility bills, all while developers benefit from public subsidies at the communities’ expense.

Although some of these problems are local, they also reflect wider concerns about AI. Some leading figures in AI have no doubt contributed to this anxiety with dramatic warnings of a white-collar-job apocalypse and even the possibility that AI will lead to human extinction. These are real issues that must be understood and addressed, but the growing public pushback against AI also suggests a deeper distributional challenge: individuals, communities, and businesses are being asked to help shepherd a transformative and potentially unsettling new technology at a time when many citizens see its financial gains going to a few people whom they increasingly distrust. AI is now a major issue in American politics: candidates running in competitive elections, no matter which party they belong to, appear increasingly averse to being associated with support for AI.

These anxieties are understandable. AI adoption risks repeating the mistakes of globalization, which generated large and widely spread economic benefits but led to concentrated losses of jobs, growth, and industry in particular communities. Government support in response was insufficient or arrived too late. Although the economy gained overall from free trade, the political bargain failed to give affected workers and communities a credible stake in the gains, even as individuals benefited as consumers from lower prices. The result was a backlash that contributed to the protectionism and fragmentation that continue to plague today’s politics and society.

Turning AI’s capabilities into broadly shared and enduring prosperity requires more than investing in the technology itself. The central challenge of the AI era is coordination and cooperation across groups responsible for the many complementary investments that promote the adoption of AI, including technological diffusion, worker empowerment, firm reorganization, and infrastructure construction. Because these complementary investments must be made across different institutions and at different times, progress requires market mechanisms to encourage cooperation as well as coalitions among organizations, firms, workers, communities, and governments that can turn AI’s technological gains into widespread economic and social benefits. To borrow a concept from game theory, AI is a “cooperative game” in which the largest gains arise only when many groups coordinate, and those gains persist only when every group expects to do better as part of shared coalitions than outside them.

But coalition building requires trust, and public trust—particularly regarding technology and who benefits from it—has eroded. Grand promises of scientific and medical breakthroughs will not overcome deep-seated hostility. Durable cooperation requires giving affected groups a concrete stake in the opportunities and gains that AI generates rather than merely promising future benefits. Without that stake, the individuals and groups whose support is needed to make AI flourish could block its progress. Governments could impose stifling regulations on the industry or stop issuing data center permits, firms could decline to adopt new AI-driven systems, and workers could avoid sharing the tacit knowledge needed to make the technology useful. As the economist and Nobel Prize laureate Michael Spence once observed: “You cannot solve a cooperative game uncooperatively.” The way to ensure that society benefits from AI’s enormous potential while mitigating its risks is to make cooperation the clear choice.

AI is staking a claim to being the next general-purpose technology—one that applies across a wide array of activities, improves over time, and generates complementary innovations. Electricity was an early general-purpose technology. When inventors discovered how to commercially harness electricity in the late nineteenth century, the ability to use it to power many types of machines transformed industrial production. Computing, another general-purpose technology, used electricity to process information itself, revolutionizing sectors as varied as engineering and health care.

But AI works through a more powerful input—intelligence—which makes it possible to interpret information, predict outcomes, diagnose problems, communicate with others, and make decisions. As a result, AI can raise productivity in existing sectors: a nurse can spend less time on paperwork and devote more time to patients, engineers can more quickly develop new designs, and small firms can scale up their analytics capabilities to compete with larger competitors. It can also increase efficiency so significantly that it makes possible wholly new products and services that were otherwise too costly or complicated to deliver.

AI also goes beyond existing general-purpose technologies by transforming the process of research and discovery. By inventing new ways of optimizing scientific processes, AI opens up previously unknown possibilities, similar to what microscopes and telescopes did in earlier eras. AlphaFold, a specialized AI model for which Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared half the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is a clear example. Determining a single protein’s three-dimensional structure from its amino acid sequence used to take months or even years; by using machine learning, AlphaFold has predicted the structures of more than 200 million proteins, fundamentally reshaping what biologists are able to investigate.

The potential of AI is thus a combination of the Industrial Revolution, whose general-purpose technologies transformed production, and the Enlightenment, which brought about inventions for making inventions—the new instruments and new paradigms that transformed the process of discovery. AI holds the promise of providing both the productivity boost and the tools to pave the way for discoveries that can address many of the problems weighing down aging, debt-ridden societies across the world.

The latest wave of AI has diffused at unprecedented speed. Google’s Gemini app and OpenAI’s ChatGPT each now reach more than one billion monthly users. Google’s AI & Economy ATLAS, a study of how people are using the company’s AI products that two of us (Imas and Manyika) worked on, analyzed 15 million interactions in more than 150 countries. It found that AI was used in tasks in 68 percent of occupations, and these occupations made up roughly 90 percent of all U.S. employment. Even automotive technicians and industrial mechanics used AI to interpret test results and diagnose electrical faults. Another study that two of us (Imas and Manyika) ran in collaboration with MIT FutureTech found that nearly half the scientists who were surveyed used some type of AI model every day, saving them time and enabling more interdisciplinary research.

But the gains of diffusion are neither guaranteed nor automatic. AI has been adopted broadly across and within sectors, but thus far its penetration remains fairly shallow. The ATLAS study found that only 21 percent of tasks in a typical occupation have been substantially affected by the technology. According to the Anthropic Economic Index, which measures how the AI model Claude is used in workplace tasks as varied as writing software, analyzing data, and managing administrative workflows, potential use far exceeds actual use. This suggests that access has spread much faster than adoption. Incorporating AI deeply enough to allow it to live up to its potential requires a bigger transformation. A firm does not change how it operates simply by buying access to an AI coding agent. It must also invest in organizational reforms and worker training and often needs to redesign its governance structure or its product lines.

The banking sector, for example, has widely adopted AI but mostly used it to perform superficial tasks. As it is currently deployed, AI gives analysts a faster way to research companies, populate spreadsheets, and identify the sources of investment returns. Deep adoption, on the other hand, requires changing workflows and job responsibilities. A bank must decide what proprietary data to feed a model, how to protect client information, and how to verify the results of the AI models it uses. Junior employees may spend less time collecting information and more time interpreting it, forming ideas, and advising clients. But many tasks that AI can automate are also forms of training. Firms will therefore need to find ways for experienced employees to help younger colleagues acquire the skills the experienced employees once developed by producing the underlying analyses themselves.

The true economic promise of AI lies in deep and transformational adoption. This requires revamping organizational processes, preparing workers to capitalize on the new technology, and applying AI in ways that enhance productivity and innovation and improve consumer welfare. Innovations that increase output and can generate new products and services have not yet appeared at a meaningful scale. But there is enormous latent demand for many new products and services, including specialized services such as individualized tutoring, health care, and legal and financial assistance, and additional demand will emerge from completely new activities that technology will make possible. By fundamentally changing how work is done and what work can be done, AI can lower the cost of providing tailored products, making new opportunities economically viable. Serving demand that previously did not make economic sense adds new value to society rather than merely redistributing a fixed economic pie.

But enlarging the economic pie does not guarantee a smooth transition for every worker. As with globalization, the new demand that AI unlocks will not necessarily arise in the same jobs, sectors, or communities in which existing work is done. This potential mismatch risks major labor market disruption and political backlash. Public anxiety is already growing, especially among younger workers seeking entry-level positions that are the most likely to be automated by AI. One study by the Stanford economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen found that the employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in occupations most exposed to AI automation was 19 percent lower than it would have been if employment had grown at the same rate as occupations less exposed to AI disruption. Yet the overall effect of AI on jobs, including entry-level positions, remains uncertain. The Economist has estimated that AI has created around one million jobs in the United States but led to about 200,000 layoffs, and the gap between the unemployment rate among 20-to-24-year-olds and the overall unemployment rate is low compared with recent decades. Most likely, as one of us (Manyika) wrote with Spence in these pages, in 2023, some jobs will be lost, some will be gained, and many more will be permanently changed.

Harnessing AI’s potential to increase prosperity without destabilizing society requires coordination. In addition to AI companies making new models, products, and tools, infrastructure developers must build the physical systems such as data centers that underpin AI. Businesses need to supply data and drive the organizational transformation to deploy models at their full potential—not just for efficiency but also to expand existing products and services or create new ones. Employers must decide how these technologies will be used, how workflows will be transformed, and how to enable workers to be more productive. Workers have to adopt the technology and invest in learning AI-relevant skills. Local communities must provide the land for data centers and consent to the technology’s expansion. And governments need to set rules, fund foundational research, and provide social insurance to support and manage transitions for those whose work or livelihoods are displaced by AI.

Each of these groups bears unique costs, captures different shares of the benefits, answers to its own constituencies, and responds to distinct incentives. This also means that unless they coordinate—whether through market mechanisms or active cooperation—these groups could slow or block AI development. Firms might underinvest in organizational change and use AI only to cut costs rather than to expand revenues, workers might resist or slow down adoption, communities might block infrastructure, and governments might restrict development. Each action might make sense in isolation, but together they lead to a suboptimal outcome for society.

This is a classic cooperative game scenario in game theory: these groups can accomplish much more when they work in concert than when they act individually and without coordination. A coalition with a common goal does not need to be a formal organization; it can be any grouping of actors who operate in ways that allow them to coordinate decisions and contribute resources to a shared project through contracts, policies, standards, investment commitments, or political bargains. Each possible coalition can generate more growth and economic value by promoting the adoption and diffusion of AI than any one actor can by operating separately.

In an ideal world, all these actors would form a single “grand coalition” to capture as much value from AI as possible. Their complementary actions and active coordination to promote AI would kick off a virtuous cycle in which wider adoption would spur advancements that would make AI more useful for society, unlock new demand and productivity growth, and encourage more people, communities, and companies to adopt the technology and support its expansion.

Such a grand coalition, however, is a benchmark rather than a blueprint. Progress is not all or nothing; smaller, more focused coalitions can still create economic and social gains that far outweigh what each actor could achieve alone. What is needed is a stable coalition—one in which no participant or group of participants can do better by leaving and doing something on their own. In the AI economy, exiting the coalition does not mean building a rival AI system. It simply means exercising a veto on increased AI use, which could take the form of imposing a local moratorium on data centers, resisting workplace adoption of AI, or blocking new regulations that encourage AI development. Because the withdrawal of any one participant would destroy more value than that participant could ever capture alone, it is critical that every essential group prefers being inside the coalition to being outside it.

A crucial question, then, is how to share the gains of working together so that cooperation remains stable over time and no coalition member wants to leave. In the case of AI, one factor that can help drive cooperation is that the technology creates conditions for what economists call a “convex game”: because the inputs to AI are complementary, each new participant makes everyone else’s contribution more valuable, causing the gains from joining the coalition to increase at an accelerating rate. Building better computing infrastructure, for instance, makes AI models and tools more capable; more capable models and tools increase the benefits for companies that want to invest in transforming their organizational processes and retraining workers, which increases productivity and spurs innovation; and wider adoption of AI in the workplace drives the need for additional computing power, which creates incentives for more infrastructure providers to build. Once a core group starts working together, the next actor that wants to join has even more to gain.

Prices, contracts, and incentives are indispensable for building a stable coalition, and market design and competition provide the architecture that enables coordination. But markets alone will not be enough. In the case of AI, the various costs and benefits will not unfold on the same timelines for all participants; some of them will benefit long before others catch up. Public institutions are necessary. Only policymakers, for instance, can create the common rules that will allow frontier labs in the coalition to coordinate on making AI safer, and only policymakers can provide enough support for workers to adapt to the AI economy. The bitter experiences that many workers and communities felt during globalization have made coalition building harder yet even more necessary.

A workable coalition does not need to bring every participant to the same negotiating table. A national bargain can establish common terms and align incentives on issues such as AI safety standards, workforce transition support, and infrastructure permitting, and smaller agreements at workplaces and in local communities can bring needed groups on board to cooperate. At both levels, the principle is the same: each group must receive a credible stake in the upside of the economic gains that the coalition creates through the overall growth of AI.

At the national level, cooperation should focus on the groups whose participation will determine whether AI technology can scale enough to generate massive economic gains. This includes the federal government, leading labs, major infrastructure builders and providers, organized labor, and large firms deploying AI. Big business matters because its use of technology and its investments in the workforce create demand that fuels the entire supply chain. Labor organizations will want to negotiate favorable terms for workforce transition, such as expanded unemployment and wage insurance, as well as for retraining; a lack of participation from organized labor will deprive the coalition of the support needed to facilitate adoption, especially in sectors such as construction in which unions have more power. For critical infrastructure, including power grids, telecommunications networks, and payment systems, the priority needs to be cybersecurity and reliability: before they integrate AI deeply into core operations, infrastructure providers need to believe that more capable models will not expose them to catastrophic risk.

The government can establish a predictable, risk-based regulatory framework to set clear standards in potentially dangerous areas such as biosecurity and to help coordinate the testing of advanced AI systems. A national framework would preempt a fragmented patchwork of idiosyncratic state-by-state bans on low-risk commercial uses of AI. Policymakers can also support AI development by funding research on foundational questions in artificial intelligence and increasing immigration and visa pathways for highly skilled workers to attract top global talent to U.S. labs. AI model and application developers, meanwhile, can participate in safety testing, and companies building out AI capacity can make available more computing power to small businesses, nonprofits, and local governments. Infrastructure providers can construct new data centers and show their support for the communities they work in by implementing ratepayer protections and paying local taxes, and large companies can invest in worker training, organizational transformation, and new business models. Finally, organized labor can supply the skilled employees needed to build the physical infrastructure underlying AI adoption, help redesign organizational workflows within companies, and lend its political weight to promoting AI nationally.

Each group benefits more than it is expected to contribute. AI model and application developers and infrastructure providers gain a predictable development path and a skilled workforce. Large firms have access to the support they need to more deeply adopt AI and improve their productivity. Workers gain new opportunities and job security during the economic transition. Washington also stands to benefit as the economy grows and the United States maintains its global technological leadership.

AI model developers and other companies in the AI ecosystem are already working together to diffuse AI more widely. Leading developers, including Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, along with partner organizations, have embedded engineers inside large organizations to identify valuable uses of AI, redesign workflows, and integrate new technology systems into production. These efforts recognize that model access is not enough: adoption requires technical assistance, organizational knowledge, and sustained engagement. A coalition can extend this capacity to smaller firms, schools, clinics, and municipalities. For AI model and application developers, supporting diffusion expands the market and provides insurance against potential political backlash. Only if the gains of AI adoption are shared with a broad swath of organizations and the general public will citizens support the expansion of the technology in society.

Frameworks for coalition building with labor groups are also emerging. Rather than working with individual firms to sign bespoke agreements, technology developers, industry associations, and policymakers are supporting worker cooperation through existing unions, apprenticeships, and retraining programs. The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, for example, is mobilizing its members to oppose data center moratoriums while calling for better labor agreements. Google is working with the IBEW’s partner organizations to train 100,000 electrical workers and 30,000 apprentices, giving workers access to well-paid jobs and providing developers with a source of skilled labor and the political support needed to build.

At the local level, new data centers may impose concentrated costs on communities even when they create national benefits for AI users. Developers should therefore negotiate agreements that protect ratepayers and provide tangible benefits for communities through increased local revenue, better infrastructure, and more employment opportunities. Templates for how to do this are taking shape in many U.S. states. Leading AI companies and “hyperscalers,” including Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, have signed on to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a voluntary commitment to pay the full cost of new power generation and grid upgrades in areas where they are building data centers so that household electricity bills do not rise. These companies are also funding local workforce programs and water-restoration projects and contributing property tax revenue that will allow communities to pay for new schools and roads.

The economic benefits that AI brings will increase the stability of emerging coalitions as long as they are shared. The distribution of benefits does not need to be equal, but for groups providing complementary inputs, benefits must be apportioned according to what each group contributes and also be adjusted as the technology evolves. In practice, determining each group’s contribution is not an exact science but an ongoing structured negotiation: tools such as utility tariffs, labor agreements, and enabling policies can allocate benefits in ways that reflect the role of different groups in supporting AI expansion and adoption. The share of the upside that each coalition member receives must be large enough to make participation more attractive than obstruction. Giving key players a real stake in the economic surplus that is generated is how those who might have been potential impediments to AI become participants in, and perhaps even advocates for, the expanded use of this new technology.

Where AI substitutes for existing tasks rather than complementing them, policymakers can also learn from what went wrong with globalization. Public programs to help displaced workers can be effective, but they must be accessible enough to provide support when technological disruption occurs. Targeted parts of the federal government’s Trade Adjustment Assistance program to compensate and retrain workers affected by globalization succeeded where they were put in place—research by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that eligibility for wage insurance under the program increased reemployment, shortened the amount of time out of work, and raised cumulative earnings—but it reached only a small portion of workers. Other research found that most support was provided through disability benefits that required workers to permanently exit the labor force. With AI, policymakers will need to set up expanded wage and unemployment insurance programs and support employer-led retraining programs that help workers transition into in-demand roles before displacement occurs rather than improvise after workers begin to suffer.

A coalition does not need to be built all at once. Cooperation should start in areas in which complementary benefits are clearest and participation constraints are easiest to identify, including promoting AI adoption and worker training in particular sectors such as health care or skilled trades, and encouraging support for new data centers. At the national level, safety cooperation can grow out of partnerships between coalitions and the government. Because AI’s development trajectory remains uncertain, cooperation agreements should center on investments that could pay out across multiple plausible scenarios and can be revised as the trajectory of AI becomes clearer.

International cooperation can grow in the same way. Although AI may well eventually require cooperation among adversaries and allies alike, Washington can start by forming a U.S.-led coalition built around trusted partners willing to accept common safety and security standards. The United States could, for example, set up a coalition among trusted partners that agrees on principles and frameworks in exchange for access to technology and cooperation. This coalition will naturally widen as its terms prove workable and more countries see the benefits of participating. It could eventually include China, which, given its advanced AI capabilities, is critical to addressing AI safety issues; this will require navigating complex questions of alignment and verification, however, including how to set up trusted validation bodies and mechanisms.

The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision provides an instructive example of international cooperation. It began in 1974 as a small forum among national regulators in 12 advanced industrialized countries and over time developed common standards for how to supervise banks around the world without empowering an imposing supranational authority, expanding its scope as those standards proved valuable. The Basel Committee was the seed for what is now the dominant international architecture that identifies and minimizes the risks of financial instability, including setting standards for how much capital banks need to hold and how to classify the riskiness of securities held on banks’ balance sheets. A future coalition for AI standards could grow through the same combination of clear entry conditions and credible commitments that have made the Basel Committee and the International Organization for Standardization, which publishes voluntary technical standards, successful.

Harnessing the potential of AI will not be easy. Critics will immediately jump to the conclusion that there are many reasons why such coalitions will not work in practice. Labs might decide that they can earn more on their own, incumbent firms might try to convert cooperation into tools to protect their market share, and governments might promise support for workers and communities and fail to deliver, as was the case with globalization.

But there is reason to be cautiously optimistic about cooperation in the age of AI. Because the technology is still relatively early in its development, it is possible to identify the groups needed to initiate cooperation, and labs, governments, communities, employers, and labor organizations have already shown interest in different parts of the bargain. Ultimately, society does not need to choose between innovation and shared prosperity. The two can be complements: cooperation will drive growth, and sharing the gains of such growth will sustain the cooperation needed to keep it going.

ALEX IMAS is Director of AGI Economics at Google DeepMind and Roger L. and Rachel M. Goetz Professor of Behavioral Science, Economics, and Applied AI at the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business.

MOHAMED A. EL-ERIAN is Rene M. Kern Professor of Practice at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, Chief Economic Adviser at Allianz, and Chair of the Board of Directors of the Center for Global Development.

JAMES MANYIKA is Senior Vice President at Google Alphabet and its President of Research, Labs, Technology, and Society. He is a Distinguished Fellow at Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute and a Visiting Professor at the University of Oxford’s Blavatnik School of Government.

#6190. Skift Commerce Summit 2026: Five Decisions in the Room

AI agents are here. Travel isn’t ready. Decisions made today will determine who controls the booking, the customer relationship, and the economics of travel commerce.

AI agents are already booking travel. One invite-only booking agent reported more than $1 billion a year in transaction volume, half of which was travel. Investors have already placed their bets on who wins and who loses. Most travel companies are still built for a traveler who searches, scrolls, and clicks.

Direct or third-party distribution used to be the primary choice travel suppliers had to make. Now an agent may decide which brands show up, which system can complete the booking, which card pays, and which loyalty program earns. Hotels alone spend more than $105 billion a year on distribution, and AI companies want a share of it.

The agents are here. Travel is not ready. Travel companies have to connect the dots inside the new travel commerce stack, and Skift Commerce Summit brings senior commerce leaders together around five decisions travel companies have to make now.

Operator Ticket $275 · for the people who run commerce at travel companies. Vendor Ticket $1,500 · capped, limited supply. Group rates: events@skift.com

AI has moved quickly into the travel customer journey for inspiration and planning, but not booking… yet. According to Skift Research, direct suppliers lead with a 49% net comfort score, followed by packaged tours at 37%, travel agents at 34%, loyalty portals at 31%, and OTAs at 20%. AI and chatbots score -7%. [1]

However, Skift Research describes the discovery path shifting from “search-scroll-compare” toward “ask-shortlist-decide.” As soon as travelers gain confidence in booking through AI platforms, space for brands “on the shelf” is poised to shrink. [2]

Hotels, airlines, or other travel retailers are racing to optimize for AI discoverability, but the more control they give to AI platforms, the more they risk losing direct customer relationships. They have to decide how to prioritize what they value most, and whether distribution alone is worth it if they become interchangeable within someone else’s interface.

Travelers are comfortable booking across a wide range of channels, but that also means today’s marketplace has a wider swath of competitors.

Travel’s AI discussion is moving downstream. It’s not only a customer relationship question, but also a technological one. Even if they’re discovered, booked, and integrated into the loyalty ecosystem, brands have to ensure the infrastructure works when an AI agent starts to handle trip management.

It’s one thing for an AI assistant to drive traffic to a brand’s site. The open decision is whether travel companies find it worthwhile to give an agent the tools to compare offers, change or cancel an order, and fix problems on the traveler’s behalf.

A better conversational front end can’t compensate for fragmented inventory, legacy servicing systems, or commerce technology designed for humans.

Banks, card issuers, retailers, membership programs, and technology platforms have built businesses around the traveler without having to own (or even sell) an airline seat or hotel room. They can make money from payments, rewards, subscriptions, advertising, financing, and the broader customer relationship surrounding a trip.

That changes the competitive economics for travel companies. A bank can use travel to increase card spend. A membership business can use it to make a subscription more valuable. A technology platform can influence the purchase while monetizing the customer elsewhere. These companies can compete for the same traveler without depending on the booking itself for most of their economics.

The decision is how much of that value suppliers and other travel-native companies can capture themselves as more of the commercial relationship moves into ecosystems built outside the industry.

Non-travel companies are profiting more and more off travel, stepping in to sell ancillaries and earn loyalty. 32% of travelers rank credit-card or bank loyalty programs as the most rewarding, ahead of hotel programs at 26% and airline programs at 20%. [1]

The direct-versus-third-party debate has shaped travel distribution strategy for decades. The economics have never been as simple as choosing one side. A direct booking can carry marketing, loyalty, technology, and acquisition costs of its own. An intermediary can bring incremental demand, reach a customer the brand would not have acquired directly, or fill inventory that otherwise would have gone unsold.

The channel mix is also getting more crowded. OTAs remain important, but banks, credit-card programs, membership platforms, social channels, AI interfaces, and other partners are creating new paths to the customer. Each comes with different costs, different access to customer data, and a different ability to generate demand.

The decision is which channels produce the strongest return for a particular customer, market, and trip. The best distribution strategy may use direct channels to deepen valuable customer relationships while paying intermediaries when they can deliver demand more efficiently than the brand can acquire it on its own.

“The competition to be a travel distributor has never been this intense,” says Skift Research, pointing to credit cards, social platforms, AI-native tools, OTAs, and suppliers all competing for a larger role in the booking journey. [3]

Travel companies can find unique growth opportunities by leveraging an existing customer base, brand, asset, or operating capability to create a new revenue stream. The challenge occurs when they find themselves wading into businesses they were not originally built to run.

The decision is how far that expansion should go. Some adjacencies strengthen the core business because they use capabilities the company already has. Others require new technology, operations, capital, or customer behavior that the company has never had to manage before. Growth can create leverage. It can also create complexity faster than revenue.

A Skift and ZS survey found that 75% of senior travel executives have non-core assets they can monetize, but only 32% described their current approach to doing so as “very” innovative. [4]

Discovery no longer guarantees ownership. Distribution extends beyond an OTA or supplier website and, indeed, beyond travel-native companies themselves. Payments and loyalty can generate value beyond the booking. AI is becoming another intermediary, another channel, and eventually the buyer itself.

Every travel company now faces the same question: which parts of the customer relationship, the transaction and the economics do you need to own before an agent stands between you and the traveler, and which can sit on someone else’s platform?

The Skift Commerce Summit is built to help you answer it, and to show you where your company is least ready.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.
