#6189. Oneworld Explains The Money Behind Your Lounge Access—And Why Credit Cards Help Decide Where Airlines Fly

Historically, if I used Royal Jordanian status to enter an American Airlines lounge while flying American, Royal Jordanian didn’t get a bill. American was carrying me and bore the lounge cost. In a new interview, oneworld’s commercial chief describes a payment model that sounds like that arrangement may still apply, despite reporting that says the rules changed. Who pays for your lounge visit helps explain why airline alliances are so difficult to run. The airline that gives you status, the one selling you a ticket, and the one providing your benefits can all be different. Each wants the customer and the revenue, and they have to agree on who picks up the costs. Roger Blackburn, oneworld’s Vice President of Commercial and Loyalty, and Gilbert Ott, its Director of Loyalty (and former blogger of God Save the Points), talk about how this works in an unusually candid interview. It’s essentially herding cats, with airlines that compete for the same customers promising to take care of each other’s passengers. Blackburn explains that a lounge hosting another airline’s passenger gets paid by: …the airline who’s … lifting that customer out of the station. At least that’s how our model works. One Mile at a Time has said its understanding is that this changed, and that the program providing status now pays when status is the reason someone gets in. This affects the economics of status matches, for instance. An airline offering status to someone who mostly flies its partners has a very different cost calculation if it’s getting a bill for every lounge visit. The lack of billing was also a limiting factor on offering status matches (confined to a formula relative to the total size of the elite pool). Blackburn describes the lounge operator as delighted to have another airline’s passenger because they’re getting paid. That true when there are empty seats. When the lounge is full, another paid visit can make the experience worse for the airline’s own customers. I’ve written about American’s lounge visits growing several times as fast as its passenger traffic. Better lounges encourage more people to use them, and to stay longer. Improving the product creates demand for more space. That’s also why Blackburn’s explanation of where oneworld builds its own lounges is helpful. They want airports served by enough member airlines to keep a lounge busy across the day. One airline might struggle to justify the rent and staffing for a single daily departure. Several airlines with departures at different times can share a better facility. Delhi and Mumbai come up in the conversation, and Blackburn hopes to have more lounge news “fairly soon.” The banks competing for that space also help pay for the airlines’ products. Ott argues that credit card and loyalty revenue supports better lounges, seats, food and inflight connectivity. He’s largely right, and the case goes further: credit cards support more flights. An airline becomes more attractive to cardmembers when it flies where they need to go. It also needs destinations they want to redeem their miles for. Delta has explicitly connected its growth in Austin and Raleigh with acquiring American Express card customers. A flight that looks weak based only on ticket revenue might make sense once you count the card spending it helps generate. As I discussed in my recent piece on Scott Kirby and credit card economics, a customer might choose an airline’s card because its Chicago schedule works for their business travel, then redeem the miles for Hawaii. Assign all the card revenue to Hawaii and you can end up cutting the flights that made someone want your card in the first place. A better seat and lounge help sell that relationship, too. And an alliance makes the card more useful by offering places to spend miles that the airline doesn’t fly to itself. Of course airlines can manage this badly. Sell more miles while planes are full, without making enough desirable award seats available, and customers wind up with growing balances they struggle to use. Sell more lounge access without adding enough capacity and the customer gets a line at the door. The alliance has to get its members to participate in making those benefits valuable. Asked whether oneworld should set minimum protections around changes to earning, status qualification and award availability, Ott describes the programs as largely sovereign and emphasizes a spirit of cooperation. Asked how much say the alliance has over the number of award seats a member releases, he calls it a collaborative process. I’d put it a different way: an alliance trying to influence airlines is pushing on a string. It’s the problem I’ve written about with airlines holding back their best awards from partners. They want to offer their members access to everyone else’s seats. But making their own best seats available can benefit another airline’s credit card business, while keeping those seats for their own members can help sell their own miles. Ott makes the case that a redemption can introduce someone to an airline and turn them into a valuable customer. That’s true as far as it goes, but those seats have an opportunity cost and getting the airline with the seat to value that speculative future business enough to release it (for a foreign customer who might not travel with them often and probably won’t take their credit card) can be a challenge. So can getting the partner buying the award seat to pay enough to make that worthwhile. Blackburn says oneworld is improving how quickly miles reach accounts following a flight across the alliance, with everyone expected on a new standard by the end of the year. He also says oneworld’s earlier artificial intelligence round the world booking assistant is gone, despite earlier claims of a fivefold increase in booking conversions. The interview returns to the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September, where I spoke about how artificial intelligence gives customers better tools to choose rewards programs. (The summit photo below is courtesy of oneworld.) Ott mentions verifying elite status without relying on screenshots that someone can easily manipulate. I saw a presentation at the summit for a product that was basically Plaid for airline status: the customer logged into their existing airline account to demonstrate their status to another company. I questioned whether airlines would allow that access to their systems. Who pays for your lounge visit helps explain why airline alliances are so difficult to run. The airline that gives you status, the one selling you a ticket, and the one providing your benefits can all be different. Each wants the customer and the revenue, and they have to agree on who picks up the costs.

Roger Blackburn, oneworld’s Vice President of Commercial and Loyalty, and Gilbert Ott, its Director of Loyalty (and former blogger of God Save the Points), talk about how this works in an unusually candid interview. It’s essentially herding cats, with airlines that compete for the same customers promising to take care of each other’s passengers.

Blackburn explains that a lounge hosting another airline’s passenger gets paid by:

…the airline who’s … lifting that customer out of the station. At least that’s how our model works.

One Mile at a Time has said its understanding is that this changed, and that the program providing status now pays when status is the reason someone gets in.

This affects the economics of status matches, for instance. An airline offering status to someone who mostly flies its partners has a very different cost calculation if it’s getting a bill for every lounge visit. The lack of billing was also a limiting factor on offering status matches (confined to a formula relative to the total size of the elite pool).

Blackburn describes the lounge operator as delighted to have another airline’s passenger because they’re getting paid. That true when there are empty seats. When the lounge is full, another paid visit can make the experience worse for the airline’s own customers.

I’ve written about American’s lounge visits growing several times as fast as its passenger traffic. Better lounges encourage more people to use them, and to stay longer. Improving the product creates demand for more space.

That’s also why Blackburn’s explanation of where oneworld builds its own lounges is helpful. They want airports served by enough member airlines to keep a lounge busy across the day. One airline might struggle to justify the rent and staffing for a single daily departure. Several airlines with departures at different times can share a better facility. Delhi and Mumbai come up in the conversation, and Blackburn hopes to have more lounge news “fairly soon.”

The banks competing for that space also help pay for the airlines’ products. Ott argues that credit card and loyalty revenue supports better lounges, seats, food and inflight connectivity. He’s largely right, and the case goes further: credit cards support more flights.

An airline becomes more attractive to cardmembers when it flies where they need to go. It also needs destinations they want to redeem their miles for. Delta has explicitly connected its growth in Austin and Raleigh with acquiring American Express card customers. A flight that looks weak based only on ticket revenue might make sense once you count the card spending it helps generate.

As I discussed in my recent piece on Scott Kirby and credit card economics, a customer might choose an airline’s card because its Chicago schedule works for their business travel, then redeem the miles for Hawaii. Assign all the card revenue to Hawaii and you can end up cutting the flights that made someone want your card in the first place.

A better seat and lounge help sell that relationship, too. And an alliance makes the card more useful by offering places to spend miles that the airline doesn’t fly to itself. Of course airlines can manage this badly. Sell more miles while planes are full, without making enough desirable award seats available, and customers wind up with growing balances they struggle to use. Sell more lounge access without adding enough capacity and the customer gets a line at the door.

The alliance has to get its members to participate in making those benefits valuable. Asked whether oneworld should set minimum protections around changes to earning, status qualification and award availability, Ott describes the programs as largely sovereign and emphasizes a spirit of cooperation. Asked how much say the alliance has over the number of award seats a member releases, he calls it a collaborative process. I’d put it a different way: an alliance trying to influence airlines is pushing on a string.

It’s the problem I’ve written about with airlines holding back their best awards from partners. They want to offer their members access to everyone else’s seats. But making their own best seats available can benefit another airline’s credit card business, while keeping those seats for their own members can help sell their own miles.

Ott makes the case that a redemption can introduce someone to an airline and turn them into a valuable customer. That’s true as far as it goes, but those seats have an opportunity cost and getting the airline with the seat to value that speculative future business enough to release it (for a foreign customer who might not travel with them often and probably won’t take their credit card) can be a challenge. So can getting the partner buying the award seat to pay enough to make that worthwhile.

Blackburn says oneworld is improving how quickly miles reach accounts following a flight across the alliance, with everyone expected on a new standard by the end of the year. He also says oneworld’s earlier artificial intelligence round the world booking assistant is gone, despite earlier claims of a fivefold increase in booking conversions.

The interview returns to the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September, where I spoke about how artificial intelligence gives customers better tools to choose rewards programs. (The summit photo below is courtesy of oneworld.)

Ott mentions verifying elite status without relying on screenshots that someone can easily manipulate. I saw a presentation at the summit for a product that was basically Plaid for airline status: the customer logged into their existing airline account to demonstrate their status to another company. I questioned whether airlines would allow that access to their systems.

#6188. DOJ faces ‘heavy lift’ in Alaska election appeal as separate criminal probe continues

Fox News contributor Josh Ritter joins 'Fox & Friends First' to sound off on the legal implications of the Justice Department's plans to appeal a court ruling dismissing its challenge to Alaska's Senate election certification.

The Justice Department faces an uphill legal battle in its bid to overturn a federal judge's dismissal of its Alaska Senate election lawsuit, according to legal experts who questioned whether the government can secure meaningful relief before voting ends Tuesday — even as a separate criminal investigation continues.

DOJ filed a notice of appeal after Obama-appointed U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed its lawsuit Sunday over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot. The judge ruled that federal officials lacked standing because they had not demonstrated how their proposed remedy could address potential voter confusion without compromising ballot secrecy.

With voting ending Tuesday, attorneys told Fox News Digital that even a successful appeal could leave the government scrambling to obtain an injunction or return to district court, while a defeat would leave the civil case dismissed without necessarily affecting potential criminal charges arising from the alleged recruitment of the second Sullivan.

"The federal judge dismissed on a procedural issue — standing," election attorney Jason Torchinsky of Virginia-based firm Holtzman Vogel told Fox News Digital. "So if the government were to prevail, it would either have to seek injunctive relief from the appeals court in the first instance, a very high bar, or go back down to the district court to seek relief."

"Given the time available between now and close of polls [Tuesday], this is a heavy lift for the government," Torchinsky added.

A reversal would not automatically change Alaska's election results. DOJ would still need to obtain specific judicial relief, potentially requiring further proceedings in district court.

Former federal prosecutor and ex-Pentagon official Cully Stimson similarly said that DOJ will have difficulty securing any immediate relief in its effort to pause the Sullivan-Peltola contest.

While Gleason was appointed by Obama, Stimson suggested the ruling did not appear partisan and said uncertainty remains because voting had not yet concluded.

"I'm not surprised that the judge did this. I don't think it would matter whether an Obama judge or any other judge appointed by any other president," Stimson told Fox News Digital.

"Asking for injunctive relief way before anything even happens is a reach," he said, adding Alaska falls under the San Francisco-based Ninth Circuit, which will hear any appeal.

But Stimson suggested DOJ may have a longer-term objective beyond winning an immediate injunction: establishing a legal record that could support further proceedings after the election, once the votes are counted.

TRUMP PROSECUTIONS UNDER BIDEN SET PRECEDENT FOR DOJ’S ALASKA ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE, EX-FEC CHAIR SAYS

Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images | Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"They may be filing these suits to establish a record and force Alaska and others supporting the status quo to defend what's happening, knowing that there's some level of confusion, and they have the legal wheels churning," he said. "So after the vote is [over], they've started the legal wheels rolling."

Former Assistant U.S. Attorney for North Florida Zack Smith added that if the Ninth Circuit does not hear the case promptly, DOJ could seek emergency review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

While the Alaska case is considered unprecedented, according to the experts, the idea of a Supreme Court expedition at election time is not.

On Dec. 9, 2000, one day after the Florida Supreme Court ordered a manual recount of disputed ballots in the Bush v. Gore presidential election dispute involving "hanging chads," then-Texas Gov. George W. Bush’s legal team successfully sought emergency intervention.

The court ultimately decided in Bush’s favor within a week.

Since the disputed 2000 election, which featured "hanging chads" on hole-punched paper ballots and the Brooks Brothers Riot at the Miami-Dade elections office, DOJ has become well-accustomed to the expedited-review process, the experts said.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S THREATS AGAINST ELECTION WORKERS AHEAD OF 2026 MIDTERMS

Dan J. Sullivan, who has filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, on June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press)

"DOJ is familiar with kind of working quickly, getting things to the Supreme Court, and so I wouldn't be completely surprised if you were to see something like that," Smith said.

Bush v. Gore offers a procedural parallel because federal courts were asked to intervene in the administration of a state-run election.

"Florida was conducting the election in the manner under Florida law, under this time, place and manners set out by Florida law even though it was a federal election," Stimson said. "They used a particular type of ballot, which had those so-called dangling chads, which were punch-holes that didn't come the whole way off, so the hole was left with a little tag, essentially like a skin tag, and eventually the Supreme Court of Florida ruled."

"But because there were federal violations, eventually the Supreme Court weighed in and stopped it. And at no point in time had the vice president’s (Albert Gore) vote count ever surpassed that of the governor (Bush) and because it was a federal interest, the Supreme Court stepped in and stopped this counting at the state level."

Alex Charns, an attorney who has argued in federal court, told Fox News Digital that the clock has run out and DOJ's goal of segregating ballots based on voter intent is no longer possible.

"I've litigated against the USDOJ for over thirteen years in federal court. I've practiced law in Durham, N.C., for 43 years. The USDOJ filed a case without legal merit and its appeal is likely to fail," he said.

"In addition, voting ends [Tuesday]. The relief they seek isn't possible — ballots already cast can't be segregated. Also, one cannot tell why any voter voted in a particular way. The appeal is unlikely to be successful."

Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, is seen against the Chugach Range. (Getty Images)

In a statement from the DOJ's "Rapid Response" (DOJ-RR) office, a spokesperson said the court "dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters."

"Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," DOJ-RR said, announcing their appeal.

Stimson cautioned that the outcome of the civil litigation would have little bearing on the separate criminal investigation, which could uncover evidence supporting additional legal action even if DOJ's appeal fails.

"As long as that criminal investigation is going on, you're not breathing easy," he said, adding that evidence uncovered by federal investigators could potentially provide grounds for a separate civil lawsuit.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

What if I told you that having a United credit card could mean the difference between paying 295,000 miles or just 72,000 miles for the exact same international business-class flight?

That's not a rare or theoretical example. It's a real award flight that a friend of mine was trying to book recently.

And while United's credit cards are currently offering welcome bonuses of up to 100,000 miles, there's another benefit that can be even more valuable long-term: Access to expanded saver award availability and dramatically lower award prices for eligible cardholders.

In fact, on some flights, the savings can quite literally be hundreds of thousands of miles per ticket.

Here's how it works — and why having a United credit card can make such a huge difference when it's time to redeem your miles.

A friend of mine was recently searching for business-class award flights from Geneva Airport (GVA) to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) for a trip next month. He knew United cardholders could access lower award prices, but he didn't have a United card, so he asked me to compare what we were seeing before deciding whether to apply.

As a non-cardholder, he was seeing business-class prices of 295,000 United miles per person, plus taxes and fees for the one-way trip from Geneva to Newark. That's a lot of miles when multiplied out for a family.

As a cardholder, I checked the same flights and saw a much lower price.

For the same business-class flights, my price was just 68,000 miles per person, plus taxes and fees.

That's 77% fewer miles for the same lie-flat seat on the same plane.

Now, I have United elite status in addition to a United credit card, which brings my award price down a little further. But even without elite status, someone with an eligible United credit card could book that flight for just 72,000 miles. That's a savings of 223,000 miles on a single one-way ticket.

Here's why the difference is so dramatic: The savings aren't simply the result of a 10% cardholder discount. Eligible United cardholders can also access expanded saver award availability, which can unlock significantly lower award prices on certain flights.

And this isn't just one route or one date.

I also searched for business-class award flights from my home airport of George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston to Sydney Airport (SYD) and quickly found a flight priced at 400,000 miles for someone without a United card.

The cardmember-only price? Just 85,000 miles, plus taxes and fees. That's a savings of 315,000 miles — or nearly 79% — on a single award ticket. Multiply it out by a family, and it gets even more incredible in a hurry.

Related: What it's like in United's new elevated business class

While lots of United award flights have really big savings like the examples above, not every flight will offer discounts that dramatic.

You'll always save at least 10% off qualifying United-operated award flights just by having a United card. That number jumps to at least 15% if you also have United elite status.

So, to give another real-world example, my family flies several times a year between George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston and Orlando International Airport (MCO).

On this example date, one-way flights were priced at either 15,000 or 21,000 United miles, depending on which flight I selected.

However, because I have the United card, those flights were priced at 12,700 miles instead of 15,000 miles, or 17,800 miles instead of 21,000 miles.

Those savings aren't as headline-grabbing as the first example, but for a family of four booking round-trip flights at those rates, the savings could add up to roughly 18,000 to 26,000 miles, depending on the flights selected.

Related: United's big mileage changes are now in effect

One thing I really love about this is that you don't need a premium United card with a high annual fee to unlock these award savings.

You can get the $0 annual fee United Gateway℠ Card (see rates and fees) and get savings, too.

If you have the United MileagePlus® Debit Rewards card or the $0 annual fee United credit card, you do have to spend $10,000 in eligible purchases on those cards in a calendar year to unlock the award discount.

For travelers who can meet that threshold through purchases they'd make anyway, the Gateway could provide a way to access lower award prices without paying an annual fee.

Another option is the United℠ Explorer Card (see rates and fees), which actually has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150 annually. Eligible Explorer cardholders can access the award discounts without meeting the Gateway's $10,000 spending requirement.

The information for the United MileagePlus Debit Rewards has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: 8 reasons to upgrade from the United Explorer Card to the United Quest Card

Beyond the ongoing award-booking savings, United's credit cards currently offer increased welcome bonuses, including some of the highest offers we've seen on these cards.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

United credit cards can offer more than bonus miles and travel perks. For eligible cardholders, access to expanded saver award availability and discounts on qualifying award flights can translate into substantial savings when redeeming MileagePlus miles.

Being able to save airline miles with a co-branded airline credit card isn't unique to United, as several airlines offer this valuable perk to their cardholders. However, the mileage savings you get with most cards and airlines are often capped at around 15%.

As the Geneva–Newark and Houston–Sydney examples show, the difference can sometimes amount to hundreds of thousands of miles on a single ticket. However, savings vary by flight, and not every cardholder automatically qualifies for these benefits.

Being able to take a lie-flat seat across the globe and make it cost in the neighborhood of 70,000-85,000 miles instead of 300,000-400,000 miles, just by having a credit card is exactly the kind of tip that brings award travel out of just the hands of a small few and puts it into the hands of many of us.

For travelers who regularly redeem United miles, these award-booking advantages could be among the most valuable reasons to carry an eligible United card.

Related: Which United credit card is right for you? Comparing the Explorer, Quest, Club and Business cards

#6186. The China Price

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

Beijing’s Green Path to Ending Dollar Dominance

In 1971, as the international monetary system was on the brink of collapse, U.S. Treasury Secretary John Connally told a group of worried European finance ministers that the dollar was “our currency, but your problem.” The dollar had become that system’s official reserve currency in 1944, under the Bretton Woods agreement, making signatories subject to the whims of U.S. monetary policy. Even after Bretton Woods collapsed and many currencies floated freely, the dollar continued to dominate. In the last half century, U.S. currency power has only expanded, as more countries have integrated into the global economy and therefore grown to depend on the dollar. China, reliant on export-driven growth, is foremost among them.

Reckoning with the possibility that Washington could someday make the dollar China’s problem, Beijing is now crafting its own solution. In a January 2024 speech, Chinese leader Xi Jinping made this effort explicit, instructing senior provincial and ministerial officials to accelerate China’s transformation into a “leading financial power.” A strong currency, he specified, was one of the essential foundations of that power. When Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, published the full text of the speech in 2026, the standard Xi had in mind became clearer: for a currency to be considered “strong,” it must be widely used in international trade, investment, and foreign exchange markets and be recognized as a global reserve currency.

Xi’s call is the latest episode in a long history of efforts by major powers to reduce their dependence on the dollar-centered global financial system. In 1965, French Finance Minister Valéry Giscard d’Estaing famously described the disproportionate advantages that dollar dominance confers on the United States as “exorbitant privilege”; the same year, France began aggressively converting a substantial share of its dollar reserves into gold, contributing to the collapse of the Bretton Woods system. In 1999, the Japanese government released a report on how to promote wider international use of the yen. That same year, the launch of the euro gave Europe what would become the world’s second most important international currency, affording it greater monetary autonomy even as the European Central Bank carefully danced around any suggestion that it might challenge the dollar.

What distinguishes Xi’s ambition is that China, unlike Europe or Japan, possesses the economic heft, military capability, and political will to rival the United States’ geopolitical power. Not since London commanded a global empire has another country’s currency stood a realistic chance of competing with the dollar. A global financial transition from “In God We Trust” to “Where the Party Leads, We Follow” can no longer be dismissed as fantasy.

The internationalization of the renminbi would afford China a measure of financial survivability should the United States ever choose to wield the dollar as a punitive weapon, as it did against Russia after the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. The United States controls both the supply of the dominant global reserve currency and many of the critical financial infrastructure chokepoints through which it circulates. Washington, if it so desired, could severely restrict China’s access to dollar liquidity by making the cost of doing business with Chinese institutions prohibitive, for example by indicting or sanctioning a major Chinese bank. Any such measure would shock the Chinese financial system, raise transaction costs for trade, and deliver a major competitive blow to China’s export sector, which accounts for roughly one-fifth of its GDP.

Survivability, however, is only a prerequisite for credible deterrence. To deter the United States from using the dollar weapon, Beijing requires a financial second-strike capability. It must be able to redirect a substantial share of global trade and finance to a renminbi-based network. The durability of that shift depends on healthy global demand for an anchor asset priced in renminbi. For China, the most likely source of such an anchor asset lies in its dominance of the green economy.

Xi does not necessarily want the renminbi to replace the dollar. His 2024 speech advocated strength, not hegemony. Placing a respectable second, or even a consequential third, would suffice to break the dollar’s effective monopoly and constrain the United States’ ability to impose financial sanctions unilaterally, while saving China the effort and cost of sustaining currency supremacy. From Beijing’s perspective, the mission is to establish the renminbi as the Pepsi to the dollar’s Coca-Cola: never the market leader, but serviceable in a pinch and more than capable of keeping the dominant incumbent honest.

The near-universal acceptance of the U.S. dollar arguably benefits China more than any other country. The Chinese economy relies on exports, and Chinese goods priced and financed in dollars can reach ready buyers almost anywhere. The resulting profits can then be invested almost anywhere and converted into liquid funds on short notice. This suits Beijing: China enjoys the benefits of global liquidity without bearing the burdens of sustaining it. To preserve the global dollar system, the United States must tolerate foreign ownership of an ever-expanding volume of dollar claims as countries conduct ever more business in the currency. U.S. markets are exposed to international volatility, and foreigners hold some influence over U.S. corporations. The Federal Reserve, which issues the dollar, backstops the system, expanding its balance sheet during periods of financial stress, when governments and private companies hoard dollars to ensure they can continue to pay their debts and buy goods. This openness and exposure has posed little threat to the U.S. economy because foreign shareholders have generally sought to operate within, rather than change, U.S. business norms, and U.S. banks have earned tidy profits intermediating the world’s capital flows through New York and London.

China’s leaders have no desire to make any such tradeoff. Maintaining a global renminbi system would be fundamentally at odds with China’s state-led economic model. For the renminbi to replicate the dollar’s functions, China would have to create broad, two-way financial channels through which foreign holders of renminbi could reinvest that money into the Chinese economy. The resulting capital inflows would fundamentally reshape China’s domestic financial markets. It would be impractical for Beijing to confine foreign investors to a narrow group of approved assets, as it does now. Once foreign investors were allowed into China’s markets in force, they would arbitrage the distortions created by financial repression and politically directed capital allocation. Such competition would undermine one of Beijing’s most effective means of securing the loyalty of China’s business class: controlling who gains access to capital, on what terms, and for what purposes.

For many wealthy Chinese citizens, including some members of the Communist Party itself, the dollar is an indispensable form of political risk insurance. Domestic political rivalries can lead to asset seizure or even imprisonment with little due process. Offshore dollar deposits and foreign corporate structures allow elites to diversify their holdings across currencies and jurisdictions. Control of a company listed overseas, especially in the United States, offers wealthy Chinese more than prestige and access to global capital; disclosure obligations, duties to shareholders, and international visibility, which extend beyond the party’s control, can give Chinese executives leverage against arbitrary demands from officials at home. These constraints cannot prevent interference by senior authorities determined to pursue their targets, but they can raise its cost, slow its implementation, and create room for negotiation. The dollar-based system is a refuge for Chinese elites who fall from grace, and because no one’s position is ever entirely secure, few wish to see that refuge disappear.

China is perfectly willing to go on living in a world that the dollar makes go round. But it cannot abide the dollar’s weaponization, and the renminbi still has a long way to go before it is strong enough to blunt that threat. If more countries and businesses are to adopt the renminbi, there must first be a global financial infrastructure for its use. China has already laid the foundation by facilitating renminbi use among firms in more than a hundred countries and across a growing array of commodity markets to settle transactions, obtain financing for trade and investment, and hedge their risks. Here, breadth matters far more than depth. Even modest daily volumes of renminbi transactions can keep payment channels operational, preserve financial relationships, and maintain the legal and administrative expertise needed to run an alternative financial system.

Because China’s relative economic strength lies in the flow of manufactured goods—it accounted for 20 percent of global manufactured exports in 2025—Beijing has concentrated its efforts on building a payment network that facilitates the commercial flows generated by its manufacturing machine. In 2005, Zhou Xiaochuan, then governor of the People’s Bank of China, publicly encouraged the already increasing use of local currencies among China’s trading partners. In 2009, the PBOC launched a pilot program for settling cross-border transactions in renminbi, followed in 2015 by the creation of the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, the backbone of China’s international renminbi network. CIPS began with 195 participants spanning 50 countries; by June 2026, it had 1,829 participants and could route payments to more than 5,200 banking institutions in 191 countries. But CIPS remains much smaller than the mature wholesale payment systems supporting the dollar and the euro. In 2025, the U.S.-based Clearing House Interbank Payments System processed an estimated 19 times as much value in international payments as CIPS, and Europe’s real-time gross settlement system, called T2, cleared about 14 times as much.

But payments alone are a misleading measure of currency power. An international transaction entails far more than a transfer of economic value; it requires a package of financial services that unfolds across five linked stages: pricing, financing, risk transfer, payment, and reinvestment. The dollar dominates international trade and finance because it is the default currency at every stage, with its strength in each reinforcing its position in all the others. For the renminbi to supplant the dollar, it would have to become competitive at every stage of the transaction cycle, not just in payments.

China’s leaders recognize that the influence of financial centers in London, New York, and Tokyo rests not only on their ability to move money but also on their institutions’ ability to create credit, set prices, insure shipments, and recycle savings. That is why Chinese state-owned enterprises are driving the expansion of the renminbi network. By denominating invoices, contracts, and overseas project financing in renminbi, these enterprises create a base of recurring demand for the currency around which Chinese banks, insurers, and other financial institutions can build competing business lines under Chinese control. To reinforce that base, the Communist Party laid out an action plan in 2025 that instructs state-owned enterprises to prioritize settlement in renminbi, rather than dollars, whenever they deal with foreign suppliers and customers. That strategy is already fostering a regional network for renminbi use in Southeast Asia. In 2024, renminbi payments involving economies in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations rose 19 percent, with two-thirds of those transactions occurring between ASEAN countries.

Beijing has largely completed the first phase of its strategy, establishing a foothold in payments, and it is now expanding upstream into pricing, financing, and risk transfer, and, cautiously, downstream into reinvestment. Only recently has Beijing begun to appreciate how much the currency in which goods are priced influences the subsequent stages of the transaction cycle. Historically, China has been content to price the goods it imports and exports mostly in dollars. According to International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates, only 6.5 percent of China’s exports were invoiced in renminbi in 2023. Chinese government statistics show that nearly 30 percent of China’s trade in goods is settled in renminbi, but much of that is essentially a dollar transaction masquerading as a renminbi one: Chinese exporters invoice in dollars, buyers obtain dollar funding and are debited in dollars, and the funds are converted into renminbi only just before reaching the mainland.

The government is seeking to reverse that pattern by promoting what it calls “China prices”: renminbi-denominated benchmark prices listed on local exchanges for major commodities that China imports. Greater autonomy over pricing means that Chinese firms can buy raw inputs and manage their exposure to commodity price swings in global markets without acquiring dollars. It also gives Chinese authorities greater influence over the reference prices used to set the terms of supply contracts for the physical delivery of those commodities. This leverage is vital for China because the steady flow of raw inputs is essential to the smooth running of its manufacturing machine.

Price autonomy matters especially for critical minerals, which feed the green industries that in Xi’s view are central to China’s economic future. China produces more than 80 percent of the world’s batteries and consumes over 75 percent of its lithium, 70 percent of its cobalt, and about 60 percent of its nickel. But the country’s position in global markets for each of these minerals does not yet reflect its dominance in production and consumption. To date, China has made the most progress in lithium; more than 90 percent of global trading in lithium-carbonate futures occurs on the Guangzhou Futures Exchange, where contracts are denominated in renminbi. In July, the exchange allowed foreign traders to trade the lithium-carbonate futures contract directly, announcing with fanfare that several overseas “leading enterprises” had joined the market. China is now poised, perhaps for the first time in modern history, to become the principal financial center for a globally important commodity. Nickel and cobalt, on the other hand, remain tied to dollar benchmarks in London and Chicago. Although China is the largest consumer of these two minerals, it is not yet the financial reference point for their markets. That is the sort of mismatch that the push for China prices is meant to resolve.

The financing stage of Beijing’s renminbi strategy is gaining momentum. In 2023, Beijing instructed Chinese financial institutions to expand their renminbi funding abroad. State-backed lenders such as the Export-Import Bank of China have increased their renminbi lending for overseas trade and infrastructure projects, and commercial banks increasingly supply renminbi trade finance. Between 2023 and mid-2026, Chinese financial institutions more than doubled their renminbi lending to overseas borrowers from 1.3 to 2.9 trillion yuan ($428 billion). The PBOC, for its part, has adopted currency swap agreements with 32 foreign central banks and monetary authorities, including those in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as the European Central Bank. In their early years, after the global financial crisis, these swap lines were largely symbolic and only lightly used, but in recent years, some have provided direct support for commercial activity. In 2025, Turkish companies borrowed four billion yuan ($557 million) to pay Chinese suppliers using a facility backed by a PBOC swap line, 70 percent more than they had borrowed a year earlier. This effort to turn the renminbi into a funding currency is starting to gain traction: in May 2026, the renminbi accounted for seven percent of the value of trade-finance messages on SWIFT, the leading global platform for exchanging payment instructions, up from 5.1 percent two years earlier and enough to overtake the euro for second place, although the dollar remained leagues ahead with an 82.5 percent share.

Beijing has also taken steps, if more modest ones, to increase the renminbi’s presence in markets for insurance and reinsurance. In 2025, Bank of China, a state-owned bank, and PICC, a state-owned property and casualty insurance company, developed new terms under which premiums and claims for cargo shipments could be settled in renminbi. The terms also specified Shanghai as the preferred venue for arbitration, part of a broader effort to shift the maritime-insurance market away from its traditional reliance on dollar settlement and English commercial law, long the standard framework for international shipping and maritime insurance contracts.

The final stage of the transaction cycle, reinvestment, completes the loop through which goods and value circulate through the global economy. Recipients of payment must decide what to do with the proceeds: hold them in a short-term account, invest them in longer-term assets, or convert them into another currency. A strong currency ecosystem becomes sustainable at scale only when recipients are willing to hold and reinvest their balances rather than routinely convert them.

Beijing has, over the past decade, given foreign holders of renminbi more ways to reinvest their balances. The Stock Connect and Bond Connect programs, which took their earliest forms in 2014 and 2017, respectively, have since expanded to allow a much broader mix of investors outside China to use renminbi to buy some mainland equities and bonds. Before these programs began, licensing and quotas restricted direct access to Chinese markets, with only about 228 large institutional investors receiving quotas in 2013; today, about 1,000 investors have that status. In 2025, foreign trading through Stock Connect averaged 212 billion yuan ($29.5 billion) per day, and Bond Connect averaged 39 billion yuan ($5.4 billion) per day. The tools available to manage the risks associated with these investments have also expanded. Swap Connect, launched in 2023, allows offshore investors to hedge against movements in onshore renminbi interest rates.

Access to China’s financial markets is no longer the biggest problem facing foreign investors, but the risk that Beijing’s unpredictable capital controls could someday trap their funds remains a worry. A 2023 survey by the Insurance Asset Management Association of China and J.P. Morgan Asset Management found that roughly two-thirds of chief investment officers at insurance companies outside China cited controls on capital moving in and out of the country as a top concern for investing there. Despite greater access than ever, foreign investors remain reluctant to hold Chinese assets at scale. In March 2026, they held only 3.2 trillion yuan ($448 billion), or 1.6 percent of the Chinese bond market, compared with roughly $15.5 trillion, or 27 percent, of the U.S. bond market. Reserve holdings recorded with the IMF reveal an even wider gap: in the first quarter of 2026, the renminbi accounted for just under two percent of global foreign-exchange reserves, compared with 57 percent for the dollar. Without a far larger pool of renminbi assets that foreigners can freely buy and sell, the renminbi cannot come close to replacing the dollar.

For China to wield anything approaching the currency power of the United States, the renminbi must dominate trade in a good that China controls and the rest of the world cannot easily do without. In the dollar system, the global oil trade has long played this role—hence the term “petrodollar.” In a renminbi-ascendant system, the corresponding anchor could be the critical minerals, clean energy equipment, and electrical infrastructure that are central to green energy technology. If China consolidates its dominance over that industrial ecosystem, using its scale and cost advantages to prevent competitors from catching up, it could gain enough leverage to price those essential, hard-to-substitute exports in renminbi, creating the foundation for a “green yuan” that might eventually replace the petrodollar.

China has spent decades methodically assembling the supply chains that have made it the world’s dominant producer of green energy technology and equipment. Beijing is now on the verge of taking a commanding position across a set of goods that the world has decided it cannot do without. China’s strategy rests on vertical integration of nearly the entire clean energy supply chain. It is the leading refiner of 19 of the 20 energy-related strategic minerals tracked by the International Energy Agency, with an average market share of 70 percent. It accounts for roughly 85 percent of global solar panel manufacturing capacity, and it supplies 78 percent of the wind-turbine capacity installed worldwide. In 2025, it produced about 70 percent of the world’s electric vehicles.

After decisively seizing the first-mover advantage, Beijing is now consolidating its market position, using economies of scale to undercut prospective rivals and promote technical standards built around technologies owned by Chinese firms. The green energy economy is more diffuse than the fossil fuel system it seeks to replace and therefore more difficult to command. But China is already beginning to turn its market-share lead into structural advantages that could lock out competitors and entrench its dominance.

Until recently, Beijing focused more on extending its industrial lead in green energy than on converting that advantage into financial power. But that is beginning to change. The proliferation of carbon-neutral investment mandates has unintentionally created a green finance industry almost tailor-made for China. In 2022, Beijing published its “Green Bond Principles,” which require green bond issuers to allocate 100 percent of proceeds to eligible green projects.

By the end of 2025, funds dedicated to sustainable investment were worth $4.13 trillion worldwide, and assets managed according to sustainability criteria were projected to reach $40 trillion by 2030. Chinese entities, meanwhile, already had 47.2 trillion yuan ($6.7 trillion) in green loans and bonds outstanding, far exceeding any other country’s green lending, but largely confined to its domestic renminbi system. In 2024, foreign institutions held only 3.2 billion yuan ($445 million) of China’s 2.2 trillion yuan ($306 billion) green bond market, a minuscule 0.15 percent.

That meager foreign participation is likely to increase. Chinese authorities are working to turn more of the country’s vast pool of green debt—a term for loans and bonds issued for projects with a positive environmental impact—developed primarily for a domestic investor base, into tradable securities that foreign investors can hold in compliance with international sustainability mandates. Their objective is to create a broad class of renminbi-denominated assets that are internationally investable, tied to green projects, and integrated into the broader renminbi ecosystem for pricing, settlement, and other financial services.

About 17 percent of China’s green bond market has already been screened against technical criteria aligned with European green finance frameworks, making those bonds easier for foreign investors and index providers to recognize and include in their portfolios. The Ministry of Finance has begun issuing renminbi-denominated sovereign green bonds outside China, with its first bond issuance raising six billion yuan ($834 million) in London in April 2025, followed by a second six-billion-yuan issuance in Hong Kong this past May, where orders were ten times the amount on offer. These issues are tiny compared with China’s domestic market, but they establish pricing reference points that make it easier for other entities to issue renminbi-denominated green debt in the future. Pakistan’s issuance, in May, of a 1.75 billion yuan ($258 million) green Panda bond—the term for renminbi-denominated debt issued in China by foreign borrowers—offers a glimpse of a future in which foreign borrowers routinely raise renminbi in China to finance their green development.

This is how industrial dominance begins to grow into financial power. The Chinese government has no formal plans to create a green yuan, but the constituent pieces of such a system are nevertheless starting to come together. The anchor asset for a green yuan would not be green technology itself, but an expanding family of renminbi claims on the green economy. Green bonds would form this economy’s tradable core, connecting China’s industrial advantage to the growing global demand for sustainable assets.

Much of the world has set deadlines for replacing fossil fuels that cannot be met without China’s green economy. Even if the political will to combat climate change fades, global dependence on imported energy has created geopolitical vulnerabilities that will likely continue to buoy demand for renewables, which almost any country can deploy to produce more energy at home. For countries and firms seeking entry into the green economy, accepting renminbi financing and Chinese technical standards may eventually become part of the ordinary price of admission. The result would be a self-reinforcing circuit of green goods and green finance, much of it denominated in renminbi.

For Washington, the prospect of a green yuan should not set off alarms about an imminent renminbi takeover. It should instead prompt a harder question: whether the petrodollar is no longer fit for purpose and what asset class, technology, or industrial system might anchor the dollar’s currency power in the future. The dollar rests on far more than the United States’ ability to secure global energy flows and its ties with major oil-producing states, but policymakers would be mistaken to treat its supremacy as permanent.

Beijing is not plotting to dethrone the dollar, and the Communist Party almost certainly does not want the financial openness such a victory would require. Whether or not the green yuan becomes a reality someday, the more immediate value to the party of an internationalized renminbi is its potential to deter China hawks in Washington from weaponizing China’s current reliance on the dollar.

As China’s renminbi-based system becomes stronger, so will Beijing’s ability to withstand the shock of potential U.S. financial sanctions. Washington’s threat to impose those sanctions will, in turn, lose some of its potency. That shift in the economic power dynamic would likely make Beijing more willing to call Washington’s bluff—which it may already be doing. In May, China issued its first-ever blocking order, instructing firms in China not to comply with U.S. sanctions on five Chinese oil refiners alleged to be major purchasers of Iranian oil.

If the reign of King Dollar ever ends, it probably won’t be because China usurped the throne but rather because the United States surrendered it. Washington must take note that the strategic asset underpinning the next monetary order may not be a barrel of oil but an industrial ecosystem. The danger is that financial markets may provide little warning that such a transition is underway. Markets can go long stretches ignoring the mounting evidence of change before a catalyst—such as a political stalemate over raising the U.S. debt limit—finally causes models to adjust and prices to snap up or down. U.S. officials are reluctant to plan for the erosion of the dollar’s dominance for fear that doing so would signal to markets that such a decline is inevitable. Their eagerness to point to price charts as proof of the dollar’s resilience, however, suggests that the lessons of the last financial crisis may already be forgotten. The United States must make contingency plans before the dollar’s exorbitant privilege is visibly tattered and signs of hedging against it become clear. By that time, the damage may no longer be possible to contain.

Zongyuan Zoe Liu is Maurice R. Greenberg Senior Fellow for China Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations and Senior Research Scholar at the Institute for Global Politics at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs. She is the author of Sovereign Funds: How the Communist Party of China Finances Its Global Ambitions.

#6185. Skift Aviation Forum 2026: Five Decisions in the Room

Jet fuel prices are still rising, and just about every variable affecting air travel is in flux — aircraft supply, air traffic volume, global partnerships, input costs. Decisions made today will determine who succeeds in aviation.

Passenger demand and airline revenues seem to be holding at a macro level. For now. Jet fuel prices continue to rise, aircraft remain scarce, and labor and airport costs keep rising. Meanwhile, global air traffic has been unpredictable throughout 2026, with wide regional differences.

Airlines at all levels of the market are shifting toward premium offerings to offset these headwinds and keep their revenues afloat. They’re redesigning cabins, loyalty programs, networks, ancillaries, and customer experiences. Skift Research describes the premium push as a normalizing trend: it’s now a baseline offering underpinning revenue expectations, rather than a stopgap strategy. [1]

The decisions industry leaders have to make today center on how to yield a competitive advantage within this industry-wide shift. The decisions underpinning every conversation at the 2026 Skift Aviation Forum will provide foundational evidence for these answers.

Fuel has become the industry’s biggest near-term margin test. Airlines entered the year with strong passenger revenue and high load factors, but the economics changed quickly as jet fuel prices climbed.

The impact is not uniform. Some airlines have more pricing power, stronger premium demand, better hedging positions, or networks that can absorb a shock more easily. Others compete in markets where travelers are more price-sensitive or where adding a fuel surcharge risks pushing demand to a rival.

The decision is how much of the fuel increase airlines can absorb before fares have to rise.

IATA expected the airline industry’s net profit to halve in 2026, a forecast made months before jet fuel prices peaked above $200 a barrel in October. [2] [3]

Airlines have spent the past several years reallocating space toward travelers who generate more revenue per seat. It’s not just major international carriers, either. Low-cost airlines have nearly doubled premium capacity since 2019.

Demand has kept up so far. More than 70% of travelers surveyed by Skift Research said they would consider paying for a premium cabin. [1]

The decision is how much further to push. Premium now affects cabin configuration, route planning, revenue management, airport strategy, and loyalty. Airlines need to know where demand still supports expansion and where the market is beginning to crowd.

U.S. domestic premium-seat capacity has grown 33% since 2020, roughly twice the 16% growth in economy seats. Premium revenues are significantly outpacing overall revenue growth and driving disproportionate value within airline revenue streams. [1]

The global traffic story has fractured by region. Middle East passenger traffic is expected to contract by 11.4% in 2026 amid airspace closures and reduced transfer demand, while Africa and Asia-Pacific will benefit from the shift. [4] Global load factors are reaching record levels because capacity remains constrained even as demand slows.

The decision is how to create the strongest return if capacity becomes more scarce. Slower global growth raises the cost of getting that call wrong.

Global air traffic growth is expected to slow to 2.1% in 2026 from 5.3% in 2025, while capacity increase is expected to be even lower at 1.6%. [4]

For many travelers, the ease of knowing they’ll get some miles and a few perks outweighs the headache of price comparison. AI changes this calculation, even for those who consider themselves somewhat loyal. Shopping tools can compare fares and products across airlines immediately. A traveler carrying points or status can still be presented with a better-priced or better-matched option somewhere else.

The decision for airlines is what loyalty has to deliver beyond points. Service, recognition, card economics, access, flexibility, and personalization can all strengthen the relationship. To avoid commoditization, airlines need to prove to travelers at every level of their programs that they can offer differentiated value.

The shift to premium is buoying revenue numbers, but AI platforms may not-so-quietly siphon off loyalty value from otherwise brand-agnostic travelers.

The industry has to make long-term commitments while near-term conditions remain volatile. Those investments have to make some assumptions about how the industry will operate years from now.

The decision is which bets deserve capital allocation. Growth alone is no longer enough justification. Airlines, airports, and manufacturers need a clear view of what each investment changes — capacity, economics, reliability, service, or competitive position.

Global airline passenger revenue is expected to approach $883 billion in 2027, but annual growth is projected to slow to about 3%. [5]

The airline industry’s next set of decisions centers on where to commit.

Airlines need to decide how much further to push premium, where capacity belongs, which rising costs customers can absorb, what keeps loyalty valuable, and which long-term investments deserve capital now.

Each decision comes back to the same constraint: airlines cannot pursue every opportunity at once. Skift Aviation Forum is focused on helping industry leaders identify where the economics still justify the strategy.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.

#6184. American Airlines Passenger Stuck Overnight Couldn’t Get A Hotel Voucher—They Got A Credit Card Pitch Instead

An American Airlines passenger says they couldn’t get a hotel voucher during a flight delay. The chat agent did, however, have something else ready: a pitch to open a Citi credit card, spend $2,500, and earn 50,000 miles. That’s not even as good as the standard offer! American’s stated purpose is “To Care for People on Life’s Journey.” That journey includes a sales presentation while you’re trying to figure out where to sleep. The passenger shared a screenshot of the exchange. It begins with the agent asking, “Does any of that work for you?” Then comes a lengthy offer for the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select Mastercard: the initial bonus, free checked bags, double miles at restaurants and gas stations, and a request for permission to send a one-time email with more information. American Airlines offered me a credit card deal during a conversation about a delayed flight and their inability to provide a hotel voucher from mildlyinfuriating Always be selling! Always be closing! It’s Glengarry Glen Ross, and the passenger asking for help is the lead. American Pays Agents To Make These Pitches In May 2023, I reported that American’s reservations agents would switch from pitching Avis rental cars to Citi credit cards. At the time, I argued that agents should judge whether the conversation had gone well enough for a customer to be receptive. American’s AAdvantage Cash support materials explain why an agent might make the ask either way: Contact center and Premium Guest Services representatives earn at least $50 for each approved application carrying their referral code. That rises to $100 as they move through annual sales tiers. There are also $100, $300, and $500 bonuses for reaching Gold, Platinum, and Diamond. They earn elite status like we do. There’s also a separate guide to pitching cards during chats, complete with prescribed transitions from talking about travel benefits to offering the card. American Already Knows When To Stop Selling I’ve written for years about credit card announcements that interrupt sleep on early morning flights. As Kevin Williamson once put it, [T]here is the Clockwork Orange sensation of being literally strapped into a seat while someone screams corporate banalities at you on a loudspeaker fifteen inches from your head… It is a “limited-time” offer in the sense that the sun eventually will run out of gas and become a dying star, first engulfing the Earth in fire and then leaving the wreck of the solar system a sterile plane of interstellar cold and utter silence, which will be interrupted only by some addled flight attendant screeching about the limited-time Barclays card offer. The airline’s guidelines at least suggest: Use the approved script, which should take about a minute. Make the announcement only once per flight segment, at cruise before descent, between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. Skip late night and redeye flights. Refrain from offering the card or making announcements during delays, cancellations, diversions, and other events affecting the customer experience. Meanwhile, the pressure to sell keeps growing. On October 15, the flight attendants union objected to American inserting a 15-minute card-sales module into mandatory fourth quarter training. Selling remains voluntary, but management made the training required and offered a $25 qualification reward. They Have A Sales Script For Your Bag Fee, Too American’s airport agent talking points for “Real Time Benefits” identify two moments to pitch: when a customer is about to pay a checked bag fee, and when they’re worried there won’t be overhead bin space for their carry-on. For most instantly approved applicants, the card’s first checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding can apply to the trip a passenger is already taking. The airline says the boarding group can take roughly seven minutes to update on a digital boarding pass. If the customer has already prepaid for bags, agents are told to shift the pitch to the miles, boarding, and free bags on a future eligible trip. I’ve even proposed plastering aircraft lavatories with credit card ads if attaching revenue to that space would persuade American to give us larger bathrooms since the space becomes monetized rather than deadweight loss. The inflight sales operation has instructions for distributing the commissions fairly among participating flight attendants. Brochures are prefilled with employee numbers, then stacked in a 1–2–3–3–2–1 sequence when three crew members participate. They’ve worked out whose referral code the next passenger gets. A Few Applications Don’t Prove This Is A Good Idea Maybe the number of applications generated from unhappy customers isn’t zero. The agent already has their attention, the sales text is ready to paste, and a small number of approvals can produce real money. But a positive response rate doesn’t establish that the pitch was worth making. You have to count the customers you make angrier, the business they take elsewhere, and whether someone who applies will actually keep and use the card. As I covered in looking at American’s Citi economics, their ambitions depend on acquiring customers, retaining them, and getting their spending. American’s deal announcement projected annual payments approaching $10 billion. They’ve finally come to realize that it matters whether customers like the airline enough to carry it in their wallet. In August, I covered their push for friendlier inflight service to increase card applications. Taking care of passengers makes them more receptive to the pitch. A customer service chat that hasn’t resolved the passenger’s hotel problem starts with.. not that. World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and I've loved redeeming my World of Hyatt points over the years on everything from cheap and cheerful Category 1 airport hotels to luxurious bespoke properties on idyllic Greek islands.

I knew that the program had expanded the ways to redeem points beyond hotel stays to experiences via its Find experiences platform. But I've never given it much thought, assuming the value (or the experiences themselves) wouldn't be that great.

So, when Hyatt recently invited me to an event that it sponsors, the Laver Cup tournament at London's The O2 arena, I jumped at the chance to go as a tennis enthusiast. I'd been to The O2 countless times for concerts and thought I knew the venue pretty well. But Hyatt was auctioning off a luxury experience in the ultra-VIP Legends Club, a space I didn't even know existed that turned out to be on a completely different level of luxury, in part due to its courtside seats for watching the action.

Seeing how few Hyatt points the winning bids went for, especially given this impressive level of premium hospitality and access, I came to the realization that this might just be the most valuable way to redeem World of Hyatt points.

Related: This is how you do a luxury all-inclusive: Zoetry Mallorca, bookable with Hyatt points

Find is World of Hyatt's experiences platform, where members can book everything from fitness workshops and chef's table dinners to Broadway tickets, paying with either cash or World of Hyatt points. You don't need to stay at a Hyatt hotel to take part, though some experiences include accommodations.

Most Find experiences are advertised with a fixed price — and that's where you might struggle to get outsize value. When TPG travel writer Rachel Craft tested a fixed-price Find dining package in Denver, it delivered less value than TPG's valuation of World of Hyatt points at the time, and she concluded that members would probably get more value redeeming their points for hotel stays.

Auctions work differently. A small number of limited-time experiences, often tied to Hyatt's sports sponsorships, go to the highest bidder, with members bidding in points rather than paying a set price.

Before you bid, it's worth knowing the rules:

Auctions are usually only a small portion of the Find options available at any one time, so here's how you can find them:

The Laver Cup packages were a savvy example of just how much value a Find auction can deliver.

Each of the three packages Hyatt auctioned included:

Starting with priority, fast-track entry to the venue, the Legends Club was a significant step up in luxury from anything else I've seen at The O2. It even surpassed my impression of the Virgin Red Room, a corporate suite at The O2 that can be booked with Virgin Red points.

The two-level hospitality suite (usually hidden behind the stage at traditional concerts) was huge and opened onto the arena, with a perfect view down the baseline.

Before the play started, there was even a Q&A with tennis legend Andy Murray, which isn't something you get with a regular ticket.

Premium food and drinks were included from 90 minutes before the session until the final ball, and the Champagne kept flowing the entire time.

When it was time for the tennis, I headed down to my own courtside seat in the second row. I was so close to the current No. 3 player in the world, Carlos Alcaraz, that I could almost have reached out and touched him.

I didn't stay at the Park Hyatt this time, but having toured the hotel, I can see why it would make the package even more appealing, with spacious rooms, marble bathrooms, views over the Thames and a 65-foot indoor pool.

Published all-in prices for a single Legends Club ticket ranged from $1,329 to $2,652 for Friday night and from $1,461 to $2,916 for either Saturday session, depending on the seat.

Standard rooms started at $633 per night when TPG reviewed the Park Hyatt, and the hotel's 60-minute "Back to Brilliance" massage cost $279 per person. Add the two-night stay and hotel credit, and I estimate each package was worth between $5,000 and $8,000 before assigning any value to the transfers.

A search engine index of Hyatt’s official Find homepage shows Hyatt auctioned off three Laver Cup packages with Legends Club single-session tickets and Park Hyatt accommodations (plus the above-mentioned inclusions) with winning bids of 81,583, 120,560 and 160,000 points, although the closed listings are no longer visible on the live page.

TPG's October 2026 valuations assign a value of 1.65 cents to every World of Hyatt point. By that valuation, the winning bids were worth about $1,346, $1,989 and $2,640, respectively. Even using the low end of my estimated package value, those redemptions delivered about 6.1, 4.1 and 3.1 cents per point, respectively, or roughly 1.9 to 3.7 times TPG's valuation, a spectacular result.

Put another way, the Category 8 Park Hyatt London River Thames costs 35,000 to 75,000 World of Hyatt points per night for a standard room, so two nights can cost 70,000 to 150,000 points. The two lower bids were below the 150,000-point threshold required for two standard award nights on top-priced dates, while the highest bid was only 10,000 points higher.

Of course, not every auction will deliver this much value. Popular experiences, such as Formula One races, can attract plenty of competition, and you have no control over where the bidding ends. However, you can decide up front what an experience is worth to you and stop bidding if the price goes past that amount.

World of Hyatt members earn points on eligible Hyatt stays and Find bookings paid for with cash, but a credit card can be the quickest way to build your balance for an auction.

You can choose between two cobranded cards:

Or, you can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to World of Hyatt from the following cards:

Chase Ultimate Rewards points held in Chase Sapphire Reserve and Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business accounts transfer to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio.

Points held in Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred accounts transfer at a 4:3 ratio, meaning 1,000 Ultimate Rewards points become 750 World of Hyatt points.

Bilt Points currently transfer to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio through Dec. 31, 2026. The ratio will drop to 4:3 on Jan. 1, 2027.

Related: How many Hyatt points do you need to transfer before the Sapphire Reserve beats the Sapphire Preferred?

Fixed-price Find experiences still would not usually tempt me away from a hotel redemption, but auctions are a different story.

This was easily the most luxurious sporting experience I have ever attended, from the VIP entry to the spectacular views and the hospitality of the Legends Club, which offered everything I could imagine, including proximity to some of the world's best tennis players.

Factor in the accommodations, transfers, food-and-beverage credits and other perks, and it's clear this is an exceptional way to redeem World of Hyatt points. You'll potentially considerably exceed our valuation of these excellent hotel points by redeeming them this way.

The 2027 Laver Cup will be played at the Intuit Dome near Los Angeles from Sept. 24 to 26, 2027. As the official hotel partner, look out for Hyatt Find experiences and auctions for next year's tournament.

#6181. Gulf Hotels’ Peak Season Stalls as Travelers Wait Out the U.S. Midterms

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Dubai's Love Lake in Al Qudra. Dubai Media Office

Bookings for the Gulf’s peak quarter are on hold until after the U.S. vote. With airlines still staying away, some operators don’t expect a real recovery until late 2027.

Gulf hotels are entering their peak season well behind last year. Leisure travelers are holding off on bookings until after Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections, and some are canceling outright.

U.S. President Donald Trump has said he would not launch an attack on Iran before the November 3 vote. Iran has not attacked the UAE since May, but the country bore the brunt of Iranian missile and drone strikes in March. Operators say guests now fear a new round of attacks once the election passes.

“Is Q4 as good as what we thought in August? No, it’s not,” said Saurabh Tiwari, vice president for the Middle East, Maldives and Sri Lanka at hotel group IHCL, which operates the Taj brand. “Leisure travelers are waiting and watching until after the U.S. midterm elections. They are thinking twice before booking their tickets, also influenced by the high airfares.”

Ali Siddiqui, research manager at consultancy Cavendish Maxwell, expects Dubai visitor numbers

Gulf hotels are heading into their most important quarter well behind last year, with operators and analysts pointing to travelers delaying or canceling trips ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections and fears of renewed strikes on the region afterward. UAE hotel occupancy fell to 67.6% in September from 79.9% a year earlier, according to CoStar, and Dubai's international visitors dropped 44% to 6.97 million in the first eight months of the year, according to Dubai's Department of Economy and Tourism. Short-term rentals have deteriorated fastest: AirDNA data shows November forward bookings down 37.5% year over year as of October 30, with December and January roughly 26% behind, a sharp decline from late September when the gap was 6% to 8%. Airline capacity is a compounding problem, with KLM, Singapore Airlines, Wizz Air, Cathay Pacific, United, Air Canada, Finnair, Luxair, and Virgin Atlantic suspending Dubai flights into 2027. Business travel is also being pulled, with ExxonMobil and Chevron reversing executive travel plans to Adipec in the UAE over security concerns, Reuters reported. Staycations, long-stay guests, and visitors from India, Russia, the UK, and Eastern Europe are cushioning the quarter, but one analyst estimates international tourists generate 70% of Gulf hotel revenue. Dubai has responded with incentives including the new invitation-only Dubai Access Club, which offers a five-year multi-entry visa, a SIM card, and AED 2,000 ($545) in spending credit.

#6180. Delta CEO Ed Bastian Slams ‘Short-Sighted’ Heathrow Shake-Up

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Delta Air Lines CEO, Ed Bastian. Delta Air Lines

Virgin Atlantic's anger over Heathrow's terminal shake-up now has heavyweight backing from Atlanta. With Ed Bastian joining the fight, the airport faces mounting pressure to rethink its plans.

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian has sharply criticized plans to separate the carrier from its joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic at London Heathrow Airport. In a LinkedIn post, Bastian described the proposals as "short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers."

The intervention marks a major escalation in the dispute over Heathrow's future terminal arrangements. It follows a series of strongly worded statements from Virgin Atlantic executives and the airline's founder, Sir Richard Branson.

Under the proposals, Delta would relocate from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 in 2028. The move would end its arrangement alongside Virgin Atlantic, which is set to remain at Terminal 3.

"For more than a decade, our airlines have served millions of customers through our co-located operation in Terminal 3, offering travelers convenient connections, premium amenities and access to an expanded global network," Bastian wrote.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian has publicly attacked Heathrow's plan to move Delta from Terminal 3 to Terminal 4 in 2028, calling it "short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers" in a LinkedIn post and saying Delta will "pursue all available remedies to correct this decision." The move, part of Heathrow's once-in-a-decade Terminal Occupancy Review, would end Delta's co-located operation with joint venture partner Virgin Atlantic, which stays in Terminal 3. Four other carriers — Finnair, Japan Airlines, Latam, and China Southern — would also switch terminals, while British Airways keeps its existing arrangements at Terminal 5. Heathrow says the changes free up capacity, reduce congestion, and improve resilience, and airport insiders cited by Sky News said airlines representing around 81% of Heathrow passengers backed the final proposal — a figure weighted by British Airways, which carries roughly half of Heathrow's traffic. Virgin Atlantic CEO Corneel Koster told The Sunday Times minimum connecting times between the two airlines could rise from 60 to 90 minutes, and said there is still time to reverse the decision before 2028. North America is Heathrow's largest market after the EU, with 1.86 million passengers in September 2026, or 25.9% of traffic.
