#6093. The New Energy Stalemate in Ukraine

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

TATIANA MITROVA is a Global Fellow at the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University.

SERGEY VAKULENKO is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin.

Why Russia’s Escalating Attacks Are Unlikely to End the War

In the days since U.S. President Donald Trump’s highly public falling out with Ukraine and growing rapprochement with Russia, Kyiv’s prospects going into the fifth winter of war look grim. The Trump administration has demanded that Ukraine suspend its attacks on Russian refineries, which have been one of Ukraine’s most effective means of putting pressure on Moscow. Meanwhile, Kyiv faces dangerous gaps in its air defenses against Russia’s jet-powered drones and stepped-up use of ballistic missiles. And Trump has entered into a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that temporarily waives U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports, offering Moscow a diplomatic win. Trump’s envoys have also proposed that Europe increase purchases of Russian gas as part of an effort to gain the Kremlin’s support for peace—further complicating the efforts of Ukraine and its remaining allies to squeeze Russia.

Yet missing from this bleak picture are the ways that Ukraine has already adapted to escalating attacks. Kyiv has developed innovative strategies to mitigate the impact of Russian energy strikes and keep its grid running, even amid intense bombardment. And despite the new U.S. pressure, Ukraine has continued to launch powerful drone strikes against Russia’s energy infrastructure, including successful mid-October attacks on an oil terminal in St. Petersburg and industrial gas processing plants as far away as Surgut and the Novy Urengoy, 1,800 miles from the Ukrainian border. Overall, since mid-2025, Ukrainian drone strikes have reduced Russian refinery throughput by roughly 30 percent; they have also eroded a significant share of Moscow’s excess refining capacity, resulting in a gasoline shortfall of about ten percent.

Still, this is only one part of a rapidly evolving energy war. Moscow has developed its own ways to limit the effects of Ukrainian strikes. And it has intensified its assault on Ukrainian infrastructure, including an October 19 barrage that damaged more than ten energy facilities. DiXi Group, a Ukrainian think tank, has estimated that Russia launched 12,800 missiles and drones at Ukrainian energy facilities in 2025 and early 2026, compared with just 2,800 during the first three years of the war combined. Although these figures count launches rather than successful strikes, they show how massive and relentless the Russian campaign has become.

Moreover, both sides are now able to target the substitutes and reserves that in the past could be used to cushion losses. Following Russian strikes on local power plants in early October, Ukrainians experienced widespread blackouts, even though Ukraine’s national grid had electricity to spare, because Russia continued hitting the lines and substations carrying the reserve power. During the summer, Ukraine hit so many of the refineries and pipelines around Moscow that Russia was forced to bring fuel by rail from as far as Lake Baikal, thousands of miles away.

If U.S. pressure and negotiations cannot stop the energy war, the central question for Ukraine is whether its remarkable capacity to adapt can keep pace with Russian attacks. At the same time, its fortunes this winter will depend on whether it can continue to hit Russian infrastructure in ways that challenge Moscow’s ability to repair and rebuild. Both Russia and Ukraine must now protect and repair their entire national networks around the clock; attackers can concentrate on the most vulnerable sites and strike again as soon as repairs are done. In such a war, defensive ingenuity matters as much as offensive capability. In the end, energy attacks alone are unlikely to force either side to accept the other’s terms, neither side may be able to gain a decisive advantage, even as both incur mounting costs. Recognizing the limits, as well as the power, of these strikes may be crucial not only to ending the present conflict but also to understanding the role that energy infrastructure will likely play in future wars.

For Ukraine, international support has been especially crucial in containing Russia’s energy barrage. As of November 2025, before the worst of last winter’s attacks, Ukraine had suffered $17.1 billion in direct damage to its electricity infrastructure, according to a report by the UN, the World Bank, and the European Commission. Yet Kyiv was able to keep the electricity flowing by drawing on the country’s remaining nuclear plants; repairing thermal generation facilities; increasing electricity, gas, and diesel imports; and compensating for lost power plants with distributed generation—smaller units running on solar, wind, gas, and diesel energy that are connected to the main grid.

Europe has also provided crucial replacement technology. In 2025, the European Commission delivered equipment from a retired Lithuanian thermal power plant to Ukraine in 149 shipments, enabling Ukraine to provide power to one million people. Such transfers have turned foreign utilities and suppliers into part of Ukraine’s rapid repair system. In September, Ukraine and the UN Development Program launched a new coordination center to speed up the installation of donated energy equipment.

Expanded use of batteries and distributed power also play a growing role. In September 2025, the Ukrainian energy company DTEK and the U.S.-based battery maker Fluence installed battery storage at six sites around Kyiv and Dnipro, with enough capacity to supply 600,000 households, roughly half of Kyiv, for two hours. Meanwhile, Kyiv has put in place 150 megawatts of distributed power generation—not enough to cover winter peak demand, but sufficient to provide more than half of the city’s essential services, including water supplies, hospitals, and heating systems. Nonetheless, Ukrainian reports suggest that 2,500 to 3,000 of Kyiv’s 12,000 apartment buildings could enter winter without an alternative heat supply.

That vulnerability is especially dangerous because restoring electricity does not automatically restore heat. Replacement boilers can help, but they must be installed locally, supplied with fuel, and connected to functioning heat networks, often while the same city remains under repeated attack. Last winter, UN monitors recorded at least 74 Russian attacks on heating infrastructure across Ukraine—attacks that left hundreds of thousands of people without heat or hot water for weeks on end in frigid temperatures. Keeping the national electric grid running did not make those homes habitable in freezing weather. Residents can try to solve the problem with electric space heaters, but their widespread use could overload the already fragile grid.

To prepare for even worse conditions this winter, Kyiv has been building up gas reserves. As of August, Ukraine’s gas stocks stood at 13.1 billion cubic meters, compared with 9.6 billion a year earlier. Still, stored gas must reach functioning heat and power plants, and electricity must pass through functioning transmission networks, both of which Russia has been continually attacking. Regardless of how resilient the national system is, Russia’s incessant targeting of particular Ukrainian cities has left them exposed, because local sources of substitute supply are often attacked before damaged facilities can be restored.

Meanwhile, Ukrainians are paying for the survival of their energy system in ways that capacity measures miss. Across the country, businesses have to run expensive generators, cut shifts, or close. Households spend more for fewer hours of reliable service. Declining industrial demand can make the electricity balance sheet look healthier, when the reality is that the economy is deteriorating under the pressure of relentless attacks. Those losses weaken the tax base and increase the need for foreign support. Russia does not have to switch off Ukraine’s power to impose an extraordinary burden.

Russia has also felt the growing effects of the energy war. In theory, Moscow has a much larger cushion: when the war began, its refineries produced more fuel than its domestic market consumed, and many had excess capacity to distill crude than to convert the resulting streams into finished motor fuel. Losing one distillation unit did not necessarily mean losing an equivalent share of gasoline or diesel supply. But Ukraine’s attacks this year have tested the limits of that flexibility.

In June, Ukrainian drones hit one of two processing units at Moscow’s Kapotnya refinery and hit the other six days later. The refinery was shut down after the June attacks and although it subsequently resumed operations, another strike again halted processing in September. Elsewhere, Ukrainian attacks have damaged complex units that are designed to raise fuel yields and improve quality; they can take six to eight months to fix, so they might remain unavailable through the coming winter heating season. Spare primary distillation capacity cannot replace damaged secondary equipment needed to turn intermediate products into finished gasoline and diesel.

To make up for these losses, the Russian government has loosened fuel standards, allowing naphtha blended with octane boosters to enter the gasoline supply, and extended state subsidies to imported gasoline. Russian companies can also send crude to its ally Belarus for processing or import finished products. These measures have helped fill consumers’ gas tanks without restoring the equipment that previously supplied them. But they come at a cost, which consumers, companies, and the state will all ultimately have to absorb.

Not all Ukrainian drone strikes have had such long-term impact. In March 2026, for example, Ukraine attacked the Ust-Luga oil terminal, which is on the Baltic Sea near St. Petersburg, continually for almost two weeks, halting oil shipments from that terminal. But shipments from Ust-Luga resumed a few weeks later, and by late April Russia’s total seaborne crude exports averaged 3.8 million barrels a day—up seven percent from March and 11 percent from a year earlier. This increase helped offset falling exports of refined products, as damage to refineries left more crude available for export.

For Moscow, the most pressing question is how to manage fuel shortages. Through higher prices and rationing, it can ensure that the military remains well supplied even if civilians have to cut back. It can also use subsidies and price controls to provide some relief to consumers. None of these options are costless, but as long as the government is willing to impose lower living standards and absorb the resulting political costs, it retains considerable room to maneuver. Ukrainian strikes can force Russia to spread its air defense thinner, absorb money and labor, and reduce its income from refining. They can somewhat reduce the oil and gas revenue that finances Russia’s war, but none of these costs are likely to make the war prohibitively expensive for the Kremlin.

Paradoxically, the growing success of Ukraine’s strikes against Russian refineries has brought new pressure on Kyiv itself. To buttress its increasingly constrained domestic market, Russia has reduced the amount of diesel it is selling abroad. Normally, higher prices should encourage refiners elsewhere to take up the slack, but the U.S. war against Iran has made that adjustment harder. Combined Russian and Middle Eastern net diesel and gasoil exports in September were 1.3 million barrels a day below their level a year earlier, according to the International Energy Agency. That global supply crunch has also affected the United States, which has now blamed Ukraine for stubbornly high U.S. diesel prices.

Ordinarily, the United States enjoys a substantial diesel surplus and is the world’s largest diesel exporter. Yet in the absence of export controls, quotas, or export tariffs, the U.S. market is exposed to galloping international prices, even when there is no U.S. fuel shortage. It is also far easier for the Trump administration to press Ukraine to stop its attacks on Russian refineries—and to enter a diesel agreement with Russia—than to restore lost Middle Eastern diesel exports.

In reality, Washington’s moves are unlikely to add much to global supply in the near term: redirecting existing exports does not create additional fuel. A larger, lasting increase would require Russian refineries to recover and stay in operation. This is where Washington has an incentive to restrain Ukraine’s attacks—even to the point of withholding, or threatening to withhold, Kyiv’s access to Starlink satellite service or U.S. intelligence, or to block European purchases of U.S. weapons for Ukraine. If Ukraine complies with U.S. demands, one risk is that Moscow could obtain protection for its refineries while continuing its assault on Ukrainian cities.

The United States is not the only external player in this widening energy war. For Europe, Ukraine’s collapse would create a security threat far greater than the cost of replacing transformers or financing fuel imports. Thus, in mid-October, the EU’s ambassador to Ukraine described a $1.1 billion energy support package Europe is preparing for the coming winter, which will enhance Ukraine’s ability to recover. But if some European countries, despite the European Commission’s opposition, accede to the Trump administration’s proposal to expand European purchases of Russian gas in the hope of lowering energy costs for households and industry—that could bolster Moscow’s earnings and its ability to finance the war. Europe’s energy choices matter on both sides of the contest.

China and India may also affect the future direction of the energy war. Thus far, both countries’ purchases of Russian crude have helped sustain Russia’s war machine. Moreover, by refining discounted barrels of Russian crude, both countries can benefit their own industries, and by exporting more refined fuel, they can ease the global crunch that is now driving U.S. pressure on Ukraine. But the ability of these countries to raise their exports depends on available crude and government approval—particularly in China. Over time, Russia’s leverage from the current diesel crunch will shrink as other suppliers recover, trade adjusts, and consumption falls. But that shift is unlikely to happen in time for this winter: the International Energy Agency expects diesel markets to remain tight well into 2027.

For both Russia and Ukraine, the aim of the energy war is clear: to disrupt or break the adversary’s economy to the point of undermining support for the war or making it unsustainable. But there are few indications that either side can achieve such an outcome. U.S. pressure could nevertheless produce a cease-fire or a broader settlement, even on terms deeply unfavorable to Ukraine. A mutual halt to energy strikes would give both sides relief and time to recover.

For now, however, an enormous gap remains between the conditions that Moscow and Kyiv deem minimally acceptable for even a temporary cease-fire. High levels of mutual distrust have increased that gap further. Moreover, a deal to protect only refineries, as the Trump administration has called for, would leave Ukraine’s cities and other infrastructure still exposed to Russian attacks. And Moscow has less incentive to accept any such deal if it can secure Ukrainian restraint through pressure by Washington, without making concessions of its own.

If diplomacy fails, the most likely scenario is another winter of sustained strikes on energy and other infrastructure by both sides. For Russia, the loss of refining capacity has been manageable thus far, but that does not preclude larger problems ahead. With each additional loss of capacity, Russia’s protection of its military energy supply becomes more expensive. Certain regions that have already been squeezed, such as occupied Crimea, could become especially vulnerable. If Moscow is unable to make repairs fast enough or otherwise compensate for further losses of refining capacity, regional fuel shortages could develop into wider disruptions to civilian transport and industry.

For Ukraine, the central risk is a cascading series of Russian attacks on the same city. During prolonged cold, repeated attacks—whether on Kyiv or Kharkiv or Odessa—could exhaust backup supplies faster than crews can restore service. Prolonged pump stoppages could lead to a disastrous local scenario of ruptured water supply, district heating, and sewage pipes, even if electricity remains available elsewhere in the country. A milder winter and timely equipment deliveries could keep Ukraine ahead of such a crisis, but delays in air defense deliveries or the loss of a critical heating facility could overwhelm a city whose electricity balance looked adequate. An indication of danger will be local power outages that continue to grow despite repairs, showing that recovery is unable to keep pace with attacks.

As it prepares for what will likely be its harshest winter yet, Kyiv faces a dilemma: if it reduces or suspends its attacks on Russian refineries to preserve U.S. military support, it will give Moscow a repair window while the Ukrainian grid remains exposed. If Kyiv refuses, it could continue its strikes but face intelligence or Starlink cutoffs that could make its infrastructure harder to defend. An additional influx of European funds and technology could soften the consequences—and perhaps provide some alternatives to U.S. communication networks—but will not fully replace U.S. intelligence and air-defense capabilities. That dilemma will not go away as long as Ukraine’s own infrastructure is exposed to attack.

As it approaches its fifth anniversary, the conflict in Ukraine has transformed energy warfare in ways that have few precedents. The advent of cheap long-range weapons has allowed each side almost unlimited access to the energy infrastructure on which the other depends. Yet at the same time, innovations in distributed power generation, batteries, and mobile equipment have given defenders novel ways to preserve essential services and continually recover, even in the face of large-scale attacks. Russia’s deep industrial reserves and Ukraine’s impressive adaptation have shown that complex energy systems can withstand enormous damage. That endurance has been far greater than a tally of destroyed assets on either side would suggest.

But this same resilience can make wars longer and more devastating. As Ukraine and Russia have shown, each side can gain confidence from its ability to sustain repeated attacks while also persuading itself that an even more intense campaign against its adversary might finally succeed. In this dynamic, each adjustment and workaround by one side invites a fresh attack by the other, and each new strike accelerates the search for new ways to endure. This adaptation spiral can continue even as economic and human losses mount. Only a true cease-fire can break the cycle. And that will depend on political choices that energy attacks alone cannot determine.

How a True “Energy Cease-Fire” Can Curb Putin

How the Shadow Fleet Enables Russia’s Hybrid Warfare in Europe

Why Ukraine’s Campaign Against Moscow’s Energy Sector Is Working

Congress Should Wield Oil Sanctions to Force Russia to Negotiate

Why the Country’s Food Insecurity Could Prevent a War Over Taiwan

Theodore Bunzel, Edward Fishman, and Addar Levi

#6090. Trump’s closing midterm argument, Reflecting Pool edition

President Donald Trump on Monday delivered an unconventional midterms closing argument after spending weeks dropping comments at rallies aimed at sowing doubts about the election — and what he might do to contest races Republicans lose.

After barnstorming states with competitive Senate races the last few weeks, Trump delivered his final message in Washington, D.C. He even chose the Reflecting Pool by the Lincoln Memorial — the site of a refurbishment he oversaw that was plagued by questionable work that continues to reverberate politically and legally.

There had been rumblings online last week that he would be in Michigan to close out his rally blitz alongside former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, who is in a Toss-up race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. That race was rocked Sunday when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost a primary to El-Sayed, endorsed the Republican nominee. Alas, Trump chose the nation’s capital and mused about pool liner colors, an issue that has not overtaken voter concerns about the cost of living, corruption, the Iran war and other issues, according to public polling.

“We resurfaced the bottom in a beautiful dark blue, very dark blue. They call it ‘American flag blue,’ but it’s very dark,” he said, wearing a suit, tie and white baseball cap. “And if you had a regular blue, like I personally love the lighter color blue, but then you wouldn’t have any reflectors.”

He also plugged his proposed arch, made questionable statements about crime rates and boasted about his other Washington, D.C., fountain and park projects. He did not mention Tuesday’s election —which he deemed “the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime” — until after the 22-minute mark. Once he moved on from boasting about his D.C. projects, Trump touted his second administration’s policy record. And himself.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime. The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history,” he said. “These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

He noted he had held 29 rallies in recent weeks. He contended Iran’s military platforms and stockpiles were “way down.” He touted statistics about the economy.

“Personal incomes are the highest in history. The poverty rate is at an all-time record low,” he said, adding. “American exports are at an all-time high, and more people are working today than at any point in the history of our country. And the United States is now by far the largest supplier of oil and natural gas anywhere in the world.”

The Reflecting Pool event came after he spent weeks on the campaign trail making warnings about elections — specifically, ones Democrats have won and might win this week.

For instance, during an Oct. 20 campaign rally in North Carolina for former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, Trump returned to casting doubt on his 2020 loss.

“What a lot of people don’t know is that we got screwed in 2020,” Trump said that evening, referring to the presidential race he lost to Joe Biden. “We did great. But you know who … didn’t allow it to happen was Michael Whatley. We were winning everything. You went to bed [at] 10:00. The race was over.

“Then all of a sudden, Georgia happened and some other things happened. Pennsylvania happened,” he said, continuing to cast doubt on his losses that year in both states despite no evidence of fraud.

“But we can’t forget,” he told loyalists in eastern North Carolina. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales lists the race as leaning toward Cooper.

Trump also offered the same crowd a preview of what his administration and political organizations have signaled for Tuesday at strategically selected polling stations with competitive House and Senate races.

“You know what didn’t happen? North Carolina didn’t happen,” he said to cheers about the 2020 election. “Because he had 619 lawyers at every station watching, watching, watching.”

Democratic lawmakers and pro-voter groups have warned for months that they fear pro-Trump election monitors — or even federal agents — could try to intimidate anti-Trump voters from casting ballots. Some sources have even raised concerns the administration might try seizing ballots in places that could swing a close outcome toward Republican candidates.

Trump’s rally rhetoric also suggests he will raise doubts not just about the outcomes the votes produce, but how they were cast.

“The whole thing is corrupt,” he told rallygoers Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa. “Go to paper ballots, everybody. Nice, beautiful paper ballots. You know, the paper ballots cost 9 percent of what these crooked machines cost, so you’d save a lot,” he said, without offering evidence that electronically cast ballots are problematic.

He even set the stage for casting doubt over or challenging Democratic-won races in states with GOP chiefs executive.

“And even Republican governors, many of them, they, they just do it,” he said of using voting machines over watermarked paper ballots. “I don’t know, it’s hard to believe. But you go to paper and you have the ballot there, and it’s so simple, and they put it in stacks.”

Still, Trump and his team have questioned the counting of paper ballots before — in 2020 in places like Arizona, Georgia and Pennsylvania, but to no avail. That didn’t stop him on Sunday, like at previous campaign stops, from alleging Democrats would still try shenanigans.

“It’s, look, they’ll try figuring something [out], but it’s much harder, because they have to cheat,” he said without providing evidence. “Because without, look, their policies are so bad.”

One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, said it was “normal” for any party to contest “some” election results.

Former Pennsylvania GOP Rep. Charlie Dent on Friday said Trump’s rally rhetoric appears mostly aimed at influencing public opinion and could be lacking a legitimate legal strategy.

“I’m not sure how he would intend to make a challenge to the certification of some members who may win by comfortable margins,” Dent said. “There might be circumstances where you have some contested outcomes shortly after the election that are very close. But then you’ll have a legal process and a recount process to go through to ultimately determine who the winner is.

“But once those winners are determined and the states certify those elections, then everything that’s done or said in Washington is merely ministerial at that point,” he added. “If there are objections to a particular outcome, there are legal remedies candidates can seek out.”

Mark Zaid, an attorney who has sued the Trump administration multiple times, said Monday that “the danger with his rhetoric is that he expects people to react to what he says and implement his words into action.

“He did that on Jan. 6 and he continues to do it now,” Zaid added, referring to the January 2021 Capitol riot by a pro-Trump mob following his fiery Ellipse speech that morning raising doubts about his loss to Biden.

“My own view is that post-Nov. 3 he will act far more like a cornered animal, more dangerous than when an avenue of escape is available — and implement a scorched-earth response to anything that is thrown at him,” he added. “I find it amazing that his rhetoric seemingly goes unchallenged by his base.”

Trump appeared in a relaxed mood on Monday, joking that he intended to rename the Reflecting Pool to include his name.

“I’m only kidding,” he said, looking toward assembled media members. “Please, don’t report it.” Later, about the midterms, he said the party of sitting presidents typically loses, adding matter-of-factly: “We gave this a very strong shot.”

#6088. The economy is on the ballot. 3 charts reveal the reality voters face as they head to the polls

Trump’s escalating trade war with Canada could raise costs for businesses and consumers in key battleground states before voters head to the polls.

Voters who have already cast ballots and those heading to the polls on Tuesday are weighing an economy shaped by rising everyday costs, surging home prices and strong gains in the stock market.

President Donald Trump vowed a better economy and a brighter financial future in his 2024 bid for office. But nearly two years into his second term, fuel prices have surged, inflation has accelerated and buying a home remains expensive — all pressures that put Republicans' affordability promises to the test in this midterm election cycle.

Three charts help exhibit the economic forces shaping voters’ choices as control of Congress hangs in the balance and the future of Trump's agenda is put on the line.

HIGH PRICES PUT TRUMP’S ECONOMY IN THE SPOTLIGHT AS THE GOP FIGHTS TO HOLD CONGRESS

Customers shop for groceries at a Target store in Salt Lake City, Utah, on Friday, July 31, 2026. Target has been overhauling its grocery aisles since the spring, hoping the upscale Tarzhay success it once had with stylish apparel and home goods in the early 2000s can be revived in food. (Kim Raff/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The latest inflation report showed consumer prices rose 3.7% over the year through September and 0.6% from August. The Consumer Price Index tracks prices across a broad range of household expenses, including food, housing, medical care and transportation.

Trade policy has added to some of those costs.

A New York Federal Reserve study found that Trump's tariffs added about 2.9 percentage points to prices across the consumer goods researchers examined.

Roughly one-third of the increase came from U.S.-made products, as domestic manufacturers faced higher costs for imported materials and components under Trump's agenda.

The impact varies by household, but these figures offer a snapshot of the price pressures voters may weigh ahead of the midterms. They show how costs have changed, though not how voters will assign responsibility.

A semi-truck driver replaces a diesel fuel pump at a Love's gas station in Eloy, Arizona, on Wednesday, March 18, 2026. U.S. diesel rose above $5 a gallon for the first time since December 2022, the latest sign of surging fuel price pressures menacing the global economy as the war in Iran continues to disrupt energy supplies. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Higher energy costs are putting pressure on households and businesses, as the wars in Iran and Ukraine disrupt global fuel supplies.

Diesel prices have climbed sharply, rising from about $3.45 per gallon in early 2025 to a peak of $6.53 in October 2026, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

The increase matters beyond the pump because trucks, freight trains and farm equipment rely on diesel.

AMERICAN-MADE GOODS ALSO GOT MORE EXPENSIVE UNDER TRUMP TARIFFS, NEW RESEARCH FINDS

Higher fuel costs can raise expenses for businesses moving groceries, packages and building materials, which may absorb some of the increase or pass it along to customers.

Gasoline prices are also adding to household costs. They jumped 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of that month’s overall increase in the Consumer Price Index.

Housing remains a major affordability challenge, particularly for prospective buyers.

Housing industry leaders say states that have prioritized homebuilding have been better positioned to accommodate population growth and economic expansion. (Joshua Lott/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.24% as of Oct. 29, while the latest median price for an existing home was $417,500 in September, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Mortgage rates shape buyers’ monthly payments, and home prices determine how much they need to borrow, making it harder for many households to enter the market.

TRUMP’S HOUSING CHIEF PAINTS A GRIM PICTURE FOR HOMEOWNERSHIP IN ONE MAJOR AMERICAN CITY

Rising home values can benefit people who already own property, but that wealth is difficult to access without selling or borrowing against a home. For renters and first-time buyers, the costs are more immediate.

The data offer a snapshot of the costs voters have faced, but the charts alone cannot show how they will weigh the economy — or which party they will hold responsible — as results come in.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

#6087. 15 moments that shaped the 2026 midterm campaign

Republicans began the 2026 election cycle on a high, with a governing trifecta in Washington and heavy optimism that the coalition that swept Donald Trump back into the White House represented a durable new voting bloc. They had a favorable Senate map and insisted there were opportunities to expand their narrow House majority.

But Trump’s policies, economic anxieties, historical trends and an unpopular war have upended  the calculus for the midterm elections. At the close of the campaign, the fight for Congress is taking place mostly on Republican turf, a striking shift in less than two years.

Here are 15 moments that shaped the 2026 midterm campaign:

Less than three months after taking office, Trump made good on a campaign promise: a 10 percent minimum tariff on all imports and higher duties on nations that run trade surpluses with the U.S. Since proclaiming “Liberation Day,” the on-and-off tariffs have injected uncertainty into the economy and hurt key sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing and consumer goods by driving up costs. Polls show the tariffs, which economists estimate have cost the average American household about $1,100, are viewed unfavorably by most voters, likely hurting Republican candidates in several states.

Republicans celebrated a key legislative achievement last summer, with the enactment of the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which they later sought to rebrand as the “Working Families Tax Cut.” The law’s tax provisions became a focal point for the GOP during the campaign, while Democrats slammed the included health care cuts. Before passage, North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis drew scorn from Trump for opposing the measure and soon announced his retirement, opening up a pivotal Senate seat that Democrat Roy Cooper is favored to flip.

Trump kicked the mid-decade redistricting wars into high gear when he directed Texas to redraw its congressional lines, resulting in five seats getting revamped in Republicans’ favor. Other GOP-led states followed suit, though Democrats have remained competitive in several of these redrawn districts. Meanwhile, California voters approved a Democrat-drawn map aimed at helping the party flip five Republican seats, and a court-approved map in Utah gives the party a prime pickup opportunity.

Democrats had a big night in the off-year elections, with a pair of decisive gubernatorial victories: former Rep. Abigail Spanberger flipped the Virginia governor’s mansion and Rep. Mikie Sherrill won in New Jersey. The two moderates focused their campaigns on cost-of-living issues, as did progressive Zohran Mamdani in his winning race for New York mayor, giving Democrats a blueprint for 2026.

The Trump administration began sending federal immigration agents to Minnesota in late 2025, but Operation Metro Surge picked up in January and ultimately led to the fatal shootings of two people by federal agents. That in turn intensified Democratic calls to “abolish ICE” and made immigration enforcement a defining issue in Democratic primaries across the country.

Not long after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, Trump predicted that the conflict would last a few weeks. It didn’t play out that way, and the ongoing war has become a focal point of the campaign. Higher oil costs have led to higher prices, the blame for which Democrats have pinned on Trump and Republicans in Congress. While Trump’s job approval ratings had fallen before the start of the war, they’ve dropped further since then.

Facing serious sexual misconduct allegations, California Democrat Eric Swalwell, who was running for governor, and Texas Republican Tony Gonzales resigned from the House just as their colleagues were preparing to expel them from the chamber. Swalwell dropped his gubernatorial bid and Gonzales left behind an open seat that has grown increasingly competitive.

In invalidating Louisiana’s congressional map, the Supreme Court pared back the Voting Rights Act and set off a new phase in the redistricting wars, as GOP-led Southern states sought to redraw districts with substantial Black populations. Not all attempts were successful, but Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee ended up with new maps.

A week before the Republican Senate primary runoff in Texas, Trump publicly backed scandal-plagued state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s challenge to Sen. John Cornyn. Paxton went on to win that contest, but has had a tougher general election fight against Democrat James Talarico. Two other incumbents the president targeted for defeat — Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy and Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie — also lost their May primaries to Trump-backed challengers. But Trump’s endorsement power had its limits: Several of his picks, including Iowa gubernatorial hopeful Randy Feenstra, lost primaries this summer.

June 23 was a big night for Mamdani as three House candidates he endorsed, including two fellow democratic socialists, won their primaries. Two of them ousted incumbent Democrats, Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat, and a third defeated the hand-picked successor of retiring Rep. Nydia L. Velázquez.  The New York primaries kicked off a strong summer for progressive candidates in states such as Colorado, Michigan and Minnesota.

Maine Democrat Graham Platner appeared to have weathered an array of controversies when he easily won his June primary to take on Republican Sen. Susan Collins. But about a month later, he ended his campaign following a report that he had sexually assaulted a woman he once dated, which he denied. That set off a weekslong scramble for Democrats to replace him on the ballot, culminating with a party convention at which former state Senate President Troy Jackson became Democrats’ new nominee.

The sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham shocked Washington but also touched off a scramble for South Carolina Republicans to replace him on the November ballot. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed the late senator’s sister, Darline Graham, to fill his seat, and she then won Trump’s support to seek a full term. Boosted by the president, Darline Graham went on to secure the nomination via a primary runoff, but her general election against Democrat Annie Andrews has tightened significantly.

Republicans gathered in Dallas for a first-ever midterm convention.  The two-day event offered them a chance to hone their message, fire up voters and lavish praise upon Trump, the gathering’s brainchild. Speakers, including Trump, stoked fears about democratic socialism, but polls showed the event didn’t provide the GOP with the bounce the party was anticipating. The president followed the convention with a series of rallies in red states, where he implored Americans to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Alaska’s competitive Senate race features two candidates with the same name: Dan S. Sullivan, the GOP incumbent, and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., listed on the ballot with no party affiliation. Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, has said she was unaware of the effort to recruit the second Sullivan, but The New York Times reported that top aides to her campaign were closely involved in the ballot-stacking plan. The Trump administration is attempting to block certification of the results if the incumbent doesn’t win, but, on Sunday, a district judge dismissed the lawsuit.

Less than 48 hours before polls were set to open on Election Day, Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens served up a November surprise Sunday, endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for Senate over Abdul El-Sayed, who had narrowly bested her in an August Democratic primary. While it was unclear how much influence her late decision could have on the race, a high-profile intraparty fight was surely not how Democrats wanted to close out the campaign. Even so, the El-Sayed campaign said Sunday was its biggest fundraising day, bringing in $2.4 million.

With just days to go until the U.S. midterm elections, many Europeans and Canadians are watching closely to see if Democrats will retake Congress and perhaps begin to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump for his final two years in office.

Canadians, who have been on the receiving end of some of Trump’s harshest trade actions, are so hungry for news about the U.S. midterms that they are searching for information at a higher rate than even Americans, according to Google search trends.

With just days to go until the U.S. midterm elections, many Europeans and Canadians are watching closely to see if Democrats will retake Congress and perhaps begin to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump for his final two years in office.

Canadians, who have been on the receiving end of some of Trump’s harshest trade actions, are so hungry for news about the U.S. midterms that they are searching for information at a higher rate than even Americans, according to Google search trends.

“Normal, average Canadians know so much more about the United States and care so much more about the United States,” said retired Royal Canadian Air Force Maj. Gen. Scott Clancy, a former director of operations for the North American Aerospace Defense Command. “Whereas Canada doesn’t even come into the daily [consideration] for the vast, vast majority of Americans in any given day.”

Europeans are also gripped by midterm fever. After Canada and the United States, midterm election information searches were the highest in Denmark, Qatar, and Norway—three countries that have also been rocked by Trump’s foreign-policy actions, from his aggressive claims on Greenland to the war against Iran.

Damian Murphy, the senior vice president for national security and international policy at the liberal Center for American Progress think tank, said that European officials he’s met with lately are “laser-focused on the midterms.” Murphy said he has been struck by the granular level of knowledge his European interlocutors have shown for the state of play of individual House races.

“What I’ve been telling them is that you shouldn’t have super high expectations for what any Congress can affirmatively do,” Murphy said. “In our system, the executive has a lot of power when it comes to the conduct of foreign policy. But what is important is the political message that it will send to the rest of the world: that the American people repudiate all of this—ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement], the Iran war, the treatment of allies.”

Other foreign observers have cautioned against high expectations of a U.S. reversion to pre-Trump foreign policies even if Democrats win control of Congress.

“Let us not overestimate the consequences of a defeat for the Trump administration in the midterm elections,” said former French Ambassador to the United States Gérard Araud in a recent post on X. “An American president holds considerable powers, particularly in foreign policy, and Trump can rely on the Supreme Court to bypass Congress.”

The experiences of Trump’s surprise 2016 and 2024 presidential election wins also continue to act as ballast against runaway hopes of a blue tidal wave.

“My philosophy of life is to have low expectations, and I apply that to the midterms as well. My mission is to stamp out any glimmer of hope of a return to normalcy after the midterms,” said one European diplomat, who requested anonymity to give an unvarnished take on the U.S. political situation.

One outcome with a strong chance of occurring in November, though, is a vote on impeaching U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over allegations of violating war powers and war crimes laws. A vote on the defense chief’s impeachment is likely to happen the week after the midterms.

Even if Republicans find the votes to protect Hegseth in the impeachment vote, a new impeachment inquiry may be launched in January if Democrats win control of the House, as is predicted.

Like the midterms, Canadians are likely to closely follow any impeachment process against Hegseth.

The former Fox News host “deeply offended” many Canadians this fall, Clancy said, when he separately appeared to disparage Canadian troop cadets and denigrated the contributions of NATO allied troops who joined the U.S.-led mission in Afghanistan.

“Personal friends of mine perished during that conflict,” Clancy said.

#6085. The Gulf Isn’t Ready for a Renewed Iran War

Analysis: The Gulf Isn’t Ready for a Renewed Iran War

By the narrow measure of barrels shipped, the Persian Gulf has weathered eight months of war better than most energy analysts expected. Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending Oct. 18, above the prewar level of 23.3 million, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. JPMorgan analysts wrote last week that energy markets are “converging on a forever conflict” and that view has encouraged a belief in the Trump administration that the region can absorb another round of fighting.

That view confuses how much oil and gas are still flowing from the Gulf with the state of the plants and terminals that move it. Since the war began on Feb. 28, Iranian missiles and drones have damaged refineries, liquefied natural gas (LNG) trains, and export terminals across the Gulf, and the Houthis have opened a second front in the Red Sea. Much of what has been lost will take years to rebuild. The cost will fall mostly on importers in Asia, Europe, and the developing world that built their energy systems around reliable Gulf supply.

By the narrow measure of barrels shipped, the Persian Gulf has weathered eight months of war better than most energy analysts expected. Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week ending Oct. 18, above the prewar level of 23.3 million, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. JPMorgan analysts wrote last week that energy markets are “converging on a forever conflict” and that view has encouraged a belief in the Trump administration that the region can absorb another round of fighting.

That view confuses how much oil and gas are still flowing from the Gulf with the state of the plants and terminals that move it. Since the war began on Feb. 28, Iranian missiles and drones have damaged refineries, liquefied natural gas (LNG) trains, and export terminals across the Gulf, and the Houthis have opened a second front in the Red Sea. Much of what has been lost will take years to rebuild. The cost will fall mostly on importers in Asia, Europe, and the developing world that built their energy systems around reliable Gulf supply.

U.S. and Israeli planners have drawn up options for a short, intensive campaign against Iran’s nuclear facilities, missile and drone arsenals, and energy infrastructure after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, the New York Times reported last week. President Trump has not approved it. This week, the Wall Street Journal reported that Washington has told Gulf governments to prepare for such an offensive. Iranian officials have responded by naming Saudi oil facilities, Gulf data centers, and undersea cables as targets. The next round would likely concentrate on the assets and importers that Gulf states can least afford to lose.

The Gulf’s reputation as a dependable supplier rests on decades of investment as much as on geology. After the 1973 oil embargo, consumer nations created the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the 1980 Carter Doctrine committed the United States to keeping the Gulf open by force. After the 1991 Gulf War and the 2003 invasion of Iraq, Gulf states invested in redundancy. Saudi Arabia expanded the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, the United Arab Emirates built a pipeline to Fujairah to bypass Hormuz, and Riyadh kept spare production capacity in reserve. All of this assumed that U.S. power would protect the region’s infrastructure or at least deter attacks on it. This year’s fighting has overturned that assumption.

A recent Reuters investigation documented at least 135 Iranian drone and missile attacks on at least 84 infrastructure sites across seven Gulf states since the war’s start. Iranian-linked strikes damaged five of Saudi Arabia’s nine largest refineries and both export manifolds at Fujairah, the UAE’s main terminal outside Hormuz. At Qatar’s Ras Laffan, the world’s largest LNG complex, strikes on the cold boxes that house liquefaction equipment took out two LNG trains representing about 17 percent of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy expects repairs to take three to five years and to cost an estimated $20 billion in annual revenue. Since much of this equipment is custom-built, the losses will outlast any cease-fire or peace agreement with Iran.

Proponents of a renewed campaign point to U.S. and Gulf air defenses, which by most measures have performed well. The UAE reported intercepting 132 of the 137 ballistic missiles fired at it on the first day of the war. The Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) estimated in March that more than 90 percent of Iranian projectiles had been intercepted across the theater. Interception rates, however, are the wrong measure for energy infrastructure. A refinery or LNG complex does not need to be hit repeatedly to be taken offline; it needs to lose only one critical component. On March 18, Qatar’s Defense Ministry said its forces intercepted four of the five ballistic missiles Iran fired at Ras Laffan. That attack took out the two trains cited above. An 80 percent interception rate still produced a loss of LNG supply that will last for years. The Financial Times reported that the missiles were maneuverable enough to evade Patriot batteries.

A second round would also begin from a weaker defensive position. JINSA estimated that by late March, Bahrain had used up to 87 percent of its Patriot interceptors and the UAE and Kuwait roughly 75 percent. Even if defenses performed better next time, a handful of missiles reaching a gas train, a pumping station, or a terminal manifold could remove capacity the market cannot replace for years. For planners, the share of Iranian missiles stopped should matter less than what the few that get through will hit.

Neither appealing to Washington nor diversifying security partners nor back-channeling with Tehran is insulating the region from the consequences of war.

Meanwhile, since declaring a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on July 20, the Houthis have struck Saudi Aramco’s 400,000-barrel-a-day Jizan refinery three times, forcing it offline for repairs in August. Drone strikes on East-West pipeline infrastructure in September led Riyadh to shut the line for 11 days, halting loadings at Yanbu. The group claimed new attacks on the pipeline’s pumping stations on Oct. 24 and Oct. 26, which Saudi Arabia has not confirmed. The pipeline built to cope with a Hormuz closure has become one of the most exposed parts of the Saudi export system.

Asia, which received nearly nine-tenths of the crude shipped through Hormuz before the war, has borne the brunt. In March, Bangladesh closed its universities early, rationed fuel at the pump, and diverted gas from four of its five state fertilizer plants to keep the grid running. Pakistan imposed a four-day workweek and closed schools. India limited households to one subsidized cooking-gas cylinder every 25 days as crowds besieged dealers. The Philippines declared a national energy emergency, and in May rotating blackouts left nearly 2 million people on Luzon without power. By September, Bangladeshi garment exporters reported canceled orders and idled production lines, hospitals in Sylhet were losing power almost hourly, and some families in Dhaka waited until midnight for enough gas pressure to cook dinner. Europe’s exposure runs mainly through refined products; European diesel premiums hit records in September.

Iranian strikes on Saudi oil facilities, combined with the Houthi campaign, would place both Saudi export routes under simultaneous attack while the region’s other bypasses are already degraded. Recovery timelines would lengthen toward a decade, and the Saudi spare capacity that has absorbed supply shocks since the 1990s would erode. Buyers and sellers are already adjusting in ways a second round would make permanent. On Oct. 22, QatarEnergy signed a deal to buy up to 4 million metric tons a year of U.S. LNG from Cheniere through 2054, supply that does not pass through Hormuz. If fighting resumes, Gulf producers may find that the market share they cede to the United States, to coal, and to other suppliers does not return.

The alternative to another round is a negotiated settlement in which both sides give ground, and the outlines of one are already visible. Qatari mediators delivered a draft agreement to Tehran on Oct. 25 that reportedly sets out a seven-day sequence of reciprocal confidence-building steps, backed by several guarantor states. A senior Iranian official dismissed it as “not an offer,” but Tehran is expected to respond this week. Washington has moved from demanding an end to Iranian enrichment to seeking a “meaningful” reduction, while Tehran’s priorities are relief from the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions. A deal that trades verifiable limits on enrichment and an unconditional reopening of Hormuz for phased relief on the blockade and sanctions would require each side to accept terms it has so far resisted.

Those concessions carry political costs, but they are cheaper than the alternative. The U.S. military’s costs had reached $47.1 billion by mid-October, according to U.S. Central Command, $29 billion of it for replacing expended munitions. A short campaign would not repair Ras Laffan or restore Saudi spare capacity, and it would invite exactly the retaliation that air defenses cannot fully stop.

Gulf producers spent five decades persuading the world that their supply could withstand regional wars. Eight months of fighting on two fronts have badly weakened that case. A negotiated end to the war would give the region time to rebuild it. Another round, on top of the Saudi-Houthi war, would leave damage to infrastructure and to importers’ confidence that markets are likely to carry for a generation.

Analysis: The Security Challenges Facing the Next Israeli Leader

Israel’s election results remain unclear, but whether current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu again emerges triumphant or a new government, perhaps led by Gadi Eisenkot, takes power, the country is at a crossroads. Although Israel has demonstrated its military power throughout the Middle East, it is trapped in endless conflict on multiple fronts, overstretched at home, and damaging its long-term relationship with the United States.

In the three years since Oct. 7, 2023, when a Hamas terrorist attack killed almost 1,200 Israelis, Israel’s regional military power has reached new heights. Not only did Israel smash Hamas after the attack, but it also took on the far more formidable Hezbollah, severely weakening its leadership, arsenal, and fighting forces in a continuing campaign. In 2025 and then again in 2026, Israel (along with the United States) attacked Iran, killing much of its senior leadership and setting back its nuclear program and military. In addition to striking its enemies, Israel now occupies around 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, large parts of Lebanon, and several miles along its border with Syria, using these buffer zones to guard against another Oct. 7-like attack and make it more difficult for terrorist groups to use drones, rockets, and other short-distance systems to strike Israel.

Israel’s election results remain unclear, but whether current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu again emerges triumphant or a new government, perhaps led by Gadi Eisenkot, takes power, the country is at a crossroads. Although Israel has demonstrated its military power throughout the Middle East, it is trapped in endless conflict on multiple fronts, overstretched at home, and damaging its long-term relationship with the United States.

In the three years since Oct. 7, 2023, when a Hamas terrorist attack killed almost 1,200 Israelis, Israel’s regional military power has reached new heights. Not only did Israel smash Hamas after the attack, but it also took on the far more formidable Hezbollah, severely weakening its leadership, arsenal, and fighting forces in a continuing campaign. In 2025 and then again in 2026, Israel (along with the United States) attacked Iran, killing much of its senior leadership and setting back its nuclear program and military. In addition to striking its enemies, Israel now occupies around 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, large parts of Lebanon, and several miles along its border with Syria, using these buffer zones to guard against another Oct. 7-like attack and make it more difficult for terrorist groups to use drones, rockets, and other short-distance systems to strike Israel.

These conflicts, however, have brought with them additional problems for Israel that its new government must address. In particular, Israel has failed to translate military success into lasting strategic gains.

The Iran war is the most pressing security challenge. What was intended as a short war is now in its ninth month, with no end in sight—and indeed escalation seems possible. Although the United States is focused on the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz and the security of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and other Gulf allies, Israel is more concerned about Iran’s long-range missile arsenal and provision of drones and money to anti-Israel proxies, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, allowing the group to rearm.

More broadly, Israel must break the cycle of endless conflict. In the last three years, Israel has used military force in eight countries and territories: Gaza, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Qatar, Syria, the West Bank, and Yemen. Israel’s enemies, however, show no sign of folding, even as the populations they claim to represent suffer tremendously. Israel can degrade its enemies’ military capabilities, but it is far harder to stop them from rebuilding or get them to abandon their hostility. Iran may emerge from the war wounded but vengeful, and it may commit at least some of the resources it gains under any cease-fire agreement, such as the one the United States proposed in June, to countering Israel. Hamas and Hezbollah are far weaker, but Hamas is still the most important Palestinian actor in Gaza, and Hezbollah, too, remains formidable.

This lack of progress makes Israel’s wars unsustainable even as their human cost is staggering. In Lebanon, Iran, and the West Bank, Israeli operations have killed thousands of civilians as well as many enemy fighters, while the civilian figure for Gaza is in the tens of thousands. Israel has devastated infrastructure in Gaza and parts of Lebanon, with mass displacement in both areas. Even if the new Israeli government places little weight on this suffering, other countries do, and support for Israel is low in most of the world.

Israeli leaders may dismiss this general collapse in support as a necessary price to pay for its security, but it also shapes how key allies treat the country. Israel has long hoped to secure an alliance with Saudi Arabia, but this is politically impossible for Riyadh when the deaths of Palestinian children are a regular feature in the news.

Pollster Dahlia Scheindlin on whether Benjamin Netanyahu can stay in power.

Main opposition parties fail to muster majority.

Early results indicate deadlock in parliamentary elections.

Far more consequential are the effects on Israel’s relationship with the United States. Polling by the Pew Research Center indicates that only 16 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans have favorable views of the Israeli government. Among young adults, those figures are 12 percent for Democrats and only 28 percent for Republicans.

The United States supports Israel militarily, economically, and diplomatically, as well as being a partner in the Iran war. Even if most forms of support continue, the coming years could see increased congressional scrutiny of military assistance to Israel, less diplomatic support in the United Nations and elsewhere, and a possible decline in financial support.

Because the endless wars draw on Israeli reservists, they are also increasing strains in Israeli society. In addition to the risk of casualties, the reservists are away from their jobs and families for long stretches, with no end in sight. There is an Israeli joke that one-third of Israelis pay taxes, one-third work, and one-third serve in the military. The joke is that it is the same third, as Israel’s large Arab population and most of its ultra-Orthodox community do not serve. Reflecting this disproportionate burden, one contentious issue in the latest election was the question of whether Israel’s large and growing Haredi population should be forced to serve in the military.

Historically, Israel has excelled at operations and tactics while having a short-term, narrow mindset about how to achieve security in general. As one Israeli security official joked to me on a recent trip, “The Hebrew word for ‘strategy’ is ‘tactics.’” This mentality has helped Israel score impressive military victories over Hezbollah and Hamas, but it has also left Israel trapped in multiple endless wars with little hope of lasting security. The new Israeli government, whether led by Netanyahu, Eisenkot, or another figure, must translate military dominance into sustainable political arrangements. Otherwise, Israeli society risks exhaustion while the country loses vital international support.
