#6081. The Israel Netanyahu Made

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

DALIA DASSA KAYE is a Distinguished Visiting Fellow at Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania and a Senior Fellow at the UCLA Burkle Center for International Relations.

Why Bibi’s National Security Vision Will Endure

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dominated his country’s politics for the last four decades, and his influence will not end even if Israelis vote him out of office. Over the course of his tenure as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu has dramatically reset the terms of the country’s national security politics. His persistent rejection of Palestinian statehood has helped push the idea firmly out of mainstream debates, and his longtime agitation for war against Iran is now widely accepted policy across Israel’s political and security establishment.

Before his first term as prime minister, Netanyahu was already a divisive figure. In 1993, as the leader of the opposition, he likened Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s Oslo agreement with Palestine Liberation Organization leader Yasir Arafat to British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s appeasement of Hitler ahead of World War II. His inflammatory rhetoric emboldened Israelis who considered any territorial compromise with the Palestinians to be treasonous, including the assassin who killed Rabin in 1995. Today, extreme policies and positions have become normalized under Netanyahu’s watch. He has presided over a three-year campaign of mass destruction and displacement in Gaza and the killing of more than 70,000 Palestinians. His government includes one politician, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was barred from serving in the army in his youth because of his involvement in terrorist groups, and another, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who has said Israel needs “to wipe out Gaza” and that it should repeat what it “did in Gaza” in the West Bank. Defense Minister Israel Katz has made similar calls for applying the “Gaza model” to the West Bank and even southern Lebanon.

Netanyahu might soon lose power. His attacks on Israel’s judiciary, corruption trials, and refusal to take responsibility for security lapses ahead of Hamas’s terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, have generated significant opposition among Israelis. A change of leadership could have profound consequences for domestic policy. But whether Netanyahu leaves politics this week or years down the road, his national security vision will outlast him. He has had catastrophic success in crushing domestic support for Palestinian national aspirations and gaining mainstream backing for a permanent war footing to confront Iran. Netanyahu has changed the baseline of how Israelis think about their country’s security and turned his own uncompromising positions into an institutionalized reality. Future leaders may bring their own styles to Israeli security policy, but for the foreseeable future, at least, they will be coloring within lines that Netanyahu has drawn for them.

Netanyahu is not the first Israeli prime minister to reject Palestinian national aspirations. In a 1969 interview, Golda Meir famously asserted that there was “no such thing” as a distinct Palestinian nation. Menachem Begin embraced the 1978 Camp David accords with Egypt only because the agreement did not require him to come to terms with the Palestinians. Yitzhak Shamir refused to allow independent Palestinian representation at the 1991 Madrid Peace Conference.

The difference today is that the idea of Palestinian statehood is not even up for debate. This change did not happen overnight. Rabin’s assassination led to the dismantling of the Oslo model, which intended to produce a Palestinian state but in practice produced limited Palestinian self-government and continued Israeli control over much of the West Bank. Attacks by Palestinian terrorist groups throughout the 1990s deepened Israelis’ skepticism about the prospects of peace, which helped to bring Netanyahu to power in 1996.

Still, when Netanyahu’s first term ended in 1999, some politicians sought to keep the possibility of a political settlement alive. Israelis elected leaders such as Ehud Barak and Ehud Olmert who were open to territorial concessions to the Palestinians and who engaged in serious, albeit unsuccessful, U.S.-backed peace negotiations. Barak also spearheaded a unilateral Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon in May 2000. Even the hawkish Ariel Sharon, whose controversial visit to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem later that year helped spark the second Palestinian intifada, evacuated around 9,000 Israeli settlers and initiated the withdrawal of ground forces from Gaza in 2005.

But in the absence of a negotiated solution, the conflict worsened on all fronts. Hamas won the 2006 elections in Gaza and took full control of the territory by 2007. Military conflict between Israel and Hamas became routine, with major wars erupting in 2008, 2012, 2014, and 2021. Netanyahu became prime minister again after the first of those wars, in 2009. As Israel contended with frequent rocket fire from Gaza and missile attacks by the Lebanon-based Hezbollah in the north, Netanyahu linked the deteriorating security conditions to Israel’s earlier withdrawals from these areas, bolstering his case against territorial compromise.

Netanyahu’s policies also changed realities on the ground in the West Bank. Even before his return to power, after the second intifada broke out, Israel built a concrete wall to separate Israel from the West Bank that encroached substantially on internationally acknowledged Palestinian territory. Israeli checkpoints throughout the West Bank also severely limited Palestinians’ freedom of movement and access to East Jerusalem. In office, Netanyahu accelerated policies, including continued settlement expansion, that threatened the viability of a future Palestinian state. And he encouraged a growing divide between Hamas in Gaza and the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank by facilitating Qatari payments to Hamas-run Gaza for more than a decade, further undermining the Palestinian national project.

Even the coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid that briefly removed Netanyahu from power from 2021 to 2022, and which promised change, did not substantially depart from Netanyahu’s positions. It is telling that this coalition—the only one able to push Netanyahu aside in the last decade and a half—boasted strong right-wing security credentials; Bennett was a longtime opponent of Palestinian statehood. Rather than taking steps to advance peace with the Palestinians, Bennett and Lapid focused on the Abraham Accords, the agreements negotiated by the first Trump administration in which several Arab states committed to normalizing relations with Israel without requiring concrete progress toward Palestinian statehood in return.

Few vocal supporters of Palestinian statehood remained within the political establishment on the eve of October 7, 2023. The attacks that day all but ensured that opposition to a Palestinian state would become the norm. No Israeli political leader, even in the opposition, speaks anymore about ending Israeli occupation of Gaza and the West Bank. After destroying much of Gaza and killing tens of thousands of Palestinians, Israel has regained military control of nearly 70 percent of the strip. Israeli settlers in the West Bank, whose numbers have more than doubled since the Oslo accords were signed, have been attacking Palestinians with alarming frequency. The settlers have ravaged Palestinian villages as the Israeli government and military look the other way, if not outright condone the violence. Palestinians, as a result, are now more focused on survival than statehood. Whether Netanyahu wins or loses this election, there is no clear path to the two-state future he has been so determined to avoid.

Netanyahu’s hardline position on Iran has been just as consistent as his hardline attitude toward the Palestinians. As early as 1992, as a member of the Knesset, he warned that Iran was “racing to develop nuclear weapons” and that the “threat must be uprooted.” More than three decades later, Netanyahu finally found in Donald Trump a U.S. president willing to launch the military campaign against Iran he had long sought. The first attack went forward in June 2025, when the United States and Israel struck key nuclear sites in Iran. Then, on February 28, they began a larger war targeting the Iranian leadership itself. As Netanyahu announced in a video message at the start of hostilities, “Together with the U.S., we will strike the terror regime hard and create the conditions that will enable the brave Iranian people to cast off the yoke of this murderous regime.”

The Israeli public and Israeli politicians expressed near-uniform support for the war in its early months; Lapid, the leader of the opposition, declared it a “just war.” By June, polls showed more public criticism of Netanyahu’s handling of the war. But few Israeli politicians have questioned the need to maintain military pressure on Iran, and active planning for renewed attacks continues. When Yair Golan, the leader of the left-wing Democrats party, called Israel’s killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khameini a “mistake” that led to an even more extremist Iranian leadership, politicians across the political spectrum condemned him.

There used to be more debate among Israel’s military, intelligence, and political elite about how to deal with Iran. When Netanyahu’s government began seriously considering a conventional military strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities in 2012, for instance—a development that drew concern in Washington—Israeli leaders did not all immediately coalesce around the idea of attacking Iran. Notable voices such as Meir Dagan, the former head of Israel’s intelligence agency, the Mossad, were arguing against a military strike and questioning what such a move could accomplish. The debate over military options became moot, however, once the Obama administration announced an interim nuclear deal with Tehran, negotiated in 2013 via back-channel diplomacy through Oman. The deal surprised and infuriated Netanyahu, who tried without success to scuttle the final nuclear agreement, which was signed in 2015.

Netanyahu’s strident opposition to U.S. President Barack Obama’s diplomacy was not supported by all Israeli politicians, either. Many worried that campaigning against the nuclear deal would damage Israel’s relations with Washington and that Netanyahu’s growing alignment with the U.S. Republican Party threatened bipartisan support for Israel. Although the Israeli government officially opposed the agreement, several prominent political leaders and members of the security establishment argued that the deal could have upsides. Benny Gantz, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, called the deal an “achievement” that could postpone Iranian nuclear capabilities for ten to 15 years. Some Israeli officials even argued against a U.S. withdrawal from the deal when Trump, with Netanyahu’s enthusiastic support, threatened to do so without first establishing an alternative arrangement. Even Barak, who had supported military strikes on Iran in the past and criticized the nuclear deal when it was signed, questioned whether Trump’s pulling out of the agreement was the “optimal” way to deal with Iran.

But these debates largely dissipated after Trump withdrew from the deal in 2018. When Iran resumed its nuclear enrichment program and with diplomatic efforts at a dead end, Netanyahu seized the opportunity to renew Israel’s shadow war with Tehran. Explosions at Iran’s Natanz nuclear facility in July 2020 and April 2021 were widely attributed to Israeli intelligence, as was the killing of Iran’s top nuclear scientist in November 2020, after the election of U.S. President Joe Biden, who had promised to restore the nuclear deal during his campaign. Even when the Bennett-Lapid coalition took over, Israeli positions on Iran remained consistent. The new government was less confrontational than Netanyahu’s, but it opposed a U.S. return to the nuclear deal. Bennett argued, as Netanyahu had done before, that an agreement would channel funds into “the Iranian terror machine.”

After October 7, with Netanyahu back in power, Israel escalated its attacks on Iran and its proxies. These actions included strikes in Tehran and Beirut that killed the heads of Hamas and Hezbollah, as well as tit-for-tat missile exchanges with Iran in April and October 2024. Aside from criticism that Netanyahu was timing the attacks to serve his own political interests, opposition figures such as Lapid and Gantz supported Netanyahu’s actions and the public backed what had become open military confrontation between Israel and Iran.

Israeli leaders have rallied behind Netanyahu’s preference for military confrontation over diplomacy, and not only with Iran. The idea that preventive military action should be used to manage any potential threat has guided Israel’s campaigns not only in Palestinian territories but also in southern Lebanon and in Syria after the fall of the Assad regime. Israel has been crossing new lines: it launched its first military attack on a Gulf Arab state in September 2025 with an airstrike in Doha targeting Hamas leaders. War has become Israel’s normal state of affairs.

Even if Netanyahu loses power, Israel’s approach to national security is unlikely to change. The opposition has articulated clear differences from the current government on matters of domestic policy, but major fissures on the Palestinian conflict, Iran, and Israel’s wider regional military campaigns are less apparent. As many Israeli analysts have put it, the political spectrum of the opposition is in essence “50 shades of right.”

Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as Netanyahu’s main rival, might slow settlement expansion in the West Bank and crack down on settler violence if he becomes prime minister. But those steps would amount to tactical adjustments, not strategic shifts. Eisenkot is not suggesting that Israel end its occupation of the West Bank or make a serious effort to advance a two-state solution. He has called the idea of a Palestinian state “delusional” in the wake of October 7. Other leading opposition figures, such as Bennett, not only oppose a Palestinian state but also avidly support settlement expansion.

A new government would not overhaul Israel’s policy in Gaza, either. There is widespread resentment among opposition politicians and the Israeli public over how Netanyahu waged the war, especially his resistance to cease-fire agreements that could have saved the lives of more hostages. Many believe Netanyahu prolonged the war to stay in power. But there is far less concern about the war’s effect on Palestinians; only a small number of Israeli human rights groups say Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. An Eisenkot government might be more inclined to advance the stalled Trump peace plan for Gaza, which has yet to make meaningful progress on reconstruction, Palestinian governance, or other key objectives. But like Netanyahu, Eisenkot does not support giving up Israeli control of Gaza without the full disarmament of Hamas.

More fundamentally, Israeli leaders across the board now consider control of territory to be essential to national security—whether in Gaza, the West Bank, southern Lebanon, or Syria. As the Middle East scholar Nathan Brown has observed, to the extent that debate about Israel’s security doctrine remains, it “is increasingly about how Israeli predominance should be exercised, not whether it should be maintained.” A new government might be willing, with Washington’s backing, to strike a nonaggression agreement with Syria that would require the removal of Israeli forces from border areas. Many leading Israeli politicians oppose such a withdrawal, however, lowering the odds of a deal going through. And it is even less likely that Israel would cede ground anywhere else.

No major Israeli politician is arguing for a change of course on Iran. The only significant domestic criticism of Netanyahu’s Iran policy has been about his failure to prevent diplomatic agreements, such as the short-lived memorandum of understanding the Trump administration reached with Tehran in June, which most Israelis see as favoring Iran and as failing to remove Tehran’s nuclear and missile threat. Israeli military leaders are already planning for the next round of war, including for a possible scenario in which Israel has to fight Iran on its own. Maintaining this war footing seems to have broad political support, too. Lapid has argued that Israel should go even further in its attacks on Iran, including by bombing “all energy facilities” to make sure the “Iranian economy is demolished.”

Netanyahu would have found it far more difficult to bring his hardline vision into the mainstream had he faced a political opponent who could powerfully advocate for a fundamentally different vision for Israel’s place in the region and path to peace. There have been no Rabins in the Israeli opposition, no leaders willing to pivot from their own previous positions, tell the public the truth about what a real peace would require, and invest in the painstaking work of diplomacy. Instead, Netanyahu’s governing style has stifled robust debate on national security questions and lined up Israel’s defense leadership behind the prime minister’s own uncompromising worldview that favors continuous reliance on military force.

Neither did Netanyahu face serious pushback from Washington as he pursued policies that thwarted any hope for peace with the Palestinians, including the relentless destruction of Gaza. Even though U.S. public attitudes toward Israel have grown increasingly unfavorable, on both sides of the political divide, American presidents have become less willing to use diplomatic and economic leverage to cajole Israeli leaders to end dangerous activities such as settlement expansion. The lack of pressure from the United States—and some Arab states’ willingness to normalize relations with Israel without demanding serious progress toward reconciliation with the Palestinians—made it easier for Netanyahu to pursue hardline policies without making concessions. It weakened dissenting voices within Israel, too, who could not convincingly criticize those policies on the grounds that they would damage Israel’s security or relationships with its most important partners.

Of course, regional realities complicate Netanyahu’s worldview. The plight of the Palestinians continues to resonate with foreign publics, limiting how far pivotal countries such as Saudi Arabia will go in normalizing relations with Israel. Yet future Israeli leaders may not be overly concerned about that problem, convinced that Israel, with its military might and technological edge, has too much to offer potential partners to be ignored or isolated. Many Israeli politicians today are dismissive of the increasingly common view in the region that Israel is as great a security threat as Iran.

A serious reversal of Netanyahu’s security policies will not be possible until a new Israeli leader emerges with a bold alternative plan for how Israel achieves lasting peace—and with the ability to bring the Israeli public on board. And as long as the United States remains Israel’s closest political and security partner, helping this shift along will require U.S. policies that stop enabling and start pushing back on Israeli settlement expansion, territorial occupation, and reckless military escalation.

None of this is happening during the current Israeli election season. In fact, there is little chance of it happening any time soon. Netanyahu has triumphed in squashing Israeli support for Palestinian national aspirations and normalizing military confrontation with Iran. It’s a powerful legacy. But it is not one that will make Israel, the region, or the world better off.

Gains Against Iran Won’t Translate Into Regional Peace

The Constraints and Costs of the New Security Consensus

Why a New Majority—Even in Gaza—Supports Compromise With Israel

Michael Robbins, Amaney A. Jamal, and Mark Tessler

Why Iran and the Houthis Keep Winning the Waterways

A Failing Peace Process Leads to Only One Outcome

Why the Country’s Food Insecurity Could Prevent a War Over Taiwan

The Case for an Economic Security Alliance

Theodore Bunzel, Edward Fishman, and Addar Levi

How Long Will Elites Stay Loyal to Kim Jong Un?

The Arab Monarchies Must Help Washington and Tehran Save Face

#6079. Why Trump’s Hail Mary on Fuel Prices Fell Short

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: Why Trump’s Hail Mary on Fuel Prices Fell Short

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Understanding the conflict four years on.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s eleventh-hour pivot back toward Moscow in a desperate bid to lower fuel prices ahead of next week’s midterm elections is not going great. But neither is his war on Iran, with oil prices climbing toward $120 a barrel and one U.S. lawmaker describing the administration’s plans for a renewed war on Iran as “insane.”

Three weeks ago, in a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump made a deal to purchase Russian diesel, which is forbidden under U.S. law. While the measure would have involved risible amounts of additional barrels into a strained global market, it has descended into farce. The three Russian tankers loaded with fuel may not be allowed to dock in U.S. ports. U.S. energy traders are unwilling to chance running afoul of long-standing sanctions against buying Russian energy. And Democratic lawmakers have said that any buyers will face congressional and legal scrutiny.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s eleventh-hour pivot back toward Moscow in a desperate bid to lower fuel prices ahead of next week’s midterm elections is not going great. But neither is his war on Iran, with oil prices climbing toward $120 a barrel and one U.S. lawmaker describing the administration’s plans for a renewed war on Iran as “insane.”

Three weeks ago, in a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump made a deal to purchase Russian diesel, which is forbidden under U.S. law. While the measure would have involved risible amounts of additional barrels into a strained global market, it has descended into farce. The three Russian tankers loaded with fuel may not be allowed to dock in U.S. ports. U.S. energy traders are unwilling to chance running afoul of long-standing sanctions against buying Russian energy. And Democratic lawmakers have said that any buyers will face congressional and legal scrutiny.

The global benchmark price of oil, which was about $70 a barrel before Trump started the Iran war in February, rose to over $117 a barrel on Friday. U.S. nationwide average gasoline prices are $4.20 a gallon, more than a dollar higher than the year before; no president ever has kept gasoline above $4 more than Trump. Diesel, which powers the entire economy, is worse: At $6.32 a gallon, it is about 70 percent higher than one year ago.

Another of Trump’s pro-Russia moves to keep energy prices in check was a pressure campaign on Kyiv to refrain from targeting Russian oil refineries with drones and missiles. U.S. negotiators including Steve Witkoff said that Kyiv should show “gratitude” toward Washington by curtailing strikes.

Ukraine complied for a spell in October, before remembering that what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calls “long-range sanctions” are the country’s best way of severing the sinews of Russia’s war machine. Overnight Thursday, Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil targets, with a devastating attack on a large Rosneft refinery that makes jet fuel for the military.

U.S. leverage over Ukraine is less than it used to be, since the Trump administration has not delivered any new military or financial assistance since Trump took office for a second time, and on several occasions, including this past month, has suspended what assistance there is, including some access to Starlink’s military-grade satellite internet service and intelligence sharing about inbound missile strikes. (While Ukraine has pleaded in vain for additional missile interceptors, the United States has pleaded poverty. This week, the United States sent a Patriot air defense system from Texas to Israel ahead of an anticipated restart to the fighting in the region.)

The U.S. pivot to Russia isn’t limited to diesel deals and strong-arming Ukraine, though. In addition to stopping future aid, U.S. officials have reportedly been cautioning countries on the front line of Russia’s shadow war to tone down their warnings about Moscow’s hostile intentions. And on Friday, the U.S. welcomed Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov to the G-20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, to the irritation of European allies. The abandonment of Ukraine has lately raised bristles in the European Parliament, where some politicians are redoubling their support for Ukraine even as Trump retreats.

“This is not one of those instances of many different shades of gray. There’s clearly an aggressor who is in the wrong, and that’s Russia, and so I think, for me, that stands clearly,” said Reinier van Lanschot, a Dutch member of the European Parliament from the Volt Europa party and a vocal critic of Russia’s invasion.

Kyiv’s energy war on Russia may hurt on the margins, but the real culprit is Trump’s war on Iran.

It won’t help consumers, won’t help Kyiv, and won’t mean riches for Moscow.

But Trump’s travails aren’t limited to his limited leverage over Ukraine. The war in Iran, which is now in its eighth month and likely to escalate in coming weeks, has kept oil prices high as shippers struggle to navigate a strait strewn with high costs, Iranian drones and missiles, and, for the first time, limpet mines.

It may get uglier after the midterms. The Trump administration is reportedly considering a sharp military attack to try to once and for all break the back of a regime that has withstood war and sanctions for nearly half a century. Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, who was briefed on defense planning, described the war plan as “insane.”

None of Trump’s moves to placate Putin will help him in the midterms, but they could haunt him in the two years remaining in his presidential term. Winter is coming for Ukrainians who endure daily and undefended assaults from Russian missiles, but it may be coming as well for an administration that has aided and abetted.

#6077. What in the World?

Quiz: What in the World?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts.

1. How did right-wing presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro react to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s runoff election victory on Sunday?

He called for his followers to protest his loss in Brasília.

He said he would request an annulment of the election.

Lula became the first Brazilian presidential candidate in history to come from behind to win the election’s second round, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports. Bolsonaro, the subject of several criminal probes, subsequently fled to Miami, where he called himself “the leader of Brazil.”

2. Student-led protests in Serbia that began in November 2024 culminated in the defeat of longtime right-wing leader Aleksandar Vucic in elections on Sunday. What incident sparked the original demonstrations?

Vucic’s decision to send military equipment to Russia

The collapse of a concrete railway station canopy

A factory spill that polluted the Danube through Belgrade

The revelation of a mass domestic surveillance network

The student protesters’ improbable victory against the Vucic regime could be instructive for their counterparts in the United States and European Union, Edward P. Joseph writes.

3. The Chinese Communist Party’s fifth plenum began on Monday. Traditionally focused on economic policy, what is the priority for this year’s gathering?

The shift in focus is a sign that Chinese President Xi Jinping is worried that his anti-corruption campaigns aren’t paying off, FP’s James Palmer writes in China Brief.

4. Early results show no clear winner from Israel’s parliamentary elections on Tuesday. But what is clear is that voter turnout was at its highest this century. About what percent of Israel’s registered voters turned out to cast a ballot on Tuesday?

Even if the opposition bloc succeeds in forming a governing coalition, there is little indication that Israel’s policies toward Palestinians will dramatically change, FP columnist Steven A. Cook writes.

5. At a Texas rally on Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump floated adding a 51st state. What territory or country did he suggest?

Trump’s “America First” foreign-policy agenda has been wildly unpopular with voters, as recent polling indicates, Jonathan Monten, Jordan Tama, and Josh Busby write.

6. The third Russia-Africa Summit began on Wednesday in Moscow. Russian President Vladimir Putin asserted that Moscow would champion greater African involvement where?

In the continent’s own critical minerals industry

At the World Bank and International Monetary Fund

African leaders’ attendance has dipped since its high point in 2019, partially driven by Moscow’s unfulfilled promises on the continent and the forced recruitment of Africans into Russia’s military ranks to fight in Ukraine, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.

7. Why were three French nationals sentenced to life in prison in Iraq on Thursday?

For spray-painting protest graffiti on Iraq’s parliament building

For smuggling weapons to the Popular Mobilization Forces

The arrests highlight how conflicts and divisions that may feel distant to Washington remain alive and pressing in the Middle East. Earlier this month, Hekmat Aboukhater wrote about how the Trump administration is inflaming sectarian divisions in Iraq.

8. Ireland said on Friday that it will set up a government body that, for the first time, would research and prepare for the possibility of what?

Sending troops to defend Palestinians in the West Bank

Unifying with the U.K.-run Northern Ireland

The announcement comes as Scotland and Wales also push for greater autonomy from London, which has reeled from years of dysfunction, Jamie Maxwell wrote in May.

9. Contestants gathered in Belgium on Monday to participate in a competition to see who could craft the most impressive sculpture made from what material?

Among the chocolate creations were birds, an elf, and a praying mantis, as photographed by The Associated Press.

10. An Australian court ruled on Monday against an inmate’s claim that his inability to have this product violated his right to “enjoy his culture as an Australian.” What product did the inmate sue to access?

The court found the ban on Vegemite, a yeast-based spread, was justified because of the product’s potential to impair drug-sniffing dogs’ ability to detect narcotics as well as its possible use in brewing alcohol, The Associated Press reports.

#6075. Talarico warms to Trump, says he wants to help fulfill some MAGA promises

James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, said he would work with President Donald Trump on a number of MAGA priorities if he is elected to the Senate. (Credit: The Diary Of A CEO Nov 2, 2026)

James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, appeared to extend an olive branch to President Donald Trump in a podcast released Monday, expressing a willingness to work with Trump on a wide range of issues.

"I would love, as the next U.S. senator from Texas, to work with Donald Trump to actually fulfill some of the promise of his political project," Talarico told Steve Bartlett, the host of "The Diary of a CEO" podcast.

"The promise of MAGA was that we were going to transform this government so that it delivered for the people who have been left behind, the people who have been forgotten in this country. And there's still time to do that," Talarico continued.

Talarico, who Trump has frequently mocked and criticized in the months leading up to the Texas state representative's crucial midterm contest against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, explained that he'd love to work with Trump on issues like healthcare and housing.

Texas state Rep. James Talarico, who is running for U.S. Senate, speaks during a town hall on Saturday, July 11, 2026, at the Plaza Theatre in El Paso, Texas. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"If the president wants to work with me or with any Democrat to expand healthcare access, I'm there. If he wants to make sure that every single kid in this country gets high-quality, accessible childcare, I'm there. If he wants to tackle the housing problem — Donald Trump is a builder — if he wants us to slash the red tape in this country so we could build millions of new homes and ensure everyone in this country has a place to call home, that I'm there. I'll work with him to do it. I would love to do that," Talarico said.

BATTLEGROUND DEM TOUTS BIPARTISAN RECORD, BUT CAN’T NAME SINGLE ISSUE SHE’D WORK WITH TRUMP ON

Talarico also indicated that a successful midterm election for Democrats could be a "rebirth" for Trump's presidency.

"If the people of Texas, if the people of this country elect leaders who are going to check the president, I think it could be a rebirth for his presidency," Talarico said.

State Representative James Talarico, a Democrat from Texas and U.S. Senate candidate, speaks during a campaign event at the University Of North Texas in Denton, Texas, on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY

Talarico added that he hoped a Democratic victory Tuesday could be a "wake-up call" for Trump and his administration, claiming that he felt the administration should "reverse course" if faced with a Democratic supermajority in Congress.

Talarico's willingness to reach across the aisle comes despite months of Trump badmouthing him on social media and the president campaigning in person for Paxton.

Trump has taken to frequently referring to Talarico as "TalaFREAKo" in posts on Truth Social, calling him "unelectable" in Texas and disparagingly referring to him as a vegan, a charge which Talarico denies.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, left, was mocked by President Donald Trump during his remarks at the Republican National Committee midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

He wants to abolish ICE. He wants to open our prisons. This is not somebody who is going to work with President Trump to secure our border and continue deporting illegal aliens," Leavitt added.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt speaks onstage during the second day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at American Airlines Center on Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"This is somebody who would join the ranks of the extremely liberal Democrat Party to engage in lawfare and obstructionism of all of the common sense policies that the Trump administration is continuing to pursue. #6074. 5 things to watch for in Tuesday’s midterm elections

Midterm elections are almost always referendums on the party in power. That’s especially true this year, when President Donald Trump has repeatedly directed Republican voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”

But Trump’s sagging poll numbers, driven by cost-of-living concerns and an unpopular war, have helped create a political environment that favors Democrats.

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales projects Democrats could net four to six seats in the Senate, a scenario considered highly unlikely at the start of the cycle. To succeed, Democrats need to flip seats in several red-leaning states, among them Alaska, Iowa and Kansas. The party would also need to hold its own vulnerable seats in New Hampshire, Minnesota and Georgia.

On the House side, the question seems to be not whether Democrats will take the majority, but rather how big their margin will be. The party needs a net gain of three seats; Inside Elections projects Democrats could wind up winning 20 to 30 seats, a significant number of them in districts that voted for Trump by double digits two years ago.

Here are five things we’ll be watching for as the votes are tallied:

Republicans appeared to win the redistricting wars that defined much of the 2026 election cycle, especially after the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act, which led to new maps in several Southern states. Democrats gained favorable lines in California and Utah, but Republicans redrew more seats in their favor. The overall GOP effort put new districts on the board in places such as Florida and Louisiana but also sought to boost Republicans’ chances of ousting longtime targets, including Reps. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio and Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez of Texas.

While some redrawn districts are clear pickups, many redrawn seats are considered Toss-ups, forcing the GOP to deploy significant resources. Still, if Republicans make the gains they hoped to make in places such as Florida and Texas, it could go a long way in helping them either somehow keep the majority or narrow a Democratic one.

Historic gains among Latino voters helped Trump win the White House in 2024 and boosted GOP candidates in swing districts across the nation. Those victories also influenced Texas Republicans’ redraw of the state’s congressional map, betting that Latino voters would stick with the party. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

Across the South, the Trump-led redistricting push that dismantled House districts with sizable Black populations has fired up Black voters in states such as North Carolina and Louisiana. Black voters could also be key to determining the winner of Michigan’s hard-fought Senate race.

Democrats’ initial midterm target list, released in April 2025, included a few Republican incumbents who represented seats that Trump had carried by double digits the previous year. The number of “reach” battleground races in traditionally red terrain that fit that description has only grown since then. One of the biggest questions heading into election night is how many of those districts Democrats will be competitive in. Wins in those districts would translate into a larger Democratic majority or, at the very least, could help offset losses by Democratic incumbents in redrawn seats.

But flipping these districts would put a bull’s-eye on the Democratic winners, since their seats would likely rank among Republicans’ best pickup opportunities in 2028.

At the start of the midterm cycle, few could have predicted that the Senate battlefield would run through states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. But concerns over rising prices driven by Trump’s tariff policy and the war in Iran have put several red-state seats in play. In the farm belt states of Iowa and Kansas, soaring diesel and fertilizer costs have GOP candidates on defense. In South Carolina, a divisive Republican primary and an untested first-time candidate have made the race unexpectedly competitive. And in Ohio, the return of a Democratic former senator, coupled with a national environment that is increasingly inhospitable to the GOP, suggests the state could shift from red to purple.

Recent surveys have shown Democrats with the advantage heading into Election Day and Trump’s job approval rating underwater, meaning more voters disapprove of the job he’s doing than approve. All signs point to Democrats retaking the House and potentially winning the Senate majority. That wouldn’t be unexpected — after all, the president’s party almost always loses seats in midterm elections. But polls have been wrong before. In August, some surveys predicted progressive Abdul El-Sayed would notch a double-digit win over Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, but El-Sayed wound up winning by less than a point. Throughout the campaign, Republicans have cautioned against reading too much into the polls, asserting that they typically undercount GOP voters.

#6072. ‘I Welcome Their Hatred’

Analysis: ‘I Welcome Their Hatred’

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

As Election Day approaches, the president of the United States is onstage, lambasting the powerful forces ranged against him—the judges, the media, the ultra-wealthy. Addressing 20,000 of the millions of regular Americans who love him, he defies his enemies, declaring, “They are unanimous in their hate for me—and I welcome their hatred!” The crowd roars.

Oct. 31 marks 90 years since President Franklin Delano Roosevelt delivered that speech at Madison Square Garden, as the 1936 presidential race neared its climax. In a world again beset by angry populists stoking economic distress, the rise of autocrats, and the floundering of moderate politicians, Roosevelt’s barnburner speech has come to seem relevant once more.

As Election Day approaches, the president of the United States is onstage, lambasting the powerful forces ranged against him—the judges, the media, the ultra-wealthy. Addressing 20,000 of the millions of regular Americans who love him, he defies his enemies, declaring, “They are unanimous in their hate for me—and I welcome their hatred!” The crowd roars.

Oct. 31 marks 90 years since President Franklin Delano Roosevelt delivered that speech at Madison Square Garden, as the 1936 presidential race neared its climax. In a world again beset by angry populists stoking economic distress, the rise of autocrats, and the floundering of moderate politicians, Roosevelt’s barnburner speech has come to seem relevant once more.

Roosevelt had entered office ready to work with established power as he launched his reflationary, state-expanding New Deal. Yet the president had grown increasingly frustrated by the obstructiveness of the Supreme Court—which had blocked programs such as the National Recovery Administration, designed to end “cut-throat” competition—and by the hostility of newspapers and tycoons. His enemies insinuated that he was a communist, and a would-be dictator. He also faced the rise of the radical right, which sought to exploit the public’s fear and frustration.

Roosevelt realized that by facing down the “economic royalists,” as he put it in his acceptance speech at the 1936 Democratic National Convention, he could cast himself as the people’s tribune, uniting the disparate groups supporting him. In that speech on Halloween, he warned that “powerful influences” were striving to bring back leaders who were “indifferent” to ordinary Americans’ economic plight. “Government by organized money,” he charged, was “just as dangerous as government by organized mob.” He hoped in his second term to become such forces’ “master.” Three days later, almost 61 percent of voters backed him, in one of the most decisive presidential election victories in U.S. history.

The speech resonates today even in that land of actual royalists, the United Kingdom. In the 2019 general election, the left-wing Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn quoted Roosevelt’s speech. But since then, political commentators, most of whom were never keen on Corbynism, have done the same. Their overarching goal is to ensure, as Roosevelt did, that power does not fall to the radical right.

In 2024, Corbyn’s successor, Keir Starmer, lead Labour to back into office, in an election marked by widespread public frustration with the long-dominant parties. From the left, the Greens and “Gaza independents” made gains, while support for the far-right party Reform UK hit 14 per cent—and has continued to rise. When it became clear that the new prime minister’s response was to remain stolidly managerial while at times adopting the language of Reform’s own arguments, liberal-left fears rose too.

In the two years that followed, a series of voices—in the Guardian, the London Times, and elsewhere—called for Starmer to learn from Roosevelt’s tub-thumping at Madison Square Garden. The prime minister, they argued, should pick battles with entrenched interests, carving out a clear narrative about how overcoming those interests would improve voters’ lives.

Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn speaks at Birmingham City University in Birmingham, England, on Nov. 21, 2019.Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

Writing in Prospect magazine, Ben Ansell, professor of comparative democratic institutions at Oxford, was one of those arguing that the speech offered the center-left a model for beating the radical right by using its own populist means against it. In January, as Starmer’s popular support plumbed terminal new depths, the veteran pollster Peter Kellner called on him to learn from Roosevelt’s speech by “declaring war” on the champions of Brexit. “Would he be taking a risk?” Kellner added. “Absolutely — and that’s the point.”

Starmer didn’t have it in him, but this was never just about his personal skillset. Across the democratic world, the center-left has been under pressure for a decade to find effective ways to respond to right-wing populism, as exacerbated by social media. Now that Starmer has been replaced by the former mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham (a politician much more ready to talk about power), those same voices reiterate their case. They point to the punchier approach taken by the prime ministers of Spain and Australia, and the success of Manuela Schwesig, the Social Democratic premier of the east German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, in holding back the advance of the extreme right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

Political scientist Robert Ford is the author of books on the radical right and Brexit. He plays his students at the University of Manchester footage of Roosevelt’s speech, he told me, because “it shows us how much bolder a center-left politician was 90 years ago.” As the center-right loses ground to its more populist rivals, he argued, the left and the radical right are “coalescing around in-group/out-group politics at a mass level, whatever politicians do.” This is forcing center-left politicians to ask themselves, “How can we best make use of this?” Roosevelt’s us-against-them speech offers a useful example, Ford suggested, because the genial president delivered “a polarizing message in a non-polarizing tone”—a trick he thinks Burnham is well-placed to copy.

Read More In this black-and-white photo, Teddy Roosevelt points to the middle of South America on a map as another man looks at the map from the other side of it. Both men wear suits, ties, and wire-frame glasses. In this black-and-white photo, Teddy Roosevelt points to the middle of South America on a map as another man looks at the map from the other side of it. Both men wear suits, ties, and wire-frame glasses. The ‘Donroe Doctrine’ Is a Roosevelt Redux Then as now, big stick diplomacy will lead to costly cycles of intervention and retrenchment. Argument | Tom Long, Carsten-Andreas Schulz

Then as now, big stick diplomacy will lead to costly cycles of intervention and retrenchment.

Within weeks of Starmer’s election, the Guardian columnist and historian Andy Beckett exhorted him to emulate Roosevelt’s speech. Now, nearly two and a half years later, Beckett told me that the more consensual tone struck so effectively by social democrats in the buoyant 1990s has been “tested to destruction.” In a period of widespread economic insecurity and visibly extreme inequality, “if social democracy has any chance now, as in the 1930s, it’s got to be much more aggressive rhetorically.” Roosevelt’s example, he said, offers a way for center-left leaders to unite with their more left-wing colleagues against a common enemy.

Each of those pointing back to the speech appears to have alighted on it independently, as they combed history for ways out of the British center-left’s constraints. This makes it all the more striking that they all homed in on the same oration, and a U.S. one at that. But then, Britain’s political pantheon lacks a figure like Roosevelt: at once centrist by instinct, radical by necessity, and charismatic by nature. Perhaps the nearest equivalent is Tony Blair, but he was never driven to declare war on entrenched power in the midst of economic crisis.

The question Roosevelt’s example raises for today’s Labour leaders is: which enemy? Ansell said that Burnham tried targeting the bond markets, which “didn’t work quite so brilliantly.” He might focus more fruitfully on exploitative gambling companies, Ansell suggested, or right-wing British tycoons who denounce their home country from tax exile. Or the heads of the United Kingdom’s notoriously inefficient privatized utility companies.

Ford, however, contends that Labour should concentrate its fire on perhaps the most aggressive expression of private power: big tech, and specifically Elon Musk. As populists have demonstrated, putting a face on the enemy can help dramatize political fights, and bolster public support. In the wake of a series of inflammatory interventions over such issues as immigration and free speech, Musk is very unpopular in the U.K. In 2025, he appeared by video link at an extreme right rally in London and told the crowd that “you either fight back or you die.” A few months later there came the scandal over Musk’s AI, Grok, producing images of child sexual abuse. Ford suggests Musk’s public stances make him “a golden opportunity for any center-left populist looking to do a bit of an FDR.”

Roosevelt signs the Glass-Steagall banking reform act at the White House in Washington on June 16, 1933.Universal Images Group/Getty Images

In the United States itself, where the radical right is already in power, Roosevelt’s speech has been pressed into service too—but not by the sort of moderates from whom critics long to hear it. In 2018, Maureen Dowd of the New York Times used it to criticize Barack Obama for failing to take an Roosevelt-style approach to the bankers who caused the 2008 crash. While this was historically unfair—Roosevelt, like Obama, initially bailed the banks out—it highlights the fact that Roosevelt’s controversial address remains the province of those to Obama’s left.

Elizabeth Warren has embraced the speech since at least 2015; Bernie Sanders has repeatedly conjured it too, as in a speech on June 13, 2019, where it triggered a raucous standing ovation. In 2025, Jamie Raskin clipped the speech in a tweet endorsing the “Rooseveltian” now-Mayor of New York City Zohran Mamdani.

In April, Democratic Rep. Greg Casar used it to help launch the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ 10-plank agenda for this year’s mid-term elections, which is focused on stopping “price gouging” by corporations and “[abolishing the unlimited spending power of Super PACs.” Much more contentiously, the far-left streamer Hasan Piker used the line on X to fend off accusations of antisemitism, after saying that “if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action.”

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders delivers a speech in Washington, D.C., on July 17, 2019. Cheriss May/Getty Images

Casar’s approach seems much more effective than Piker’s, explicitly aiming to bring left and moderate Democrats together around economic policies intended to re-channel populist anger away from the targets that President Donald Trump attacks, toward those the left blames for the cost-of-living crisis. For this to work, however, moderate Democrats might need to go beyond their attacks on “billionaires” and “the Epstein class,” and strive to match the bravura of their most successful ancestor.

The real lesson of the speech is not that welcoming the hatred of plutocrats is always effective, no matter who says it. Those lines landed precisely because they were not delivered by an angry leftist, but a cool-tempered centrist, driven finally to declare that the vested interests had gone too far.

In the United States, as in the U.K. and elsewhere, the potential impact of adopting Roosevelt’s strategy lies in that clarifying surprise.

Phil Tinline is a documentarian and journalist and the author of Ghosts of Iron Mountain: The Hoax of the Century, Its Enduring Impact, and What It Reveals About America.

#6069. Is Netflix’s ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ for Real?

Review: Is Netflix’s ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment’ for Real?

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

I had to chuckle when I got the email. A PR blast announced “Netflix presents The New Stanford Prison Experiment.” Was this an attempt to one-up the satirically dystopian phrases in David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest? A “yes, and” to Wallace’s “Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment”? Alas, no. And for the streaming service that only became more ubiquitous after the global success of the gleefully sadistic Squid Game, it seemed apt.

The phrase “Stanford prison experiment,” like Lord of the Flies, is pretty much synonymous with violence, anarchy, and the bleakest confirmation of man’s inhumanity to man. Do we really need a “new” one?

I had to chuckle when I got the email. A PR blast announced “Netflix presents The New Stanford Prison Experiment.” Was this an attempt to one-up the satirically dystopian phrases in David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest? A “yes, and” to Wallace’s “Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment”? Alas, no. And for the streaming service that only became more ubiquitous after the global success of the gleefully sadistic Squid Game, it seemed apt.

The phrase “Stanford prison experiment,” like Lord of the Flies, is pretty much synonymous with violence, anarchy, and the bleakest confirmation of man’s inhumanity to man. Do we really need a “new” one?

Chances are you know about the original Stanford prison experiment. In August 1971, with the campus on break, a psychology professor at Stanford University named Philip Zimbardo offered a paying gig to students willing to run through an unusual and morally questionable exercise. The basement of a university building was made up to resemble a prison. Twenty-four students (all male, all white except for one Asian-American; “good boys,” Zimbardo called them) were randomly split into groups of inmates or guards and given appropriate uniforms. For two weeks, the professor thought, he would take notes on how unchecked power in an enclosed system would reveal itself. The experiment, funded by the U.S. Office of Naval Research, ended after six days, and that’s only because Zimbardo’s girlfriend stopped by and said, “Holy crap, what the hell is happening here?!”

Stanford professor Philip Zimbardo discusses the Stanford prison experiment on Aug. 20, 1971.Duke Downey/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images

At least that’s the lore. Zimbardo—a wonderful self-promoter later taken to wearing t-shirts with the letter Z resembling Superman’s logo—seemed eager not just to lean into his experiment’s findings, but to allow that he, too, lost his ethical mooring, suggesting that all closed institutions are incubators of depersonalization and madness.

You can watch this all play out in a pretty good fictionalized version of the experiment produced in 2015 called The Stanford Prison Experiment, adapted from Zimbardo’s 2007 book The Lucifer Experiment. In it, Billy Crudup plays Zimbardo, Michael Angarano plays a guard nicknamed John Wayne, and Ezra Miller and Tye Sheridan play the inmates who suffered the most, eventually quitting.

Indeed, the fact that the experiment went haywire and needed to be canceled surely aided in spreading its premise—that merely donning the costume of guard or inmate in a sealed-off environment would radically alter someone’s personality, and rather quickly. These findings, plus the inherent “wait, they let students do this?” question, made Zimbardo a notable and sought-after voice on cable news during the Abu Ghraib scandal.

But recent research and a three-part 2024 documentary that aired on the National Geographic channel, The Stanford Prison Experiment: Unlocking the Truth, offers firsthand testimony from the participants that they were coaxed to behave in ways that would conform to the experiment’s thesis. John Wayne, for example, wasn’t really a skull-cracking bully as the film clips suggest, but a pot-smoking theater kid who wanted to please his director. One of the kids who quit wasn’t on the verge of psychological collapse; he just thought the experiment was annoying and was told the only way to get out of it was to pretend he was losing it.

All these decades later, it’s hard to know which version is accurate. (As with so much in life, it is likely somewhere in between.) But the suspicion surrounding Zimbardo’s data is, I suppose, reason enough to call for a redo.

The punchline, of course, is that however bogus the original may actually be, this new iteration is a hundred times more manufactured.

Trymaine Lee and host Alison Wood Brooks in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

Enter television producers Jane Lipsitz and Dan Cutforth, whose previous work includes competition shows like Project Runway, Top Chef, Nailed It!, and my personal favorite, the ongoing Is it Cake? franchise, which has somehow managed to stretch the act of wondering whether something is cake for three seasons plus five holiday-themed specials. With that eternal question still lingering, they decided it was time to turn their reality TV lens to issues of crime and punishment. (One wonders how Rodion Raskolnikov’s life would have been different had he had access to fondant.)

“Does power corrupt?” is the big question laid out in the first of six episodes in The New Stanford Prison Experiment. Our host—the Ryan Seacrest of this affair—is Alison Wood Brooks, an associate professor of business administration at Harvard University and a behavioral scientist, and she assures us this experiment will answer this question once and for all. Her two associates offering color commentary are Trymaine Lee, a Pulitzer-winning journalist and author, and Michael Cantrell, a retired federal corrections officer and podcaster.

In a decommissioned wing of an actual county correctional facility in Georgia, the trio sit before a bank of monitors from their panopticon’s perch, which naturally includes a whiteboard featuring circled names, flowchart markings, and vague phrases like “test ourselves.” They observe the activity of the show’s willing participants as though they were Harry Lime on a Ferris wheel, strikingly detached from humanity.

And who are the participants? Unlike Zimbardo’s crew—kids looking for a summer gig—these are adults with a full understanding of what they are doing. If there is a financial incentive, it is never mentioned. What is mentioned is that everyone involved considers this is a test of their character, and that the experiment may lead to an important conclusion. What’s more, the show has intentionally kept the pool of applicants diverse in age, race, and class—CEOs and bartenders walk side by side in their civilian clothes before the selection begins.

Contestants wait to join the experiment in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

The original experiment left who would be an inmate versus a guard completely up to chance. Not so here. The producers have predetermined this, but the audience isn’t privy to how they made their decisions. (The three women are guards because someone must have wisely realized that mixing genders in a locked-down 24-hour quasi-jail was something no insurance company would cover.)

But there’s an elephant in the room. Unpleasant though this may be, no one is actually incarcerated or in anything resembling danger. There are cameras everywhere, and all anyone needs to do is say the safe word (“pineapple”) and they are free to go.

Also, all of the inmates have clearly been encouraged to give periodic first-person addresses (cleverly shot through glass to resemble a visiting room)—a very common reality show trope to add narration and assist in the editing process. Annoyingly, while watching the finished product, we have no idea how scripted these moments are, or when during production they were recorded. Also, everyone, from all walks of life, uses Instagram-friendly therapy speak phrases. Great for marketing clips.

This is the perfect project for the creator of ‘Adolescence.’

Vince Gilligan’s “Pluribus” asks whether an AI-led society would really be that bad.

Over time, some personalities begin to shine. One of the younger inmates, Pete, who has a Jesse Eisenberg-like quality, is a fifth-grade social studies teacher who feels compelled to instigate and push back against authority. His reasoning is hazy, but he seems to be working toward some poorly defined, somewhat utopian ideal. (The show works mostly in soundbites, not thorough arguments.) He quickly finds some teammates in the art of pushing back, one specifically who seems even more eager to be a thorn in the guards’ side, even though Pete is quietly calling the shots.

The guards, meanwhile, are split into a night and day shift, and an alpha male soon finds himself the unelected leader of each. On night shift, there is Chris, an entrepreneur with a coaching business and an intense desire to be liked. He enforces rules but does it with a smile. On the day shift, there’s Chet, a supervisor on an oil rig, who seems more than eager to carry the metaphorical big stick.

The guards get printed memos (not unlike directives from the Gamemakers in The Hunger Games) with certain tasks and directives. They are to vote for a head guard among them on their shifts (in one case reversing what seemed like natural selection) then each shift must elect what is effectively a shop steward from among the inmates. As the choices are made, our three observers titter and murmur in fascination.

Things move along largely as expected. There is discord. Much of this is due, so the experts conclude, from too much individuality, which is anathema in a prison. Chris and Chet have different styles, and this imbalance causes a rupture. When penalties (such as removing a common clock) aren’t enforced, it creates a mess.

On the seventh day of the show, longer than the original experiment ever went, there comes a new twist. Some of the guards and inmates are directed to trade places. Wouldn’t you know it, the troublemakers are now wearing the badges. How will this change things?

Naturally, the show milks this reversal for as much drama as possible, but it is ultimately quite anticlimactic. This isn’t a real prison, it isn’t even a rogue college experiment from the early 1970s; it’s a Netflix reality show. It’s meaningless! You keep waiting for a hockey brawl to break out, but nothing like that ever happens.

Guard and inmate contestants in The New Stanford Prison Experiment.Netflix

At first, the new guards try to act like “good” guards but soon realize this makes them seem like hypocrites. Instead, they ease up on restrictions, leading to a bit of a party atmosphere. Meanwhile, many of the inmates realize this is all kind of dumb (as will a great number of home viewers, I’m sure!) and start saying “pineapple.” Others are determined to make it to the end, to fulfill some sort of promise they’ve made to themselves. (Does Netflix cut them a bonus check if they last 14 days? None of that is ever discussed.)

Finally (to risk spoiling things), a decision emerges from the ranks. If the inmates all decide to leave as one, as a collective instead of individuals who have had enough, then they will have “taken power” and used it in the name of righteousness. Beaming with pride, our three overseers are delighted to conclude that, wowee, power doesn’t always corrupt! What a relief! The world’s systems can stay in place now. Or something.

If all this sounds preposterous, just know I’m leaving tons of extra nonsense out. I watched this series in awe of its stupidity. I am not one who automatically dismisses all competition shows. The Great British Baking Show is charming and RuPaul’s Drag Race is chock full of puns and creativity. But The New Stanford Prison Experiment is a round peg in a square hole—a ludicrous scenario desperate to rationalize its own existence.

Zimbardo’s experiment may have been unethical, but this is just humiliating, both to the audience and to the people who had to spend nearly two weeks in uncomfortable conditions before landing on a milquetoast and meaningless conclusion. If I were forced to watch all six episodes again, it would feel like a jail sentence.

Jordan Hoffman is a film critic and entertainment journalist living in central New Jersey. He also publishes at Vanity Fair, Entertainment Weekly, and the Times of Israel. He is a member of the New York Film Critics Circle and co-author of The Star Trek Book of Friendship. X: @jhoffman

#6066. Fame, Fortune, and Murder in 1960s France

Review: Fame, Fortune, and Murder in 1960s France

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

It helps if you think of the so-called Markovic affair as an accordion. At the beginning, the story is at its thinnest—small and compact. The year is 1968, and a dead body is found, by accident, in a ditch. The corpse is assumed to be that of a vagabond. He receives a half-hearted autopsy—his skull was smashed in, an obvious cause of death—and gets put in the ground.

Still, the judge investigating the case studies the autopsy report and wonders if there is more to it than meets the eye. Would a random, lowly criminal really have perfectly manicured fingernails? A fingerprint match confirms his hunch: The body belonged to Stevan Markovic, an associate of Alain Delon. That’s where Murder in Paris ’68 really picks up.

It helps if you think of the so-called Markovic affair as an accordion. At the beginning, the story is at its thinnest—small and compact. The year is 1968, and a dead body is found, by accident, in a ditch. The corpse is assumed to be that of a vagabond. He receives a half-hearted autopsy—his skull was smashed in, an obvious cause of death—and gets put in the ground.

Murder in Paris ’68: A True Story of Death and Glamour, Edward Chisholm, Pegasus Crime, 416 pp., $32, November 2026

Still, the judge investigating the case studies the autopsy report and wonders if there is more to it than meets the eye. Would a random, lowly criminal really have perfectly manicured fingernails? A fingerprint match confirms his hunch: The body belonged to Stevan Markovic, an associate of Alain Delon. That’s where Murder in Paris ’68 really picks up.

“Associate” is a loose term, but, as author Edward Chisholm explains over the course of roughly 400 pages, it’s better to be vague than incorrect. It’s tough to describe what the two men meant to each other. Markovic was a young man from Yugoslavia who had come to France illegally in hope of a better life. Delon was a movie star, and one of the most beautiful men in the world. They liked and loathed each other, acting as close friends and betraying one another remorselessly. Before his death, Markovic wrote to his brother saying that, if anything were to happen to him, Delon would be “10,000% responsible.”

The scandal following both Markovic’s death centered on this murky and complex relationship. But, according to Chisholm, it had to do with much more than that. The affair was about the nature of fame and fortune in the 1960s, the influence World War II still had on French politics, and a country desperately trying to move toward the future yet weighed down by its heavy past. There was one man at the center of it, sure, but in Chisholm’s telling, you can easily grab the accordion and open it wide, showcasing its countless folds.

Delon with his wife, Nathalie, and their son in Monte Carlo in 1965.Archive Photos via Getty Images

Really, the story begins a decade earlier. In 1955, a 19-year-old Delon left the army after three years. His military record was far from spotless. He spent nearly a third of his time there in prison—for “[o]perating a vehicle without authorization and without a valid licence, resulting in a serious accident,” “[p]ossession of a prohibited weapon,” and “[c]ausing public scandal while ashore,” among other offences. His file concluded that he was “[a] bad element in every respect.”

Now a civilian again, his first port of call was Toulon, in the south of France. He was there to see an old acquaintance, François Marcantoni, a Corsican gangster and former French Resistance fighter who, like many others at the time, moved relentlessly between worlds.

France in the 1950s and 1960s was still fundamentally shaped by the war—by the Nazi occupation and its collaborators in the Vichy government, and by those who fought back. Marcantoni was “arrested in ’44 in a stolen car, running an op for the Resistance. The Gestapo had tortured him,” Chisholm writes. For someone like him, “the post-war years offered two paths: the police, or Pigalle [a neighborhood in Paris]. For François, the choice was obvious. The cops had collaborated, they were the enemy then—and they still were.”

Pigalle was where not-so-reformed Corsican gangsters set up their dodgy bars in the years following the liberation, and where Delon wound up in the late 1950s, when he landed his breakout role in Purple Noon, an adaptation of Patricia Highsmith’s The Talented Mr. Ripley.

A 21-year-old Markovic, meanwhile, made his escape from Josip Broz Tito’s Belgrade to Western Europe in 1958, the same year that Charles de Gaulle, once venerated then cast into the political wilderness, returned to the French presidency.

After a short prison stint in 1965, Markovic, who sustained himself through odd jobs and low-level crime, was in need of a place to stay. His best friend, Milos Milosevic, had managed to befriend Delon a few years earlier while the actor was filming in Belgrade. (Milosevic had staged a fake mugging, before “stepping in” to rescue Delon, and eventually became part of Delon’s entourage.) Milosevic soon convinced Delon to host his friend.

Protest and radicalization are the answer to an authoritarian, centralized state.

François Mitterrand’s U-turn decades ago holds lessons for today.

What happened afterward is complicated. Milosevic died in Hollywood in 1966, in what looked like a murky murder-suicide involving the estranged wife of actor Mickey Rooney. After that, Markovic became an integral part of Delon’s life. As Chisholm explains, Markovic was “[n]ot quite a secretary, not a bodyguard, not an employee. Delon doesn’t pay him—unless you count the occasional envelope. His job is more…ambient.”

“He’s become the man in the background. Pushing the pram through Parc Monceau, driving [Delon’s wife] Nathalie’s Alfa, standing behind the couple at film galas, cocktail in hand,” Chisholm adds. “He’s always there.”

The situation may seem idyllic from the outside; it wasn’t. The nature of the trio’s dynamic was not entirely clear, but the Delons’ marriage was unstable and violent. Sometimes, Markovic felt like he was part of the family; often, the couple put him firmly back in his place. The letters he sent to friends in those years indicate that he was frustrated by this state of affairs, and by Delon’s frequent refusal to sign his residency papers, keeping his legal status irregular.

In 1967, the couple separated. Nathalie moved out, Markovic followed her, and the pair watched as Delon unilaterally announced the divorce on television. What followed was a short-lived affair between the two, which may have sealed his fate.

Markovic’s body was found just over a year later. While much remains unknown, Chisholm makes it clear that the events surrounding the murder cannot be explained without one man: Marcantoni. He was a friend of Delon’s, still, and knew Markovic. He spent the 1960s arguing that he was no longer a gangster—retired long ago—and merely a “victim of [his] reputation,” which few people bought even then. He’s mentioned by name in the infamous letter Markovic sent to his brother. Was he a murderer?

The book alleges that he is (it can afford to—Marcantoni died in 2010), but the murder was never solved. There are, Chisholm explains, four prevailing theories. The first is that Delon had Markovic killed for sleeping with his wife, probably enlisting Marcantoni’s help. The second is that Markovic planned to sell stories and pictures of the Delons, but they found out and had him killed, likely with Marcantoni. The third is that Markovic’s personal dealings with the underworld got him killed, possibly by Marcantoni, possibly by someone else.

The fourth—watch as the accordion expands—is that, through his association with the Delons, Markovic had made his way into the upper echelons of French society, where politicians, singers, actors, and high-end criminals partied and slept together in secret. Could the young Yugoslav have gone to those events, taking covert pictures of the Parisian elite in compromising positions? We know now that no evidence exists (or remains) of this, but the theory tantalized France for months after his death.

Most shocking of all were snaps that emerged of a woman engaged in a tryst with another woman, which made their way to the Parisian police. The woman was believed to be Claude, the wife of Prime Minister Georges Pompidou. These were so obviously doctored that they did not even become a part of the police investigation, but the story was too salacious to die quietly. De Gaulle, aging, tired, did little to protect the man who had been faithfully at his side since his return to the Élysée Palace a decade earlier. Meanwhile, political opponents, hungry journalists, and at least one Czech spy conspired to ensure that the Pompidou name would keep being embroiled in the Markovic affair.

It helped Marcantoni, as the main suspect, that this merry band of interested parties was invested in turning the story into a political scandal. In 1969, he was arrested and held in custody after investigators had traced the plastic in which the body had been wrapped to packaging used by a mattress brand that Marcantoni had in his house. He spent just under a year behind bars, then left a free man. With no one talking, there just wasn’t enough there for a conviction.

Though the case rumbled on after that, the Markovic affair was essentially over. France had turned a new leaf too. The riots of May ’68, which had united students, workers, and millions of others in protesting for a brighter future, had initially failed to remove de Gaulle from his post. But a year later, despite the success of his party and the support of figures including Delon, de Gaulle resigned. Pompidou, a man who did not fight during the war and whose love of contemporary art and friendships in the entertainment world shocked his predecessors, took his place. Finally, the future of France was taking form. Everyone was moving on.

Marcantoni, now free for good, published multiple books concerning the affair, including the provocatively titled But Who Killed Markovic?. He became famous for claiming that “only three people know the truth. Delon, me and God. And God never snitches.” Delon died two years ago, and though his career continued for decades after the murder, it largely peaked in the 1960s. Maybe there was a reason he supported de Gaulle and not the idealist youths in 1968. On some level, he knew that, despite being in his early 30s, he could only ever be part of the old guard.

Delon (center) leaves court in Versailles in 1973.AFP via Getty Images

That is the book’s thesis anyway. Much of Murder in Paris ’68 tries to convince us that the affair was, in some way, about all of human life. “At first, I thought this was a story about a murder,” Chisholm writes. “Then it became a story about cinema. Then politics, espionage, a cover-up. But somewhere along the way, it became something else. A story about power. About what happens when someone tries to become more than they are allowed to be.”

This is one way to interpret it, but it is equally easy to read Chisholm’s yarn and come to another conclusion altogether. Delon was a cold, unpleasant man with a large ego who relished the company of outlaws. His wife was young, unreliable, and prone to follow her husband’s lead in toying with those she deemed beneath her. Many of the people they socialized with were either low-level swindlers or hardened criminals, always looking to make a quick buck.

Markovic was a man who got lucky and unlucky; who cheated and stole his way through life, then, for a short while, found himself attached to a man who happened to be a god. Always, he returned to what he knew: petty, lazy crime. It’s possible to squint and follow Chisholm in comparing him to Brutus or Iago—Shakespeare’s second men—but, really, he may have just been a minor crook who died in the way minor crooks sometimes did in those days.

By dragging Markovic’s lifeless body back in the spotlight today, Chisholm has merely become the latest in a long line of people, from Pompidou’s detractors to Marcantoni’s publishers, willing to use him for their own ends. It makes for a compelling read, though you should remember that, even as an accordion is at its widest, it’s only ever full of air.
